巴蒂·冈利夫下一趟下来时，走近马拉奇棚子的那段路，果然觉得寸步难行；可他还是闯下来了。可怜的玛莉眼见她辛辛苦苦垒起的石块被人一一推到一旁、滚出路外，那一股子存心欺她、不肯罢休的狠劲，几乎逼得她发狂。
「好啊，巴蒂，你真是个好孩子，」老格洛斯坐在棚门口望着闯入者说。
「我不害谁，谁也别害我，」巴蒂说。「海是大家的，马拉奇。」
「天也是大家的，可我不能爬上你家大谷仓的顶上去看天，」玛莉说；她正站在礁石中间，手里握着一柄长钩。那长钩就是她从浪里钩海草的家什。「可你是一点公道也没有，一点血性也没有，不然你不会上这儿来气这样一个老人家。」
「我不想气他，也不想气你，玛莉。你且容我些时日，往后咱们总能做朋友。」
「朋友！」玛莉嚷道。「谁要你这样的人做朋友？你挪那些石头干什么？那些石头是祖父的。」她怒极了，作势便要朝他扑过去。
「由他去，玛莉，」老人说；「由他去。自会有报应。哪天风向着岸他还下来，早晚要淹死在这儿。」
「那就叫他淹死好了！」玛莉怒道。「他若是掉进那边石头里那个大坑，海水半潮往里灌，我才不伸一根指头救他。」
「你会救的，玛莉；你会用你的钩子把我捞上来，像捞一根大海草。」
他说这话时，她轻蔑地扭过身去，进了棚子。她该收拾收拾干活了；而她受的欺凌里，顶重的一条便在这里——巴蒂·冈利夫这号人，竟要在她于激浪中劳作时跑来看她。
那是四月的一个下午，四点过一些。一早晨刮着猛烈的西北风，夹着阵雨；海鸥成天在湾里进进出出——玛莉认准，这是涨潮时海草要铺满礁石的兆头。

===Original===

The quick waves were now returning with wonderful celerity over the low reefs, and the time had come at which the treasure must be seized, if it was to be garnered on that day. By seven o’clock it would be growing dark, at nine it would be high water, and before daylight the crop would be carried out again if not collected. All this Mally understood very well, and some of this Barty was beginning to understand also.
As Mally came down with her bare feet, bearing her long hook in her hand, she saw Barty’s pony standing patiently on the sand, and in her heart she longed to attack the brute. Barty at this moment, with a common three-pronged fork in his hand, was standing down on a large rock, gazing forth towards the waters. He had declared that he would gather the weed only at places which were inaccessible to Mally, and he was looking out that he might settle where he would begin.
“Let un be, let un be,” shouted the old man to Mally, as he saw her take a step towards the beast, which she hated almost as much as she hated the man.
Hearing her grandfather’s voice through the wind, she desisted from her purpose, if any purpose she had had, and went forth to her work. As she passed down the cove, and scrambled in among the rocks, she saw Barty still standing on his perch; out beyond, the white-curling waves were cresting and breaking themselves with violence, and the wind was howling among the caverns and abutments of the cliff.
Every now and then there came a squall of rain, and though there was sufficient light, the heavens were black with clouds. A scene more beautiful might hardly be found by those who love the glories of the coast. The light for such objects was perfect. Nothing could exceed the grandeur of the colours﻿—the blue of the open sea, the white of the breaking waves, the yellow sands, or the streaks of red and brown which gave such richness to the cliff.
But neither Mally nor Barty were thinking of such things as these. Indeed they were hardly thinking of their trade after its ordinary forms. Barty was meditating how he could best accomplish his purpose of working beyond the reach of Mally’s feminine powers, and Mally was resolving that wherever Barty went she would go farther.
And, in many respects, Mally had the advantage. She knew every rock in the spot, and was sure of those which gave a good foothold, and sure also of those which did not.

===Chinese===

急浪此刻正以惊人的速度漫过低矮的礁群折返回来；要把这份财宝当天收进，时辰已经到了。到七点天就要黑，九点满潮；若不及早收拢，天亮之前这茬收成又要被带出海去。这些玛莉全明白，其中几分，巴蒂也开始明白了。
玛莉赤着一双脚、提着长钩下来时，望见巴蒂的矮种马正耐心地立在沙地上，她心里直想扑上去收拾那畜生。此刻巴蒂手里握着一柄寻常的三齿草叉，站在下方一块大礁石上，朝海面眺望。他说过只捡玛莉够不着的地方的海草，此刻正观望，想定下从哪里下手。
「由它去，由它去，」老人见她朝那畜生挪了一步——那畜生她恨得几乎同恨它的主人一样——便朝玛莉喊道。
风声里听得见祖父的话，她便打消了念头——倘若真有过这念头——自去干活。她顺着湾下去，攀进礁石丛中时，看见巴蒂还立在他的高台上；再往外，白浪翻卷着涌起，猛烈地自我破碎，风在悬崖的岩洞与凸壁之间嚎啕。
时时来一阵骤雨；天光虽还够亮，天上却乌云密布。爱海岸之壮丽的人，怕再难寻见比这更美的景致。照这样的景物，光线再好不过。色彩的富丽无可复加——外海的蓝，碎浪的白，黄沙，还有给崖壁平添这般丰采的一道道红与棕。
可玛莉和巴蒂谁也无心顾及这些。说真的，他们连营生的常轨也无心顾及。巴蒂心里盘算的，是如何把活计干到玛莉那女子之力所不及的地方；玛莉打定的主意，则是巴蒂到哪里，她到哪里还要更远。
而在许多方面，占便宜的是玛莉。这一带的礁石她块块认得，哪一块立得稳脚、哪一块立不稳，她都心中有数。

===Original===

And then her activity had been made perfect by practice for the purpose to which it was to be devoted. Barty, no doubt, was stronger than she, and quite as active. But Barty could not jump among the waves from one stone to another as she could do, nor was he as yet able to get aid in his work from the very force of the water as she could get it. She had been hunting seaweed in that cove since she had been an urchin of six years old, and she knew every hole and corner and every spot of vantage. The waves were her friends, and she could use them. She could measure their strength, and knew when and where it would cease.
Mally was great down in the salt pools of her own cove﻿—great, and very fearless. As she watched Barty make his way forward from rock to rock, she told herself, gleefully, that he was going astray. The curl of the wind as it blew into the cove would not carry the weed up to the northern buttresses of the cove; and then there was the great hole just there﻿—the great hole of which she had spoken when she wished him evil.
And now she went to work, hooking up the dishevelled hairs of the ocean, and landing many a cargo on the extreme margin of the sand, from whence she would be able in the evening to drag it back before the invading waters would return to reclaim the spoil.
And on his side also Barty made his heap up against the northern buttresses of which I have spoken. Barty’s heap became big and still bigger, so that he knew, let the pony work as he might, he could not take it all up that evening. But still it was not as large as Mally’s heap. Mally’s hook was better than his fork, and Mally’s skill was better than his strength. And when he failed in some haul Mally would jeer him with a wild, weird laughter, and shriek to him through the wind that he was not half a man. At first he answered her with laughing words, but before long, as she boasted of her success and pointed to his failure, he became angry, and then he answered her no more. He became angry with himself, in that he missed so much of the plunder before him.
The broken sea was full of the long straggling growth which the waves had torn up from the bottom of the ocean, but the masses were carried past him, away from him﻿—nay, once or twice over him; and then Mally’s weird voice would sound in his ear, jeering him.

===Chinese===

再说，她那身手的敏捷，又经年累月为着这份用途磨炼得炉火纯青。巴蒂无疑比她壮，也同她一样灵巧。可巴蒂不能像她那样在浪里从一块石头跳上另一块石头，也还不能像她那样借水势本身之力来助自己的活计。她从六岁顽童年纪起就在这湾里猎取海草，每一个洞窟、每一处角落、每一个有利的位置，她都了如指掌。海浪是她的朋友，她会驱使它们。她量得出它们的力气，也知道那力气何时何地便会衰竭。
在自家湾里的咸水潭间，玛莉是了不起的——了不起，而且毫无惧色。她望着巴蒂从一块石头挪向另一块石头，心里窃喜，知道他走岔了道。风灌进湾里的那个走向，不会把海草送上湾北的岩壁；更何况，就在那边，还有那个大坑——她咒他遭殃时提过的那个大坑。
于是她动手干起活来，把大洋披散的发丝一绺绺钩起，一趟趟卸在沙沿尽头；到晚间，趁着入侵的海水回来抢夺之前，她还要把这一堆堆拖上去。
巴蒂那边，也在我说过的湾北岩壁下堆起了他的草堆。巴蒂的草堆越堆越大，大到他心里明白，任凭矮种马怎么驮，今晚也驮不完。可到底还是不及玛莉的堆大。玛莉的钩强过他的叉，玛莉的巧强过他的力。他一叉失手，玛莉便用一种狂野古怪的笑声讥诮他，迎着风尖声喊他半个男人都算不上。起初他还用玩笑话回敬，可不多时，她夸耀自己的得手、指点他的失手，他动了怒，便再不答理她。他恼的是自己——眼见眼前的横财一次次错失。
碎浪的海水里尽是长长的蔓生海草，是浪从大洋底下撕卷上来的；可那一团团偏偏从他身旁漂过、离他而去——不，有一两回干脆从他头顶漫过去；这时玛莉那古怪的嗓音便在他耳边响起，讥诮他。

===Original===

The gloom among the rocks was now becoming thicker and thicker, the tide was beating in with increased strength, and the gusts of wind came with quicker and greater violence. But still he worked on. While Mally worked he would work, and he would work for some time after she was driven in. He would not be beaten by a girl.
The great hole was now full of water, but of water which seemed to be boiling as though in a pot. And the pot was full of floating masses﻿—large treasures of seaweed which were thrown to and fro upon its surface, but lying there so thick that one would seem almost able to rest upon it without sinking.
Mally knew well how useless it was to attempt to rescue aught from the fury of that boiling cauldron. The hole went in under the rocks, and the side of it towards the shore lay high, slippery, and steep. The hole, even at low water, was never empty; and Mally believed that there was no bottom to it. Fish thrown in there could escape out to the ocean, miles away﻿—so Mally in her softer moods would tell the visitors to the cove. She knew the hole well. Poulnadioul she was accustomed to call it; which was supposed, when translated, to mean that this was the hole of the Evil One. Never did Mally attempt to make her own of weed which had found its way into that pot.
But Barty Gunliffe knew no better, and she watched him as he endeavoured to steady himself on the treacherously slippery edge of the pool. He fixed himself there and made a haul, with some small success. How he managed it she hardly knew, but she stood still for a while watching him anxiously, and then she saw him slip. He slipped, and recovered himself;﻿—slipped again, and again recovered himself.
“Barty, you fool!” she screamed, “if you get yourself pitched in there, you’ll never come out no more.”
Whether she simply wished to frighten him, or whether her heart relented and she had thought of his danger with dismay, who shall say? She could not have told herself. She hated him as much as ever﻿—but she could hardly have wished to see him drowned before her eyes.
“You go on, and don’t mind me,” said he, speaking in a hoarse angry tone.
“Mind you!﻿—who minds you?” retorted the girl. And then she again prepared herself for her work.

===Chinese===

礁石间的昏暗这时越来越浓，潮水扑打得越来越猛，阵风来得一阵急似一阵、一阵猛似一阵。可他仍旧干下去。玛莉干多久他便干多久，她被逼进棚之后，他还要再干上一阵。他不能输给一个丫头。
那大坑如今已灌满了水——满坑的水仿佛在锅里沸腾。锅里浮着满满的团块——大片大片海草的财宝，在水面抛来掷去，堆得那样厚，人几乎可以躺在上面不沉。
要从那口沸滚的大锅里抢救出任何东西都是徒劳，这层玛莉知道得透亮。那坑往岩石底下凹陷进去，朝岸的这一边坡高、滑、陡。那坑即便退潮也从不干涸；玛莉相信它没有底。鱼扔进去还能逃出大海，远在几英里外——玛莉心气平和的时节，会这样告诉来湾里的游人。这坑她熟得很。她惯常管它叫普尔纳迪乌尔（Poulnadioul）；翻译出来，据说是「恶魔之坑」的意思。凡是落进那口锅里的海草，玛莉从不试图据为己有。
可巴蒂·冈利夫不知深浅；她望着他在水潭那奸滑的滑沿上稳住身子。他立定了，捞了一把，小有所获。他是怎么对付的，她几乎说不上来；她呆立了一会儿，提心吊胆地望着，随后就见他滑了一下。滑了一下，又稳住了；又滑了一下，又稳住了。
「巴蒂，你这傻子！」她尖叫道，「你要是栽进那儿去，就再也出不来了。」
她是只想吓唬他呢，还是软了心肠、想起他的危险惊慌了呢？谁说得清？她自己怕也说不上来。她还像先前一样恨他——可她总不至于愿意见他淹死在自己眼前吧。
「你干你的，别管我，」他说，嗓音沙哑而恼怒。
「管你！——谁管你？」姑娘顶了一句。随即她又自去张罗自己的活计。

===Original===

But as she went down over the rocks with her long hook balanced in her hands, she suddenly heard a splash, and, turning quickly round, saw the body of her enemy tumbling amidst the eddying waves in the pool. The tide had now come up so far that every succeeding wave washed into it and over it from the side nearest to the sea, and then ran down again back from the rocks, as the rolling wave receded, with a noise like the fall of a cataract. And then, when the surplus water had retreated for a moment, the surface of the pool would be partly calm, though the fretting bubbles would still boil up and down, and there was ever a simmer on the surface, as though, in truth, the cauldron were heated. But this time of comparative rest was but a moment, for the succeeding breaker would come up almost as soon as the foam of the preceding one had gone, and then again the waters would be dashed upon the rocks, and the sides would echo with the roar of the angry wave.
Instantly Mally hurried across to the edge of the pool, crouching down upon her hands and knees for security as she did so. As a wave receded, Barty’s head and face was carried round near to her, and she could see that his forehead was covered with blood. Whether he were alive or dead she did not know. She had seen nothing but his blood, and the light-coloured hair of his head lying amidst the foam. Then his body was drawn along by the suction of the retreating wave; but the mass of water that escaped was not on this occasion large enough to carry the man out with it.
Instantly Mally was at work with her hook, and getting it fixed into his coat, dragged him towards the spot on which she was kneeling. During the half minute of repose she got him so close that she could touch his shoulder. Straining herself down, laying herself over the long bending handle of the hook, she strove to grasp him with her right hand. But she could not do it; she could only touch him.
Then came the next breaker, forcing itself on with a roar, looking to Mally as though it must certainly knock her from her resting-place, and destroy them both. But she had nothing for it but to kneel, and hold by her hook.
What prayer passed through her mind at that moment for herself or for him, or for that old man who was sitting unconsciously up at the cabin, who can say?

===Chinese===

可她正双手端平长钩往礁石下走，忽听得扑通一声水响；急回头，只见她仇人的身子正在潭中打旋的浪涛里翻滚。这时潮已涨得极满，每一番后续的浪都从临海那一面涌进潭里、漫过潭沿，随后随着翻滚的浪退去，又从礁石上倒流回来，声如瀑布倾泻。待多余的水退净片刻，潭面会暂得几分平静，只是那恼人的水泡仍在上下翻沸，水面上始终有一层微滚，仿佛那口大锅当真烧着似的。可这点相对的安歇不过一瞬，因为前一番浪的泡沫刚退，后一番碎浪几乎立刻便到，于是海水再度猛砸在礁石上，四壁回响着怒浪的咆哮。
玛莉立即抢到潭边，为着稳当，手脚并用地伏下身去。趁一浪退去，巴蒂的头和脸被卷得转过来，挨近了她；她看见他额上满是血。他是死是活，她不知道。她只看见了他的血，看见他那头浅色的头发浮在泡沫中间。随后他的身子被退浪的吸力拖走；可这一回逃逸的水量不够大，带不走这个人。
玛莉立刻用钩子干起活来，钩尖咬住他的外衣，把他朝自己跪着的地方拖。趁着那半分钟的间歇，她把他拖得近了，近到能触到他的肩膀。她极力俯下身去，整个人伏在长钩那根弯弯的柄上，拼命用右手去抓他。可抓不着；她只碰得到他。
接着下一番碎浪吼着压上来，在玛莉看来，它势必要把她从立足之地砸下去，教两个同归于尽。可她毫无办法，只有跪住，握紧她的钩子。
那一刻她心里为自己、为他、还是为那个坐在上头棚里浑然不觉的老人，默祷了什么话，谁说得清呢？

===Original===

The great wave came and rushed over her as she lay almost prostrate, and when the water was gone from her eyes, and the tumult of the foam, and the violence of the roaring breaker had passed by her, she found herself at her length upon the rock, while his body had been lifted up, free from her hook, and was lying upon the slippery ledge, half in the water and half out of it. As she looked at him, in that instant, she could see that his eyes were open and that he was struggling with his hands.
“Hold by the hook, Barty,” she cried, pushing the stick of it before him, while she seized the collar of his coat in her hands.
Had he been her brother, her lover, her father, she could not have clung to him with more of the energy of despair. He did contrive to hold by the stick which she had given him, and when the succeeding wave had passed by, he was still on the ledge. In the next moment she was seated a yard or two above the hole, in comparative safety, while Barty lay upon the rocks with his still bleeding head resting upon her lap.
What could she do now? She could not carry him; and in fifteen minutes the sea would be up where she was sitting. He was quite insensible, and very pale, and the blood was coming slowly﻿—very slowly﻿—from the wound on his forehead. Ever so gently she put her hand upon his hair to move it back from his face; and then she bent over his mouth to see if he breathed, and as she looked at him she knew that he was beautiful.
What would she not give that he might live? Nothing now was so precious to her as his life﻿—as this life which she had so far rescued from the waters. But what could she do? Her grandfather could scarcely get himself down over the rocks, if indeed he could succeed in doing so much as that. Could she drag the wounded man backwards, if it were only a few feet, so that he might lie above the reach of the waves till further assistance could be procured?
She set herself to work and she moved him, almost lifting him. As she did so she wondered at her own strength, but she was very strong at that moment. Slowly, tenderly, falling on the rocks herself so that he might fall on her, she got him back to the margin of the sand, to a spot which the waters would not reach for the next two hours.
Here her grandfather met them, having seen at last what had happened from the door.

===Chinese===

大浪扑来，从她几乎伏倒的身上冲了过去；待水从她眼里退去，泡沫的喧嚣和怒吼的碎浪从她身旁滚过，她发觉自己直挺挺伏在礁石上，而他的身子已被托了起来，脱开了她的钩子，躺在那滑溜的石台上，半在水里，半在水外。她在那一瞬望着他，看见他眼睛睁开了，两只手正在挣扎。
「抓住钩子，巴蒂！」她喊道，一面把钩杆推到他面前，一面双手揪住他外衣的领子。
纵然他是她的兄弟、她的情人、她的父亲，她也不能怀着更大的、绝望一般的气力不放他。他果真设法抓住了她递给他的杆子；后一番浪滚过去后，他还在石台上。再一转眼，她已坐在离大坑一两码的高处，算是比较安全了；巴蒂躺在礁石上，那颗还在流血的头，枕在她的膝上。
此刻她能怎么办？她抱不动他；而十五分钟后，海水就要涨到她坐的地方。他全然不省人事，脸色惨白，血正慢慢地——极慢地——从他额上的伤口渗出来。她轻轻又轻轻，把手放到他的头发上，把发丝从他脸上拂开；随后她俯下身到他嘴边，看他还有没有气；她望着他，头一回知道他生得美。
但愿他能活，她什么不肯给？此刻再没有什么比他的性命更珍贵的了——这条她刚刚从水里救回来的性命。可她能怎么办？她祖父连自己下礁石都难，果真能挪得下来就算好的了。她能不能把伤者往后拖，哪怕只拖几英尺，好让他躺在浪头够不着的地方，等救援到来？
她打起精神动手，几乎是把他抱了起来，一寸寸挪动。她一面挪，一面惊异自己的力气；可那一刻她的确力气极大。慢慢地、柔柔地，她自己一次次跌倒在礁石上，好让他跌在自己身上，终于把他挪到了沙沿上——往后的两个钟头，海水都漫不到那里。
祖父在那里迎着他们；他到底从门口望见了出的事。

===Original===

“Dada,” she said, “he fell into the pool yonder, and was battered against the rocks. See there at his forehead.”
“Mally, I’m thinking that he’s dead already,” said old Glos, peering down over the body.
“No, dada; he is not dead; but mayhap he’s dying. But I’ll go at once up to the farm.”
“Mally,” said the old man, “look at his head. They’ll say we murdered him.”
“Who’ll say so? Who’ll lie like that? Didn’t I pull him out of the hole?”
“What matters that? His father’ll say we killed him.”
It was manifest to Mally that whatever anyone might say hereafter, her present course was plain before her. She must run up the path to Gunliffe’s farm and get necessary assistance. If the world were as bad as her grandfather said, it would be so bad that she would not care to live longer in it. But be that as it might, there was no doubt as to what she must do now.
So away she went as fast as her naked feet could carry her up the cliff. When at the top she looked round to see if any person might be within ken, but she saw no one. So she ran with all her speed along the headland of the cornfield which led in the direction of old Gunliffe’s house, and as she drew near to the homestead she saw that Barty’s mother was leaning on the gate. As she approached she attempted to call, but her breath failed her for any purpose of loud speech, so she ran on till she was able to grasp Mrs. Gunliffe by the arm.
“Where’s himself?” she said, holding her hand upon her beating heart that she might husband her breath.
“Who is it you mean?” said Mrs. Gunliffe, who participated in the family feud against Trenglos and his granddaughter. “What does the girl clutch me for in that way?”
“He’s dying then, that’s all.”
“Who is dying? Is it old Malachi? If the old man’s bad, we’ll send someone down.”
“It aint dada; it’s Barty! Where’s himself? where’s the master?” But by this time Mrs. Gunliffe was in an agony of despair, and was calling out for assistance lustily. Happily Gunliffe, the father, was at hand, and with him a man from the neighbouring village.
“Will you not send for the doctor?” said Mally. “Oh, man, you should send for the doctor!”
Whether any orders were given for the doctor she did not know, but in a very few minutes she was hurrying across the field again towards the path to the cove, and Gunliffe with the other man and his wife were following her.

===Chinese===

「爹爹，」她说，「他掉进那边潭里了，叫礁石磕的。瞧他额头那儿。」
「玛莉，我看他已经死了，」老格洛斯俯身端详着那身子说。
「没死，爹爹；可怕是快死了。我这就跑上农场去。」
「玛莉，」老人说，「瞧他的头。人家会说咱们害死了他。」
「谁这样说？谁那样血口喷人？不是我把他从坑里拖出来的吗？」
「那有什么要紧？他爹会说咱们害了他。」
玛莉心里明白，往后随人家怎么说，眼下的路却是明摆着的。她必须跑上小径，到冈利夫家的农场搬救兵。哪怕世人真像祖父说的那样坏，坏到那份上，她也犯不着再活在世上。可那是后话；此刻她该怎么办，半点无疑。
于是她赤着一双脚，能跑多快跑多快，一路奔上悬崖。到了顶上，她四下张望，看有没有人影，一个人也没有。她便顺着庄稼地边的丘垄，朝老冈利夫家的方向拼命跑；临近农舍时，看见巴蒂的母亲正倚在大门上。她一边奔一边想喊，可气力接不上，出不了大声；她索性直跑到冈利夫太太跟前，一把抓住她的胳膊。
「他爹呢？」她说，一只手按着狂跳的心口，好省着点气。
「你说谁？」冈利夫太太说——她于两家同特伦格洛斯爷孙的宿怨，也是一伙的。「这丫头抓着我做什么？」
「他要死了，就这么一句。」
「谁要死了？是老马拉奇吗？老人家要是不行了，我们派人下去。」
「不是爹爹；是巴蒂！他爹呢？主人家呢？」可这时冈利夫太太已急得魂飞魄散，放声喊起人来。幸好冈利夫，那位父亲，就在手边，同他一起的还有邻村来的一个男人。
「还不快去请大夫？」玛莉说。「唉，你们该去请大夫！」
大夫那头究竟吩咐了没有，她不得而知；可不过几分钟，她已重新赶过田地，朝通往湾里的小径奔去，冈利夫带着那人和他的妻子跟在后面。

===Original===

As Mally went along she recovered her voice, for their step was not so quick as hers, and that which to them was a hurried movement, allowed her to get her breath again. And as she went she tried to explain to the father what had happened, saying but little, however, of her own doings in the matter. The wife hung behind listening, exclaiming every now and again that her boy was killed, and then asking wild questions as to his being yet alive. The father, as he went, said little. He was known as a silent, sober man, well spoken of for diligence and general conduct, but supposed to be stern and very hard when angered.
As they drew near to the top of the path the other man whispered something to him, and then he turned round upon Mally and stopped her.
“If he has come by his death between you, your blood shall be taken for his,” said he.
Then the wife shrieked out that her child had been murdered, and Mally, looking round into the faces of the three, saw that her grandfather’s words had come true. They suspected her of having taken the life, in saving which she had nearly lost her own.
She looked round at them with awe in her face, and then, without saying a word, preceded them down the path. What had she to answer when such a charge as that was made against her? If they chose to say that she pushed him into the pool and hit him with her hook as he lay amidst the waters, how could she show that it was not so?
Poor Mally knew little of the law of evidence, and it seemed to her that she was in their hands. But as she went down the steep track with a hurried step﻿—a step so quick that they could not keep up with her﻿—her heart was very full﻿—very full and very high. She had striven for the man’s life as though he had been her brother. The blood was yet not dry on her own legs and arms, where she had torn them in his service. At one moment she had felt sure that she would die with him in that pool. And now they said that she had murdered him! It may be that he was not dead, and what would he say if ever he should speak again? Then she thought of that moment when his eyes had opened, and he had seemed to see her. She had no fear for herself, for her heart was very high. But it was full also﻿—full of scorn, disdain, and wrath.

===Chinese===

一路走着，玛莉缓过了嗓音，因为他们的脚步不及她快；在他们算得赶路的步子，倒容她把气匀过来。她一面走，一面向那位父亲讲说事情的经过，只是自己干的事，讲得极少。做母亲的落在后头听着，时时喊一声她的孩子遭了毒手，又时时疯疯癫癫地问人他可还活着。做父亲的一路少言寡语。他是个出了名的沉默、端方的人，勤谨持正，口碑极好，只是据说性子狠，动了怒便硬得出奇。
将到小径顶上，同行那人俯耳对他说了句什么；他随即回身拦住玛莉。
「他若真死在你们手里，你们就血债血偿。」他说。
那位母亲便尖叫起来，说她的孩子遭了谋杀；玛莉环视这三张脸，明白祖父的话应验了。他们疑心她害了那条性命——为救那条性命，她险些搭上了自己的。
她满面惶然望了他们一眼，一言不发，抢在前头引路下崖。这样的罪名扣到头上，她还有什么可分辩的？他们若咬定是她把他推进潭里、又趁他在水里时用钩子打他，她又如何证明不是？
可怜的玛莉不大懂证据的法度，只觉得自己已攥在他们手心里。可她顺着陡径急步而下——步子快得他们跟不上——她的心涨得满满的——满得很，高得很。为这条性命，她拼死拼活，仿佛他是她的亲兄弟。她自己腿上臂上的血还未干，那是为他出力时磕破的。有一瞬她拿准自己要同他一道死在那潭里了。如今他们竟说她谋害了他！也许他没有死；可他若还能开口，会说什么呢？随后她想起他睁眼的那一瞬，想起他仿佛望见了她。她对自己毫无惧意，因为她的心高得很。可它也满得很——满载着轻蔑、鄙夷和愤怒。

===Original===

When she had reached the bottom, she stood close to the door of the hut waiting for them, so that they might precede her to the other group, which was there in front of them, at a little distance on the sand.
“He is there, and dada is with him. Go and look at him,” said Mally.
The father and mother ran on stumbling over the stones, but Mally remained behind by the door of the hut.
Barty Gunliffe was lying on the sand where Mally had left him, and old Malachi Trenglos was standing over him, resting himself with difficulty upon a stick.
“Not a move he’s moved since she left him,” said he; “not a move. I put his head on the old rug as you see, and I tried ’un with a drop of gin, but he wouldn’t take it﻿—he wouldn’t take it.”
“Oh, my boy! my boy!” said the mother, throwing herself beside her son upon the sand.
“Haud your tongue, woman,” said the father, kneeling down slowly by the lad’s head, “whimpering that way will do ’un no good.”
Then having gazed for a minute or two upon the pale face beneath him, he looked up sternly into that of Malachi Trenglos.
The old man hardly knew how to bear this terrible inquisition.
“He would come,” said Malachi; “he brought it all upon hisself.”
“Who was it struck him?” said the father.
“Sure he struck hisself, as he fell among the breakers.”
“Liar!” said the father, looking up at the old man.
“They have murdered him!﻿—they have murdered him!” shrieked the mother.
“Haud your peace, woman!” said the husband again. “They shall give us blood for blood.”
Mally, leaning against the corner of the hovel, heard it all, but did not stir. They might say what they liked. They might make it out to be murder. They might drag her and her grandfather to Camelford Gaol, and then to Bodmin, and the gallows; but they could not take from her the conscious feeling that was her own. She had done her best to save him﻿—her very best. And she had saved him!
She remembered her threat to him before they had gone down on the rocks together, and her evil wish. Those words had been very wicked; but since that she had risked her life to save his. They might say what they pleased of her, and do what they pleased. She knew what she knew.
Then the father raised his son’s head and shoulders in his arms, and called on the others to assist him in carrying Barty towards the path.

===Chinese===

下到崖底，她紧挨棚门站住等他们，好让他们先走向前方沙地上那一小群人——离得不多远。
「他在那儿，爹爹守着他。你们去看吧。」玛莉说。
父亲和母亲跌跌撞撞奔过石头去了，玛莉却留在棚门边。
巴蒂·冈利夫还躺在玛莉撂下他的沙地上，老马拉奇·特伦格洛斯拄着棍子，吃力地站在他身旁。
「她走后他动也没动一动，」老人说；「动也没动。我把他的头搁在这块旧毯子上了，你们瞧见啦；我又拿一滴酒试着喂他，他不肯喝——他不肯喝。」
「哦，我的儿！我的儿！」母亲喊着，扑倒在儿子身旁的沙地上。
「住嘴，婆娘，」父亲缓缓跪到孩子头边，说，「这样呜呜咽咽，于他无益。」
随后他对着身下那张苍白的脸凝望了一两分钟，抬起头，冷冷逼视着马拉奇·特伦格洛斯的脸。
老人几乎受不住这可怕的诘问。
「是他自己要来的，」马拉奇说；「这都是他自己招来的。」
「是谁打的他？」父亲问。
「当然是他自己磕的，他摔在碎浪里了。」
「撒谎！」父亲说，抬眼望着老人。
「他们害死了他！——他们害死了他！」母亲尖声喊。
「住你的嘴，婆娘！」丈夫又说。「他们得血债血偿。」
玛莉倚着棚屋的墙角，把这些话全听了进去，一动不动。他们爱怎么说就怎么说。他们要说是谋杀就说是谋杀。他们尽可以把她和祖父拖去卡梅尔福德监狱，再解到博德明（Bodmin），上绞架；可有一样他们夺不走——她心里自己明白的那份知觉。她已尽了全力救他——尽了她的全力。而且她救下了他！
她记得他们一同下礁石之前她对他说过的威胁，记得自己那个歹毒的心愿。那些话说得实在恶毒；可自那以后，她拿性命去换过他的性命。他们爱说她什么就说什么，爱怎么处置就怎么处置。她知道的她知道。
随后父亲抱起儿子的头和肩膀，唤其他人帮着抬巴蒂往小径那边去。

===Original===

They raised him between them carefully and tenderly, and lifted their burden on towards the spot at which Mally was standing. She never moved, but watched them at their work; and the old man followed them, hobbling after them with his crutch.
When they had reached the end of the hut she looked upon Barty’s face, and saw that it was very pale. There was no longer blood upon the forehead, but the great gash was to be seen there plainly, with its jagged cut, and the skin livid and blue round the orifice. His light brown hair was hanging back, as she had made it to hang when she had gathered it with her hand after the big wave had passed over them. Ah, how beautiful he was in Mally’s eyes with that pale face, and the sad scar upon his brow! She turned her face away, that they might not see her tears; but she did not move, nor did she speak.
But now, when they had passed the end of the hut, shuffling along with their burden, she heard a sound which stirred her. She roused herself quickly from her leaning posture, and stretched forth her head as though to listen; then she moved to follow them. Yes, they had stopped at the bottom of the path, and had again laid the body on the rocks. She heard that sound again, as of a long, long sigh, and then, regardless of any of them, she ran to the wounded man’s head.
“He is not dead,” she said. “There; he is not dead.”
As she spoke Barty’s eyes opened, and he looked about him.
“Barty, my boy, speak to me,” said the mother.
Barty turned his face upon his mother, smiled, and then stared about him wildly.
“How is it with thee, lad?” said his father. Then Barty turned his face again to the latter voice, and as he did so his eyes fell upon Mally.
“Mally!” he said, “Mally!”
It could have wanted nothing further to any of those present to teach them that, according to Barty’s own view of the case, Mally had not been his enemy; and, in truth, Mally herself wanted no further triumph. That word had vindicated her, and she withdrew back to the hut.
“Dada,” she said, “Barty is not dead, and I’m thinking they won’t say anything more about our hurting him.”
Old Glos shook his head. He was glad the lad hadn’t met his death there; he didn’t want the young man’s blood, but he knew what folk would say. The poorer he was the more sure the world would be to trample on him. Mally said what she could to comfort him, being full of comfort herself.

===Chinese===

他们小心翼翼、轻轻软软地把他架在中间，抬着这份重负，朝玛莉站的地方走来。她一动不动，只看着他们忙活；老人拄着拐杖，一瘸一拐跟在后头。
走到棚屋尽头，她望了望巴蒂的脸，见它白得厉害。额头上血已不流了，可那道大口子看得清清楚楚，豁着参差的边缘，伤口四周的皮肉青紫。他那头浅棕色的头发向后披着——正是大浪漫过他们之后，她用手替他拢开的模样。啊，那苍白的一张脸、眉上那道凄然的疤，在玛莉眼里他多美啊！她把脸扭过去，免得让人瞧见她的眼泪；可她不挪步，也不作声。
可这时，他们抬着重负、挨着棚屋尽头蹭蹭前行时，她听见了一样声音，教她浑身一震。她猛地从倚着的姿势里直起身，伸长头颈细听；随后便移动脚步跟了上去。不错，他们在小径脚下停下了，又把那身子放在了礁石上。她又听见了那声音，像一声悠长悠长的叹息；于是她什么也顾不得，径直奔到伤者头边。
「他没有死，」她说。「听；他没有死。」
她说话时，巴蒂的眼睛睁开了，四下张望。
「巴蒂，我的儿，跟我说句话。」母亲说。
巴蒂把脸转向母亲，笑了笑，随即怔怔地环顾四周。
「你觉得怎么样，孩子？」他父亲问。巴蒂又把脸转向后一个声音，一转眼，他的目光落在了玛莉身上。
「玛莉！」他说，「玛莉！」
在场的谁也不需要再听什么，便都明白了：照巴蒂自己的说法，玛莉不是他的仇人；而说实在的，玛莉自己也无需再多的昭雪了。这一个字已替她洗清了冤屈；她退回到棚屋里去。
「爹爹，」她说，「巴蒂没死，我想他们再不会说什么我们害他了。」
老格洛斯摇了摇头。孩子没在那里送命，他高兴；他并不要那小伙子的血；可他知道世人会怎么说。他越穷，世人越要作践他。玛莉好言宽慰他——她自己心里正满是宽慰。

===Original===

She would have crept up to the farm if she dared, to ask how Barty was. But her courage failed her when she thought of that, so she went to work again, dragging back the weed she had saved to the spot at which on the morrow she would load the donkey. As she did this she saw Barty’s pony still standing patiently under the rock; so she got a lock of fodder and threw it down before the beast.
It had become dark down in the cove, but she was still dragging back the seaweed, when she saw the glimmer of a lantern coming down the pathway. It was a most unusual sight, for lanterns were not common down in Malachi’s Cove. Down came the lantern rather slowly﻿—much more slowly than she was in the habit of descending, and then through the gloom she saw the figure of a man standing at the bottom of the path. She went up to him, and saw that it was Mr. Gunliffe, the father.
“Is that Mally?” said Gunliffe.
“Yes, it is Mally; and how is Barty, Mr. Gunliffe?”
“You must come to ’un yourself, now at once,” said the farmer. “He won’t sleep a wink till he’s seed you. You must not say but you’ll come.”
“Sure I’ll come if I’m wanted,” said Mally.
Gunliffe waited a moment, thinking that Mally might have to prepare herself, but Mally needed no preparation. She was dripping with salt water from the weed which she had been dragging, and her elfin locks were streaming wildly from her head; but, such as she was, she was ready.
“Dada’s in bed,” she said, “and I can go now if you please.”
Then Gunliffe turned round and followed her up the path, wondering at the life which this girl led so far away from all her sex. It was now dark night, and he had found her working at the very edge of the rolling waves by herself, in the darkness, while the only human being who might seem to be her protector had already gone to his bed.
When they were at the top of the cliff Gunliffe took her by her hand, and led her along. She did not comprehend this, but she made no attempt to take her hand from his. Something he said about falling on the cliffs, but it was muttered so lowly that Mally hardly understood him. But in truth the man knew that she had saved his boy’s life, and that he had injured her instead of thanking her. He was now taking her to his heart, and as words were wanting to him, he was showing his love after this silent fashion.

===Chinese===

若敢的话，她真想悄悄溜上农场，去问问巴蒂怎么样了。可一想到那层，她又没了胆气，便重新干起活来，把她抢下的海草拖回那处明日要给驴子装驮的地方。干着活，她望见巴蒂的矮种马还耐心地立在礁石下；她便抱来一抱草料，扔在那畜生面前。
湾里已经黑了，她还在拖海草，忽见一点灯笼的光顺着小径下来。这是极罕见的事，因为马拉奇湾里向来少有灯笼。灯笼下得颇慢——比她惯常下行的速度慢得多；透过暮色，她看见一个人影立在径底。她走上前去，认出是老冈利夫，那位父亲。
「是玛莉吗？」冈利夫说。
「是，是玛莉；巴蒂怎么样了，冈利夫先生？」
「你得自己来看他，这就去，」庄稼汉说。「不见着你，他合不上眼。你可别说不来。」
「要我来说，我自然来。」玛莉说。
冈利夫等了片刻，心想玛莉兴许要收拾收拾；可玛莉用不着收拾。她浑身还滴着拖海草带下的咸水，那头精灵似的乱发披散着；可就是这样一副样子，她也算收拾停当了。
「爹爹睡了，」她说，「我这就去，随您。」
于是冈利夫转身跟她上径，心里暗暗惊异这姑娘过的日子——离一切同性的人那样远。此刻已是黑夜，他方才发现她独自一人在翻滚的浪边上摸黑干活，而那个似乎是唯一护着她的人，早已经上床睡了。
到了崖顶，冈利夫牵起她的手，引着她走。她不懂这是何意，可也不曾想把手抽回来。他咕哝了句崖上怕摔之类的话，声音低得玛莉几乎没有听清。其实这汉子的心里明白：她救了他儿子的命，而他非但没有谢她，反倒冤枉了她。此刻他是在把她往自己心坎上引；言语既不够用，他便用这沉默的样子表他的疼爱。

===Original===

He held her by the hand as though she were a child, and Mally tripped along at his side asking him no questions.
When they were at the farmyard gate he stopped there for a moment.
“Mally, my girl,” he said, “he’ll not be content till he sees thee, but thou must not stay long wi’ him, lass. Doctor says he’s weak like, and wants sleep badly.”
Mally merely nodded her head, and then they entered the house. Mally had never been within it before, and looked about with wondering eyes at the furniture of the big kitchen. Did any idea of her future destiny flash upon her then, I wonder? But she did not pause here a moment, but was led up to the bedroom above stairs, where Barty was lying on his mother’s bed.
“Is it Mally herself?” said the voice of the weak youth.
“It’s Mally herself,” said the mother, “so now you can say what you please.”
“Mally,” said he, “Mally, it’s along of you that I’m alive this moment.”
“I’ll not forget it on her,” said the father, with his eyes turned away from her. “I’ll never forget it on her.”
“We hadn’t a one but only him,” said the mother, with her apron up to her face.
“Mally, you’ll be friends with me now?” said Barty.
To have been made lady of the manor of the cove forever, Mally couldn’t have spoken a word now. It was not only that the words and presence of the people there cowed her and made her speechless, but the big bed, and the looking-glass, and the unheard-of wonders of the chamber, made her feel her own insignificance. But she crept up to Barty’s side, and put her hand upon his.
“I’ll come and get the weed, Mally; but it shall all be for you,” said Barty.
“Indeed, you won’t then, Barty dear,” said the mother; “you’ll never go near the awesome place again. What would we do if you were took from us?”
“He mustn’t go near the hole if he does,” said Mally, speaking at last in a solemn voice, and imparting the knowledge which she had kept to herself while Barty was her enemy; “ ’specially not if the wind’s anyway from the nor’rard.”
“She’d better go down now,” said the father.
Barty kissed the hand which he held, and Mally, looking at him as he did so, thought that he was like an angel.
“You’ll come and see us tomorrow, Mally?” said he.
To this she made no answer, but followed Mrs. Gunliffe out of the room.

===Chinese===

他牵着她，仿佛她是个孩子；玛莉在他身边碎步趋行，一句也不问。
到了场院大门，他停了片刻。
「玛莉，我的姑娘，」他说，「不见着你，他安不下心；可你别在他跟前多待，丫头。大夫说他身子虚，急等着睡呢。」
玛莉只点了点头，两人便进了屋。玛莉从没进过这屋子，睁着眼惊奇地打量大厨房里的家什。她日后的命数，那时可曾有一星半点闪过心头？我不知道。可她在此一刻也没停，便被引上楼，进了那间卧房，巴蒂正躺在他母亲的床上。
「真是玛莉本人吗？」那虚弱的后生说。
「真是玛莉本人，」母亲说，「如今你有话尽管说吧。」
「玛莉，」他说，「玛莉，我这条命这会儿还在，全亏了你。」
「这份情我记在她身上，」父亲说，眼睛偏向一旁不看她。「我永远记在她身上。」
「我们就这一个独苗苗，」母亲说着，围裙掩住了脸。
「玛莉，你这会儿肯跟我做朋友了？」巴蒂说。
即便此刻封她做这湾子永世的女主人，玛莉也说不出一句话来。不光是那里的人言人语、亲亲切切叫她怯了、哑了；那张大床，那面穿衣镜，那间屋子里闻所未闻的种种奇珍，都叫她觉出了自己的微贱。可她还是蹭到巴蒂床边，把手放到了他的手上。
「我还要来捞海草，玛莉；可捞上来全归你。」巴蒂说。
「那可不行，亲爱的巴蒂，」母亲说；「你再也别近那个吓死人的地方了。你要是没了，我们可怎么好？」
「去也行，可千万别近那个坑，」玛莉终于开口了，声音郑重，说出了巴蒂还与她为敌时她一直藏着的那点学问；「尤其是风稍稍偏北的时候。」
「她这会儿该下去了。」父亲说。
巴蒂吻了吻握着的那只手；玛莉望着他吻，心想他就像一位天使。
「你明天再来看我们，好吗，玛莉？」他说。
这话她没有答，只随着冈利夫太太走出了房间。

===Original===

When they were down in the kitchen the mother had tea for her, and thick milk, and a hot cake﻿—all the delicacies which the farm could afford. I don’t know that Mally cared much for the eating and drinking that night, but she began to think that the Gunliffes were good people﻿—very good people. It was better thus, at any rate, than being accused of murder and carried off to Camelford prison.
“I’ll never forget it on her﻿—never,” the father had said.
Those words stuck to her from that moment, and seemed to sound in her ears all the night. How glad she was that Barty had come down to the cove﻿—oh, yes, how glad! There was no question of his dying now, and as for the blow on his forehead, what harm was that to a lad like him?
“But father shall go with you,” said Mrs. Gunliffe, when Mally prepared to start for the cove by herself. Mally, however, would not hear of this. She could find her way to the cove whether it was light or dark.
“Mally, thou art my child now, and I shall think of thee so,” said the mother, as the girl went off by herself.
Mally thought of this, too, as she walked home. How could she become Mrs. Gunliffe’s child; ah, how?
I need not, I think, tell the tale any further. That Mally did become Mrs. Gunliffe’s child, and how she became so the reader will understand; and in process of time the big kitchen and all the wonders of the farmhouse were her own. The people said that Barty Gunliffe had married a mermaid out of the sea; but when it was said in Mally’s hearing I doubt whether she liked it; and when Barty himself would call her a mermaid she would frown at him, and throw about her black hair, and pretend to cuff him with her little hand.
Old Glos was brought up to the top of the cliff, and lived his few remaining days under the roof of Mr. Gunliffe’s house; and as for the cove and the right of seaweed, from that time forth all that has been supposed to attach itself to Gunliffe’s farm, and I do not know that any of the neighbours are prepared to dispute the right.

===Chinese===

到了楼下厨房，母亲给她端上茶，还有稠奶、一块热饼——农场拿得出的种种美食，都拿出来了。说不上玛莉那晚上多么在意吃吃喝喝；可她开始觉得冈利夫一家是好人——顶好的人。无论如何，这总比被安上谋杀的罪名、押进卡梅尔福德监狱强得多。
「这份情我记在她身上——永远记着。」那位父亲说过。
这句话从那一刻起便粘住了她，整夜整夜在她耳边响。巴蒂下了趟湾，她多高兴啊——哦，是啊，多高兴！他死不死的话，再没人提了；至于额上那一记磕碰，像他这样的小伙子，算得了什么伤？
「可叫你爹送你回去，」冈利夫太太见玛莉要独自动身回湾，便这样说。玛莉却听不进这个。去湾里的路，无论天亮天黑，她都摸得到。
「玛莉，你如今就是我的孩子了，我往后就这样看待你。」姑娘独自离去时，母亲这样说。
回家的路上，玛莉也想着这句话。她怎么就能做成冈利夫太太的孩子呢；啊，怎么才能呢？
我想，故事到此不必再讲下去了。玛莉后来当真做了冈利夫太太的孩子，怎样做成的，读者自会明白；久而久之，那间大厨房、农舍里种种的奇珍，都归了她所有。人们说，巴蒂·冈利夫娶了海里来的一条美人鱼；可这话当着玛莉的面说时，我怕她并不喜欢听；巴蒂自己喊她美人鱼时，她会朝他皱眉，甩动她那头黑发，装模作样用她那双小手打他。
老格洛斯被接上了崖顶，在冈利夫先生的屋顶下度过了他残存的岁月；至于那湾和捞海草的权利，从那时起，人人都认定归了冈利夫家的农场；左近乡邻，据我所知，也无意再争这份权利。

## The Gentle Euphemia Or, “Love Shall Still Be Lord of All” / 温柔的尤菲米娅，或「爱情仍将主宰一切」
===Original===

> “Lo, I must tell a tale of chivalry,

For large white plumes are dancing in mine eye.”
> — Keats

===Chinese===

> 「看哪，我须讲一个骑士的故事，

因为硕大的白羽正在我眼前舞动。」
> ——济慈

### I / 一
===Original===

> “Knowledge, so my daughter held,

Was all in all.”
> — Tennyson

The gentle Euphemia lived in a castle, and her father was the Count Grandnostrel. The wise Alasco, who had dwelt for fifty years in the mullioned chamber of the North Tower, was her tutor, and he taught her poetry, arithmetic and philosophy, to love virtue, and the use of the globes.
And there came the lord of Mountfidget to her father’s halls to drink the bloodred wine, and make exchange of the beeves and swine of Mountfidget against the olives and dried fruits which grow upon the slopes of Grandnostrel. For the pastures of Mountfidget are very rich, and its beeves and swine are fat.
“And peradventure I shall see the fair Euphemia,” said the young lord to Lieutenant Hossbach, of the Marines, who sojourned oft at Grange of Mountfidget, and delighted more in the racket-court, the billiard-table, and the game of cards, than in guiding the manoeuvres of his trusty men-at-arms. “Peradventure,” said the young lord, “I shall see the fair Euphemia﻿—for the poets of Grandnostrel sing of her peerless beauty, and declare her to be the pearl of pearls.”
“Nay, my lord,” said the lieutenant, “but an you behold the girl once in that spirit, thou art but a lost man, a kestrel with a broken wing, a spavined steed, a noseless hound, a fish out of water; for credit me, the fair Euphemia wants but a husband;﻿—and therefore do the poets sing so loudly.” For Lieutenant Hossbach knew that were there a lady at the Grange the spigot would not turn so freely.
“By my halidome,” said the young lord, “I will know whether the poets sing sooth or not.”
So the lord of Mountfidget departed for the Castle of Grandnostrel, and his beeves and his swine were driven before him.
Alasco the Wise sat in the mullioned chamber, with the globes before him and Aristotle’s volume under his arm, and the gentle Euphemia sat lowly on a stool at his feet. And she asked him as to the lore of the ancient schools. “Teach me,” she said, “as Plato taught, and the learned Esculapius and Aristides the Just; for I would fain walk in the paths of knowledge, and be guided by the rules of virtue.” But he answered her not at all, nor did he open the books of wisdom. “Nay, my father,” she said; “but the winged hours pass by, and my soul is athirst!”

===Chinese===

> 「知识，我女儿如此认定，

便是一切的一切。」
> ——丁尼生

温柔的尤菲米娅住在一座城堡里，她的父亲是格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵（Count Grandnostrel）。睿智的阿拉斯科（Alasco）在北塔那间带直棂窗的屋子里住了五十年，是她的师傅；他教她诗学、算术与哲学，教她爱美德，还教她使用地球仪。
芒特菲吉特老爷（lord of Mountfidget）来到她父亲的厅堂，饮那血红的酒，用芒特菲吉特的牛猪，换格兰诺斯特雷尔坡地上出产的橄榄和果干。因为芒特菲吉特的牧场丰饶，牛猪肥硕。
「说不定我能见上美丽的尤菲米娅一面，」年轻的老爷对海军陆战队的霍斯巴赫中尉（Lieutenant Hossbach）说。这位中尉常在芒特菲吉特田庄做客，比起操练他那些可靠的兵卒，他更醉心于网球场、台球桌和牌局。「说不定，」年轻的老爷说，「我能见上美丽的尤菲米娅——因为格兰诺斯特雷尔的诗人们歌咏她无双的容貌，称她为珠中之珠。」
「不然，老爷，」中尉说，「您若带着那心思看那姑娘一眼，您就是个完了的人——折翅的茶隼、患腿病的骏马、没了鼻子的猎犬、离水的鱼儿；请相信我，美丽的尤菲米娅缺的不过是一个丈夫；——所以诗人们才唱得那样响。」因为霍斯巴赫中尉深知：田庄里若坐了一位女主人，酒桶的龙头便拧不得那样畅快了。
「以我的圣物起誓，」年轻的老爷说，「我倒要弄明白，诗人们唱的是不是实话。」
于是芒特菲吉特老爷动身前往格兰诺斯特雷尔城堡，他的牛群猪群被赶在前头。
睿智的阿拉斯科坐在直棂窗的屋子里，面前摆着地球仪，臂下夹着亚里士多德的卷册；温柔的尤菲米娅谦卑地坐在他脚边一张凳子上。她向他求问古代学派的学问。「教我吧，」她说，「像柏拉图那样教，像博学的埃斯库拉庇乌斯和正义的阿里斯提得斯那样教；因为我不愿离开知识的小径，愿受美德的规矩指引。」可他全不回答，也不打开智慧之书。「不，师父，」她说；「可长翅膀的时光一小时一小时飞过去了，我的灵魂渴着呢！」

===Original===

Then he answered her and said; “My daughter, there cometh hither this day the young lord of Mountfidget, whose beeves and swine are as the stars of heaven in number, and whose ready money in many banks brings in rich harvest of interest. He cometh hither to drink the bloodred wine with your father, and to exchange his beeves and swine for the olives and the dried fruits which grow upon the slopes of Grandnostrel; and peradventure he will ask to see thy father’s daughter. Then wilt thou no longer desire to hear what Plato teaches, or how the just man did according to justice.”
But Euphemia replied; “Nay, my father. Am I no better than other girls that I should care for the glance of the young man’s eye? Have I not sat at your feet since I was but as high as your knee? Teach me still as Plato taught.”
But Alasco said; “Love will still be lord of all.”
“He shall never be lord of me,” said Euphemia.

===Chinese===

于是他回答她说：「我的女儿，今日芒特菲吉特的年轻老爷要到此地来，他的牛猪多如天上的星辰，他存在多家银行里的现钱生出利息的丰年。他来是要同你父亲饮那血红的酒，拿他的牛猪换格兰诺斯特雷尔坡地上出的橄榄和果干；说不定他还会求见你父亲的女儿。到那时，你就再不想听柏拉图教些什么，也不想听正义的人怎样行正义了。」
可尤菲米娅答道：「不，师父。难道我不比旁的姑娘强些，倒要去在意年轻男人的一瞥？我不从只到您膝盖那么高的时候起，就坐在您脚下了么？还是照柏拉图那样教我吧。」
可阿拉斯科说：「爱情仍将主宰一切。」
「它永远主宰不了我。」尤菲米娅说。

### II / 二
===Original===

> “And from the platform spare ye not

To fire a noble salvo shot﻿—

Lord Marmion waits below.”
> — Scott

===Chinese===

> 「从平台上且莫吝惜，

放一记响亮的礼炮——

马米恩大人在下面等候。」
> ——司各特

===Original===

And in those days there was the rinderpest in the land among the cattle, and the swine were plagued with a sore disease, and there had gone forth an edict and a command from the Queen’s Councillors that no beeves or swine should be driven on the Queen’s highways. So there came upon the lord of Mountfidget men armed with authority from the Queen, and they slew his beeves and his swine, and buried their carcases twenty fathom deep beneath the ground.
And the young lord was angered much, for he loved his beeves and his swine, and he said to himself, “What will my lord, the Count Grandnostrel, say unto me, if I visit him with empty hands? Will the bloodred wine be poured, or shall I see the gentle Euphemia?” For the Count Grandnostrel was a hard man, and loved a bargain well. “But I have much money in many banks,” said the lord of Mountfidget, in council with himself. “And though my beeves and my swine are slain and buried, yet will he receive me; for the rich are ever welcome, though their hands be empty.” So he went up the slopes which led to the Castle of Grandnostrel.
And at the portal, within the safeguard of the drawbridge, there were huge heaps of dried fruits, and mountains of olives. And there came out to him the Count Grandnostrel, and demanded of him where were his beeves and his swine. And the lord told the count how men in authority from the Queen had come upon him on the road, and had slain the beasts, and buried them twenty fathom beneath the earth﻿—because of the rinderpest which raged in the land, and because of the disease among the swine. Then said the Count Grandnostrel: “And art thou come empty-handed to drink the bloodred wine; and hast thou never a horn or a tusk? If my butler draw but a sorry pint for thee, I’ll butler him with a bastinado! No;﻿—not a cork! Get thee gone to thy Grange.” So he drew up the drawbridge, and the sweet scent of the olives and of the dried fruits were borne aloft by the zephyrs, and struck upon the envious senses of the young lord.
“And shall I not see thy daughter, the gentle Euphemia?” said he.
Then the Count Grandnostrel called to his archers and bade them twang their bows; and the archers twanged their bows, and seven arrows struck the Lord Mountfidget full upon his breast. But their points availed nought against his steel cuirass; so he smiled and turned away.

===Chinese===

那时国中牛群闹着牛瘟，猪也害着恶疾，女王的枢密诸臣已颁布敕令：不得在女王的官道上驱赶任何牛猪。于是带着女王授权的差官赶上了芒特菲吉特老爷，宰了他的牛猪，把尸首埋到地下二十寻深。
年轻的老爷大为恼怒，因为他疼爱自己的牛猪；他自言自语道：「我若空着两手去见格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵大人，他会怎么说呢？血红的酒还倒不倒？我还见得着温柔的尤菲米娅么？」要知道格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵是个狠人，最会算计买卖。「不过我在许多银行里有的是钱，」芒特菲吉特老爷心里盘算着，「牛猪虽被宰了埋了，他还是会接待我的；因为有钱人永远受欢迎，哪怕两手空空。」于是他登上通往格兰诺斯特雷尔城堡的坡道。
堡门口、吊桥防卫圈之内，堆着小山似的果干和成座的橄榄。格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵出来迎他，问他牛猪何在。老爷便告诉伯爵，路上如何来了女王的命官，宰了牲口，埋到地下二十寻深——因为国中牛瘟肆虐，又因为猪群害病。格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵便道：「你就这样空着手来喝血红的酒？连一支角、一根獠牙也没有？我的司酒若给你斟出一品脱寒酸的酒，我就用棍子给他『斟』一顿！不，——软木塞也别想拔！滚回你的田庄去。」说罢他便收起吊桥；橄榄与果干的甜香被和风托起，扑向年轻老爷那眼红的感官。
「我就见不着你的女儿、温柔的尤菲米娅了么？」他说。
于是格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵唤来弓箭手，命他们拉弓；弓箭手们把弓拉得铮铮响，七支箭正中芒特菲吉特老爷的胸膛。可箭尖碰上他的钢胸甲，全然无用；他便微微一笑，转身而去。

===Original===

“Nay, my lord, Count Grandnostrel,” said he, “thou shalt rue the day when thou treated thus one who has ready money in many banks; I will set the lawyers at thee, and ruin thee with many costs.”
Then, as he walked away, the archers twanged again, and struck him on the back. The good steel turned the points, and the arrows of Grandnostrel fell blunted to the ground. But I fear there was one arrow which entered just above the joint of the knight’s harness, and galled the neck of the young lord.
But as he went down the slopes there waved a kerchief from the oriel window over the eastern parapet.

===Chinese===

「哼，格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵大人，」他说，「你这样对待一个在多家银行存着现钱的人，日后必悔；我要叫律师跟你打官司，用讼费把你拖垮。」
他走开时，弓箭手又拉弓，射中他的后背。精良的钢甲弹开箭尖，格兰诺斯特雷尔的箭纷纷钝落地上。只是我怕有一支箭，恰恰从甲胄接缝上方钻了进去，擦伤了年轻老爷的脖颈。
可当他沿坡道而下时，东边雉堞上那扇凸窗里，有一方手帕在挥动。

### III / 三
===Original===

> “Oh coz, coz, coz, coz, my pretty little coz,

Dost know how many fathom deep I am in love?”
> — Shakespeare

’Twas midnight, and there came a soft knock at the door of Alasco the Wise. But Alasco heard it not, for he was drinking in the wisdom of the ancients with all his senses, and his ears were deaf to all earthly sounds.
“Sleepest thou, my father?” said the gentle Euphemia, as she opened the door, “or is thy soul buried amidst thy books?”
“Daughter,” said Alasco the Wise, “my soul is buried among my books. The hour is short, and the night cometh, and he who maketh not his hay while the sun of life shineth, shall hardly garner his crop beneath the cold, damp hand of death. But for thee, my child, and thy needs, all other things shall give way.” Then he wiped his pen, and put a mark in his book, and closed his lexicon.
“My father,” said the girl, “didst thou hear my father’s archers, how their bows twanged this morn?”
“I heard a rattling as of dried peas against a windowpane,” said the sage.
“It was the noise, father, of the arrows as they fell upon the breast of the Lord Mountfidget. And they fell upon his back, also, and alack! one has struck him on the nape of his neck! And then he rode away. Oh, father!”
“And is it thus with thee, my child?” said Alasco.
“Thus, father,” said Euphemia. And she hid her face upon the serge of his mantle.
“Did I not say that love should still be lord of all?” said the sage.
“Spare me, father,” said the damsel. “Spare the child that has stood at thy footstool since she was as high as thy knee. Spare me, and aid me to save my lord!”
Then they sallied forth from the small wicket which opens into the forest from beneath the west barbican.

===Chinese===

> 「哦表妹，表妹，表妹，表妹，我的小乖乖表妹，

你可知我陷在爱情里，有多少寻深？」
> ——莎士比亚

时当午夜，睿智的阿拉斯科门上响起轻轻的叩门声。可阿拉斯科没有听见，因为他正以全部感官畅饮古人的智慧，双耳对尘世的一切声响都已充耳不闻。
「师父睡着了么？」温柔的尤菲米娅推开门说，「还是您的灵魂埋在书堆里了？」
「女儿，」睿智的阿拉斯科说，「我的灵魂正埋在书里。光阴短促，黑夜将临，谁不在生命的太阳照耀时晒好干草，就很难在死亡那又冷又湿的手底下收进庄稼。但为了你，我的孩子，为了你的需要，一切别的事都可以让路。」说罢他擦净笔，在书里夹了个记号，合上词典。
「师父，」姑娘说，「今天早晨我父亲的弓箭手拉弓，您听见那弓弦响了么？」
「我听见一阵响动，像干豌豆打在窗玻璃上。」圣哲说。
「师父，那是箭落在芒特菲吉特老爷胸膛上的声音。还落在他的背上，哎呀！有一支射中了他的后颈！然后他就骑马走了。哦，师父！」
「原来你也到这一步了么，我的孩子？」阿拉斯科说。
「到这一步了，师父。」尤菲米娅说。她把脸埋在他披风的粗呢上。
「我不是说过，爱情仍将主宰一切么？」圣哲说。
「饶了我吧，师父，」姑娘说，「饶了这从只到您膝盖那么高时就站在您脚凳边的孩子吧。饶了我，帮我去救我的老爷！」
于是他们从西碉楼下面那扇通向森林的小边门出了城堡。

### IV / 四
===Original===

> “Come back! come back! he cried in grief,

My daughter, oh, my daughter!”
> — Campbell

> “When he found she’d levanted, the Count of Alsace

At first turned remarkably red in the face.”
> — Barham

===Chinese===

> 「回来！回来！他悲声喊道，

===Original===

And in the morning the Count of Grandnostrel called for his daughter. And his eyes were red with drinking, and his breath was thick, and he sat with his head between his hands. For he had drunk the bloodred wine sitting all alone through the night, laughing, as he quaffed down goblet after goblet, at the discomfiture of the lord of Mountfidget. “Rinderpest, indeed!” he had said. “He that cometh hither empty-handed is likely to return a-dry. Ho! there, butler! another stoup of Malvoisie, and let it be that with the yellow seal.” But in the morning he had called for a cool tankard, and now he demanded his daughter’s presence, that she might pour for him the cup which cheers but not inebriates. “Where is the Lady Euphemia? Why tarries the Lady Euphemia?” But the attendants answered him never a word. Then he called again. “Why cometh not my child to pour for her father the beverage which he loves? Now, by cock and pie, an that old greybeard detain her, he shall hence from the mullioned chamber﻿—and that with a flea in each ear.” But still they answered him not a word. Then he up with the tankard from which he had taken his morning’s brewst, and flung it at the menial’s head. “Thou churl, thou sot, thou knave, thou clod! why answerest thou not thy liege and lord?” But the menial put his hands to his bruised head, and still answered he never a word.
Then there entered Dame Ulrica, a poor and aged cousin of the house, who went abroad to dances and to tea-parties with the gentle Euphemia. “An please you, my lord count,” said dame Ulrica, “Euphemuia has fled this morning by the small wicket which leads from beneath the west barbican into the forest, and Alasco the Wise has gone with her.”
Then the Count Grandnostrel stood up in his wrath, and sat down in his wrath, and stood up in his wrath once again. “That tankard full of gold pieces,” said he, “to him who shall bring me the greybeard’s head!”
Then the archers twanged their bows, and the men-at-arms sharpened their sabres, and the volunteers looked to their rifles, and the drummers drummed, and the fifers fifed, and they let down the drawbridge, and they went forth in pursuit of the wise Alasco and the gentle Euphemia.

早晨，格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵唤女儿前来。他两眼喝得通红，呼吸粗浊，双手抱着头坐着。原来他独坐痛饮血红的酒饮了一整夜，一杯一杯灌下去，一面笑着芒特菲吉特老爷的狼狈。「牛瘟，倒真是！」他先前说过，「空手来的人，回去时多半要干着嗓子。喂！司酒的！再来一壶白葡萄酒，要黄封的那一种。」可到了早晨，他要了一大杯凉凉的饮料，如今又召女儿前来，好让她替他斟那「暖人而不醉人」的一杯。「尤菲米娅小姐在哪里？尤菲米娅小姐为何迟迟不来？」侍从们却一言不发。他又唤。「我的孩子为何不来给她父亲斟他心爱的饮料？哼，老天在上，若是那老胡子扣住了她，他就得从直棂窗的屋子里滚蛋——而且两只耳朵里各夹一只跳蚤地滚蛋。」他们仍一言不发。他便抄起早晨喝那一大杯的酒壶，朝仆人的脑袋掷去。「你这村夫，你这酒桶，你这恶棍，你这土块！为何不应答你的君上和主人？」那仆人双手捂住挨了砸的脑袋，仍旧一言不发。
这时进来一位乌尔丽卡夫人（Dame Ulrica），她是本家一位穷而年老的表亲，平日陪着温柔的尤菲米娅出门赴舞会和茶会。「启禀伯爵大人，」乌尔丽卡夫人说，「尤菲米娅今晨从西碉楼下通森林的那扇小边门逃走了，睿智的阿拉斯科也随她去了。」
格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵盛怒之下站起身，又盛怒之下坐下，再盛怒之下站起身。「那一满罐金币，」他说，「赏给把那老胡子的脑袋拿来的人！」
于是弓箭手拉响弓弦，兵卒磨快马刀，义勇兵检查步枪，鼓手擂鼓，笛手吹笛；他们放下吊桥，出发追捕睿智的阿拉斯科和温柔的尤菲米娅。

===Original===

“By cock and pie,” said the Count Grandnostrel, “an it be as I expect, and that sorry knave from Mountfidget is at the bottom of this﻿—”
“In that case it will be meetest, my lord, that she should be his wife,” said the Dame Ulrica, who was riding on a palfrey at his right hand. And when she spoke the ancient virtue of the old race was to be seen in her eye, and might be heard in her voice.
“Thou sayest well, dame,” answered the count.
“And the lord of Mountfidget has beeves and swine numerous as the stars, and ready money in many banks,” said Dame Ulrica. For Dame Ulrica was not virtuous only, but prudent also.
“By cock and pie thou sayest sooth,” said the Count Grandnostrel. And as they had now reached the Fiery Nostril, a hostel that standeth on the hill overlooking the olive gardens of the castle, the count called loudly for the landlord’s ale. “By cock and pie this is dry work,” said the Count Grandnostrel. “But we will squeeze Mountfidget drier before we have done with him.”
Then the menials laughed, and the potbellied landlord swayed his huge paunch hither and thither, as he shook his sides with merriment. “Faix, and it is my lord the count is ever ready with his joke,” said the landlord.
So they paid for the beer and rode on.

「老天在上，」格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵说，「倘若不出我所料，这事根子就出在那个芒特菲吉特来的混账身上——」
「若果真如此，老爷，那她最合适做他的妻子，」乌尔丽卡夫人说；她骑着一匹矮脚马，行在他右手。她说话时，眼里看得出旧族古风的德性，声音里也听得出。
「你说得对，夫人。」伯爵答道。
「况且芒特菲吉特老爷牛猪多如繁星，多家银行里存着现钱。」乌尔丽卡夫人说。原来乌尔丽卡夫人不但有德，而且有心计。
「老天在上，你说的是实话。」格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵说。这时他们已到达「火鼻」客栈——那客栈坐落在山冈上，俯瞰城堡的橄榄园——伯爵大声叫店主上麦酒。「老天在上，这可是叫人口干的话，」格兰诺斯特雷尔伯爵说，「不过等我们收拾完芒特菲吉特，还要叫他更干。」
仆从们哄笑起来；大腹便便的店主笑得浑身乱颤，那大肚皮左右直晃。「真的咧，伯爵大人开口就是笑话。」店主说。
于是他们付了酒钱，继续赶路。

### V / 五
===Original===

> “A breathing but devoted warrior lay.

T’was Lara bleeding fast from life away.”
> — Byron

In the upper chamber of a small cottage, covered with ivy and vines, lay the lord of Mountfidget, hurt unto death. For one of the arrows had touched him on the nape of the neck, and the point had been dipped in the oil of strychnine. And there leaned over his couch a widow, watching him from moment to moment, touching his lips ever and anon with orange juice mixed with brandy, and wiping the clammy dew from his cold brow. “Lord of Mountfidget,” she said, “when my dear husband was torn from my widowed arms, thy father gave unto the poor widow this cottage. Would I could repay the debt with my heart’s blood.”
“Aha! alas! alack! and well-a-day,” said the young lord. “Nought can repay me now﻿—either interest or principal. All my money at all the banks cannot prolong my life one hour. No, nor my beeves and swine, though they outnumber the stars of heaven, and are fatter than a butter-tub. It is all up with poor Mountfidget.”
“Nay; say not so, my lord. If only I could reach the wise man that liveth in the mullioned chamber of the north tower, he hath a medicine that might yet be of avail.”
Then Mountfidget demanded who was the wise man, and where was the mullioned chamber of the north tower; and when he learned that aid could be had only from the Castle of Grandnostrel, he sighed amain, and sighed again, and then thus he addressed the widow; “Ay, help from Grandnostrel;﻿—yes; but not such aid as that. I want no greybearded senior to rack my dying brains with wise saws; but, if it might be given me to let my eyes rest but once on the form of the gentle Euphemia, methinks I could die contented.”
Then the door of the chamber was opened, and there entered a young page, whose slashed doublet and silken hose were foul with the mud of many lanes, and the dirt of the forest clung to his short cloak, and his hair was wet with the dropping of the leaves, and his cap was crushed and his jacket was torn. “He is here! he is here!” said the page. “I have followed him by his blood through the forest.” Then the page fell at the bed-foot, and there he fainted.

> 「躺着一个尚有气息的忠勇战士，

那是拉拉，生命正飞快地流走。」
> ——拜伦

在一座爬满常春藤和葡萄藤的小村舍楼上的房间里，躺着芒特菲吉特老爷，伤得只剩一口气。原来有一支箭擦中了他的后颈，而箭尖浸过马钱子油。床边俯着一位寡妇，时时刻刻看护着他，不时用掺了白兰地的橙汁润他的嘴唇，揩去他冷额上黏湿的冷汗。「芒特菲吉特老爷，」她说，「我亲爱的丈夫从我这对寡妇的臂弯里被夺走时，您的父亲把这村舍给了穷寡妇。但愿我能用心头的血来偿还这笔债。」
「哎呀！苦哇！完了完了，没指望喽，」年轻的老爷说，「如今什么都救不了我——利息也罢，本金也罢。我在各家银行的钱，一小时寿命也续不上。牛猪也一样，虽说多得赛过天上的星，肥得赛过黄油桶。可怜的芒特菲吉特这回全完了。」
「不，老爷，别这么说。只要我能找到住在北塔直棂窗屋子里的那位智者，他有副药，也许还救得回来。」
芒特菲吉特便问智者是谁，北塔的直棂窗屋子又在哪里；待他得知救兵只能出自格兰诺斯特雷尔城堡，他长叹一声，再叹一声，然后这样对寡妇说：「是啊，向格兰诺斯特雷尔求救；——对；可不是那样的救法。我不要什么白胡子老先生，临死还拿格言把我这颗脑袋磨折；只是，倘若能让我这双眼睛在温柔的尤菲米娅的身上歇上一歇，我想我就能死得瞑目了。」
这时房门开了，进来一个年轻的侍童；他那开衩的紧身上衣和丝绸袜裤沾满了条条小巷的泥污，森林的尘土黏在短斗篷上，头发被滴落的露水打湿，帽子压瘪了，上衣也撕破了。「他在这里！他在这里！」侍童说，「我循着他的血迹一路穿过森林。」说罢侍童倒在床脚，就此晕了过去。

### VI / 六
===Original===

> “Meanwhile war arose.”
> — Milton

But as the page sank upon the floor, a small bottle fell from his breast coat-pocket, and the widow saw that it was labelled “antidote for the oil of strychnine.” Then the widow’s heart leaped for joy, and as she poured the precious drops into the gaping wound, she said a prayer that the page might recover also.
But what noise is this of horses and of men around the humble vinevard of that poor widow? “Tiraloo, Tiraloo, Tiraloo-ooh,” “Ha!” said the Mountfidget, raising himself on his elbow, “ ’tis the war-cry of the Grandnostrel!” “Rowdadow, Rowdadow, Rowdadow-dow,” then greeted his ears. “Ha! ha!” he cried. “Rowdadow, a Rowdadow, Rowdadow-dow; ’tis the war-cry of the Mountfidget!” And he grasped the sword which lay beneath his pillow. “Mountfidget to the rescue! Shall a man lie still and perish beneath the bedclothes? Ho, a Hossbach! Ho, a Walker!” For Walker was the captain of the men-at-arms at Mountfidget, and the lord knew the voice of his trusty clansman.
Then the widow looked through the lattice-window, and told him how the fight went. But no one thought of the page upon whose brow the clammy hand of death was falling as he lay at the bed-foot.

> 「其时，战事骤起。」

可这又是甚么声响？穷寡妇那寒酸的葡萄园四周，怎么有马蹄与人声？「提拉卢，提拉卢，提拉卢——呜。」「哈！」芒特菲吉特撑起胳膊肘说，「这是格兰诺斯特雷尔的战号！」接着「劳达道，劳达道，劳达道——道」又灌进他耳朵。「哈！哈！」他喊道。「劳达道，啊劳达道，劳达道——道；这是芒特菲吉特的战号！」他一把抓住枕头底下的剑。「芒特菲吉特人来救驾！大丈夫岂能躺着不动、闷死在被窝里？霍，霍斯巴赫家的人！霍，沃克家的人！」原来沃克是芒特菲吉特兵卒的队长，老爷听得出他这位可靠族人的嗓音。
寡妇便从花格窗里张望，把战况讲给他听。可谁也没有想到床脚那个侍童；他躺在那里，死亡冰冷黏湿的手正落上他的额头。

### VII / 七
===Original===

> “Close against her heaving breast

Something in her hand is pressed.”
> — Longfellow

Alascco the Wise had been left in the forest, and was unable to stir another step. “ ’Tis the blood of the Mountfidget,” he had said, when he saw the gouts upon the path. “I know it by its purple hue, and by its violet-scented perfume. Follow it on, but take that bottle with thee. And stay, lest thy sex betray thee to ill-usage from the boors, take this page’s raiment which I carry in my wallet, and put the bottle in thy breast coat-pocket. If thou find, as is too likely, a gaping wound in the nape of the neck, naught can restore him but this. Pour it in freely, and he shall live. But if he shall first have heard the war-cry of thy father to disturb him, then he shall surely die.” So the gentle Euphemia had gone through the forest, and had reached the chamber of the widow in which lay the lord of Mountfidget.
And as she lay at the foot of the bed, slowly there came back upon her mind a knowledge that she was there. She put her hand to her bosom in haste, and found that the bottle was gone. Then a terrible sound greeted her ears, and she heard the war-cry of her father. Tiraloo, Tiraloo, Tiraloo-ooh! “He is dead,” she cried, springing to her feet. “He is dead, and I will die also.”
Then the widow knew that it was the gentle Euphemia. “No, thou gentlest one,” she said; “he shall not die. He shall live to count the fat beeves and the many swine of Mountfidget, and shall be the possessor of much money in many banks; and thou, thou gentlest one, shall share his blessings. For love shall still be lord of all.”
“I do confess,” said the gentle Euphemia in a silvern whisper﻿—in a silvern whisper that was heard by him beneath the bedclothes﻿—“I do confess that love is lord of me.” Then she sank upon the floor.

> 「紧紧贴着她起伏的胸脯，

睿智的阿拉斯科被留在了森林里，一步也挪不动了。「这是芒特菲吉特的血，」他看见路上的血点时说过，「我认得出它，凭它紫红的色泽，凭它紫罗兰的芬芳。你循着血迹走下去，带上这只瓶子。且慢——为了免得你的女儿身教那些粗汉欺负，换上我这行囊里侍童的衣裳，把瓶子放进胸前口袋。你若找到——十有八九会找到——后颈上一个敞开的伤口，能救他的只有这药。放心倒进去，他就能活。但他若先听见你父亲的战号、受了惊扰，那他就必死无疑。」于是温柔的尤菲米娅独自穿过森林，到了寡妇的房中，芒特菲吉特老爷就躺在那里。
她躺在床脚，慢慢地，意识回到了她身上，明白了自己身在何处。她急忙把手伸向怀里——瓶子不见了。这时一声可怕的声响灌进耳朵，她听见了父亲的战号。提拉卢，提拉卢，提拉卢——呜！「他死了，」她跳起来喊道，「他死了，我也不活了。」
寡妇这才明白，她就是温柔的尤菲米娅。「不，最温柔的人儿，」她说，「他不会死的。他要活着数芒特菲吉特的肥牛肥猪，做多家银行里许多钱财的主人；而你，最温柔的人儿，将共享他的福气。因为爱情仍将主宰一切。」
「我招认，」温柔的尤菲米娅用银铃般的低语说——那银铃般的低语，被子底下的他听得见——「我招认，爱情主宰了我。」说罢她也倒在地板上。

And then they all returned to the Castle of Grandnostrel, and on their way they took up the wise Alasco, who had remained in the forest.
“Nay, father,” said the damsel smiling, “but thou hast been right in all things, and hast taught me better than Plato ever taught.”
“And was not I young once myself!” said the sage. So when the bloodred wine had warmed his old veins, and made supple the joints of his aged legs, he tripped a measure in the castle hall, and was very jocund.
So the lord of Mountfidget was married to the gentle Euphemia. But when three months were passed and gone, Lieutenant Hossbach had returned to his regimental duties.
And love shall still be lord of all.

于是众人一齐返回格兰诺斯特雷尔城堡，路上捎带了仍留在森林里的睿智的阿拉斯科。
「不，师父，」姑娘微笑着说，「倒是您样样都说对了，您教我的，比柏拉图教得还好。」
「想当年，我自己不也年轻过么！」圣哲说。于是，当血红的酒暖了他衰老的血管、活络了他老腿的关节，他就在城堡大厅里跳起舞步，快活得很。
就这样，芒特菲吉特老爷娶了温柔的尤菲米娅。只是三个月过去之后，霍斯巴赫中尉已经回团里办公务去了。
而爱情仍将主宰一切。

## Father Giles of Ballymoy / 巴利莫伊的贾尔斯神父
===Original===

It is nearly thirty years since I, Archibald Green, first entered the little town of Ballymoy, in the west of Ireland, and became acquainted with one of the honestest fellows and best Christians whom it has ever been my good fortune to know. For twenty years he and I were fast friends, though he was much my elder. As he has now been ten years beneath the sod, I may tell the story of our first meeting.
Ballymoy is a so-called town﻿—or was in the days of which I am speaking﻿—lying close to the shores of Lough Corrib, in the county of Galway. It is on the road to no place, and, as the end of a road, has in itself nothing to attract a traveller. The scenery of Lough Corrib is grand; but the lake is very large, and the fine scenery is on the side opposite to Ballymoy, and hardly to be reached, or even seen, from that place. There is fishing﻿—but it is lake fishing. The salmon fishing of Lough Corrib is far away from Ballymoy, where the little river runs away from the lake down to the town of Galway. There was then in Ballymoy one single street, of which the characteristic at first sight most striking to a stranger was its general appearance of being thoroughly wet through. It was not simply that the rain water was generally running down its unguttered streets in muddy, random rivulets, hurrying towards the lake with true Irish impetuosity, but that each separate house looked as though the walls were reeking with wet; and the alternated roofs of thatch and slate﻿—the slated houses being just double the height of those that were thatched﻿—assisted the eye and mind of the spectator in forming this opinion. The lines were broken everywhere, and at every break it seemed as though there was a free entrance for the waters of heaven. The population of Ballymoy was its second wonder. There had been no famine then; no rot among the potatoes; and land around Ballymoy had been let for nine, ten, and even eleven pounds an acre. At all hours of the day, and at nearly all hours of the night, able-bodied men were to be seen standing in the streets, with knee-breeches unbuttoned, with stockings rolled down over their brogues, and with swallow-tailed frieze coats. Nor, though thus idle, did they seem to suffer any of the distress of poverty. There were plenty of beggars, no doubt, in Ballymoy, but it never struck me that there was much distress in those days.

===Chinese===

我，阿奇博尔德·格林（Archibald Green），初次踏进爱尔兰西部小镇巴利莫伊（Ballymoy），结识了一位我有生以来有幸认识的最诚实的人、最好的基督徒，至今差不多三十年了。此后二十年里，他同我是莫逆之交，虽然他比我年长许多。如今他已在黄土之下躺了十年，我可以讲一讲我们初次相遇的故事了。
巴利莫伊算是一座镇子——至少在我讲的那些年头还算——坐落在戈尔韦郡（Galway）科里布湖（Lough Corrib）湖畔近旁。它不在通往任何地方的路上；作为一条路的尽头，本身也没有什么能吸引旅人的景致。科里布湖的风光是壮美的；可湖面很大，好景致都在巴利莫伊对岸，从镇上难以抵达，甚至难以望见。有鱼可钓——但那是湖钓。科里布湖的鲑鱼渔场离巴利莫伊很远；一条小河从湖里流出，直泻戈尔韦城。
那时的巴利莫伊只有一条街，陌生人一眼看去，印象最深的特点便是它整体透湿的样子。这不单是因为雨水常沿着没有阴沟的街面，化作一道道泥泞散乱的细流，以地道的爱尔兰急脾气奔向湖里；还因为每一座房子看去都像墙壁里渗着水汽；茅草顶与石板顶相间——盖石板顶的屋子正好比茅草顶的高一倍——更帮着观者的眼睛和头脑认定了这一印象。线条处处残破，而每一处残破，仿佛都是天上雨水自由出入的门。
巴利莫伊的人口是它的第二奇观。那时还没有饥荒，土豆还没有烂在地里，巴利莫伊四周的地租得出每英亩九镑、十镑甚至十一镑的价钱。白天任何时辰、夜里几乎任何时辰，都看得见精壮的汉子站在街上：膝扣裤敞着扣，长袜卷到粗皮鞋上，身上披着燕尾式的粗呢外套。他们虽然这样闲着，却似乎不沾一点穷苦的窘迫。巴利莫伊无疑有的是乞丐，可我从不觉得那些年头有多少真正的困苦。

===Original===

The earth gave forth its potatoes freely, and neither man nor pig wanted more.
It was to be my destiny to stay a week at Ballymoy, on business, as to the nature of which I need not trouble the present reader. I was not, at that time, so well acquainted with the manners of the people of Connaught as I became afterwards, and I had certain misgivings as I was driven into the village on a jaunting-car from Tuam. I had just come down from Dublin, and had been informed there that there were two “hotels” in Ballymoy, but that one of the “hotels” might, perhaps, be found deficient in some of those comforts which I, as an Englishman, might require. I was therefore to ask for the “hotel” kept by Pat Kirwan. The other hotel was kept by Larry Kirwan; so that it behoved me to be particular. I had made the journey down from Dublin in a night and a day, travelling, as we then did travel in Ireland, by canal boats and by Bianconi’s long cars; and I had dined at Tuam, and been driven over, after dinner on an April evening; and when I reached Ballymoy I was tired to death and very cold.
“Pat Kirwan’s hotel,” I said to the driver, almost angrily. “Mind you don’t go to the other.”
“Shure, yer honour, and why not to Larry’s? You’d be getting better enthertainment at Larry’s, because of Father Giles.”
I understood nothing about Father Giles, and wished to understand nothing. But I did understand that I was to go to Pat Kirwan’s “hotel,” and thither I insisted on being taken.
It was dusk at this time, and the wind was blowing down the street of Ballymoy, carrying before it wild gusts of rain. In the west of Ireland March weather comes in April, and it comes with a violence of its own, though not with the cruelty of the English east wind. At this moment my neck was ricked by my futile endeavours to keep my head straight on the side car, and the water had got under me upon the seat, and the horse had come to a standstill half-a-dozen times in the last two minutes, and my apron had been trailed in the mud, and I was very unhappy. For the last ten minutes I had been thinking evil of everything Irish, and especially of Connaught.
I was driven up to a queerly-shaped, three-cornered house, that stood at the bottom of the street, and which seemed to possess none of the outside appurtenances of an inn.
“Is this Pat Kirwan’s hotel?” said I.

===Chinese===

土地慷慨地出产土豆，人和猪便都别无所求了。
我命里注定要在巴利莫伊住上一星期办公事，公事的性质不必劳今天的读者分神。那时我还不像后来那样熟稔康诺特（Connaught）人的脾性，所以坐在从图阿姆（Tuam）驶来的侧座长车上进村时，心里怀着几分忐忑。我刚从都柏林（Dublin）下来，在那里便听人说过，巴利莫伊有两家「旅馆」，只是其中一家，恐怕缺些我这个英国人可能需要的舒适。因此我得指名住帕特·柯万（Pat Kirwan）开的那家「旅馆」。另一家是拉里·柯万（Larry Kirwan）开的；所以我须拿得精确。从都柏林下来的这一夜一天，我坐的是运河船和比安柯尼式的长车——那时我们在爱尔兰旅行就是这样走的；我在图阿姆吃了饭，四月的一个傍晚饭后赶了过来；到巴利莫伊时，我已累得要死，而且很冷。
「帕特·柯万的旅馆，」我近乎恼怒地对车夫说，「当心别去了那一家。」
「真的咧，老爷，为啥不去拉里家？去拉里家您招待得还好些呢，因为有贾尔斯神父（Father Giles）。」
贾尔斯神父是怎么回事，我一概不知，也一概不想知。我只知道我该去帕特·柯万的「旅馆」，便执意要车夫把我送到那里。
这时天已擦黑，风顺着巴利莫伊的街道刮下来，卷着一阵阵急雨。在爱尔兰西部，三月的天气会拖到四月里来，来时自有它的一股凶劲，虽不及英国东风那般狠毒。此时此刻，我在侧座长车上枉费力气要把头摆正，脖子已经扭了；座垫底下的水浸了上来；前两分钟里马已经停了六回；挡雨的围裙拖在了泥里；我苦恼透了。近十分钟里，我把爱尔兰的一切都骂遍了，尤其骂康诺特。
车把我拉到街尾一座模样古怪的三面临街的三角屋前，那屋子看去没有半点客栈的外表行头。
「这就是帕特·柯万的旅馆？」我说。

===Original===

“Faix, and it is then, yer honour,” said the driver. “And barring only that Father Giles﻿—”
But I had rung the bell, and as the door was now opened by a barefooted girl, I entered the little passage without hearing anything further about Father Giles.
“Could I have a bedroom immediately, with a fire in it?”
Not answering me directly, the girl led me into a sitting-room, in which my nose was at once greeted by that peculiar perfume which is given out by the relics of hot whisky-punch mixed with a great deal of sugar, and there she left me.
“Where is Pat Kirwan himself?” said I, coming to the door, and blustering somewhat. For, let it be remembered, I was very tired; and it may be a fair question whether in the far west of Ireland a little bluster may not sometimes be of service. “If you have not a room ready, I will go to Larry Kirwan’s,” said I, showing that I understood the bearings of the place.
“It’s right away at the furder end then, yer honour,” said the driver, putting in his word, “and we comed by it ever so long since. But shure yer honour wouldn’t think of leaving this house for that?”
This he said because Pat Kirwan’s wife was close behind him.
Then Mrs. Kirwan assured me that I could and should be accommodated. The house, to be sure, was crowded, but she had already made arrangements, and had a bed ready. As for a fire in my bedroom, she could not recommend that, “becase the wind blew so mortial sthrong down the chimney since the pot had blown off﻿—bad cess to it; and that loon, Mick Hackett, wouldn’t lend a hand to put it up again, becase there were jobs going on at the big house﻿—bad luck to every joint of his body, thin,” said Mrs. Kirwan, with great energy. Nevertheless, she and Mick Hackett the mason were excellent friends.
I professed myself ready to go at once to the bedroom without the fire, and was led away upstairs. I asked where I was to eat my breakfast and dine on the next day, and was assured that I should have the room so strongly perfumed with whisky all to myself. I had been rather cross before, but on hearing this, I became decidedly sulky. It was not that I could not eat my breakfast in the chamber in question, but that I saw before me seven days of absolute misery, if I could have no other place of refuge for myself than a room in which, as was too plain, all Ballymoy came to drink and smoke.

===Chinese===

「千真万确就是，老爷，」车夫说。「别的不说，单讲贾尔斯神父——」
可我已经拉了铃，门由一个赤脚姑娘开了，我便走进小门厅，没再听下去关于贾尔斯神父的事。
「能马上给我一间卧室吗？要生着火的。」
姑娘没有直接回答，把我领进一间客厅；一进去，我的鼻子立刻受到那股特殊香气的迎接——热威士忌潘趣酒掺了大量白糖的残迹所散发的气味。她把我摆在那里。
「帕特·柯万本人在哪儿？」我说着走到门口，虚张了几分声势。要知道，我是疲惫已极；而且不妨这样问一句：在爱尔兰极西的地方，稍稍唬人一下，有时是不是也能起点作用？「你们若没有现成房间，我就去拉里·柯万家了。」我说，以显示我摸得清此地的门道。
「那家可在老远的另一头呢，老爷，」车夫插嘴道，「咱们打它跟前过都过去好久啦。不过老爷您总不会想着丢下这家去那家吧？」
他这么说，是因为帕特·柯万的太太正紧跟在他背后。
于是柯万太太（Mrs. Kirwan）向我保证，一定可以也一定给我安排住处。屋子确实客满，可她早已作了安排，现成有一张床。至于卧室里生火，她可不敢恭维：「打从锅盖被风刮跑以后——遭瘟的——烟囱里的风就刮得凶得吓人；那个懒汉米克·哈克特（Mick Hackett）又不肯搭把手把它安回去，因为大宅那边有活计——那就叫他的骨节一根一根都倒霉吧。」柯万太太说得气壮山河。尽管如此，她同泥瓦匠米克·哈克特却是极好的朋友。
我表示不生火也行，这就上卧室去，于是被引上了楼。我问第二天在哪儿用早餐、吃正餐，得到的保证是：那间威士忌气味浓烈的房间，归我一人独用。我先前已经有些烦躁，听到这话，索性拉下脸来。倒不是不能在那间屋里吃早餐，而是我望见了眼前整整七天的绝对苦役——倘若我除了一间分明是全巴利莫伊人都来喝酒抽烟的屋子之外，再没有别的藏身之处的话。

===Original===

But there was no alternative, at any rate for that night and the following morning, and I therefore gulped down my anger without further spoken complaint, and followed the barefooted maiden upstairs, seeing my portmanteau carried up before me.
Ireland is not very well known now to all Englishmen, but it is much better known than it was in those days. On this my first visit into Connaught, I own that I was somewhat scared lest I should be made a victim to the wild lawlessness and general savagery of the people; and I fancied, as in the wet, windy gloom of the night, I could see the crowd of natives standing round the doors of the inn, and just discern their naked legs and old battered hats, that Ballymoy was probably one of those places so far removed from civilisation and law, as to be an unsafe residence for an English Protestant. I had undertaken the service on which I was employed, with my eyes more or less open, and was determined to go through with it;﻿—but I confess that I was by this time alive to its dangers. It was an early resolution with me that I would not allow my portmanteau to be out of my sight. To that I would cling; with that ever close to me would I live; on that, if needful, would I die. I therefore required that it should be carried up the narrow stairs before me, and I saw it deposited safely in the bedroom.
The stairs were very narrow and very steep. Ascending them was like climbing into a loft. The whole house was built in a barbarous, uncivilised manner, and as fit to be an hotel as it was to be a church. It was triangular and all corners﻿—the most uncomfortably arranged building I had ever seen. From the top of the stairs I was called upon to turn abruptly into the room destined for me; but there was a side step which I had not noticed under the glimmer of the small tallow candle, and I stumbled headlong into the chamber, uttering imprecations against Pat Kirwan, Ballymoy, and all Connaught.
I hope the reader will remember that I had travelled for thirty consecutive hours, had passed sixteen in a small comfortless canal boat without the power of stretching my legs, and that the wind had been at work upon me sideways for the last three hours. I was terribly tired, and I spoke very uncivilly to the young woman.

===Chinese===

只是别无选择——至少当夜和次日早晨别无选择——我便把怒气咽了下去，没再口头抱怨，跟着赤脚姑娘上楼，看着我的旅行箱被人先抬了上去。
如今的爱尔兰，英国人也未必都很了解，但比起那个年代已经强多了。我承认，头一回进康诺特，我心里颇有几分害怕，怕自己会做了这地方野悍不法与普遍蛮性的牺牲品；在湿漉漉、风声呼呼的夜色里，我望得见一群当地人围在客栈门口，刚能辨出他们的光腿和压瘪的旧帽子，我便觉得巴利莫伊多半是那种远离文明与法律、英国新教徒住着不保险的地方。我承担这项差事时，眼睛算是半睁半闭，也打定了主意要办到底；——但我承认，到这时我已感到它的凶险了。我早早拿定一条主意：旅行箱绝不离我的视线。我要死抱住它；要与它贴身共处；必要时，要死在它上面。于是我吩咐人把它先抬上那道窄楼梯，亲眼看着它在卧室里安顿妥当。
楼梯又窄又陡，爬上去像上阁楼。整座屋子造得野蛮、不开化，当旅馆同当教堂一样不合格。它呈三角形，浑身是角——是我平生所见安排得最不舒服的建筑。到了楼梯顶上，要我猛一转弯进那间分派给我的屋子；可小牛油烛的光影里有一道侧台阶我没留意，一个跟头栽进屋里，嘴里咒骂着帕特·柯万、巴利莫伊和整个康诺特。
请读者记住：我已经连续赶了三十个钟头的路，其中十六个钟头闷在一条狭小无趣的运河船上，连腿都伸不直；近三个钟头，风又一直从侧面修理我。我累得要死，对那年轻姑娘说话非常无礼。

===Original===

“Shure, yer honour, it’s as clane as clane, and as dhry as dhry, and has been slept in every night since the big storm,” said the girl, good-humouredly. Then she went on to tell me something more about Father Giles, of which, however, I could catch nothing, as she was bending over the bed, folding down the bedclothes. “Feel of ’em,” said she, “they’s dhry as dhry.”
I did feel them, and the sheets were dry and clean, and the bed, though very small, looked as if it would be comfortable. So I somewhat softened my tone to her, and bade her call me the next morning at eight.
“Shure, yer honour, and Father Giles will call yer hisself,” said the girl.
I begged that Father Giles might be instructed to do no such thing. The girl, however, insisted that he would, and then left me. Could it be that in this savage place, it was considered to be the duty of the parish priest to go round, with matins perhaps, or some other abominable papist ceremony, to the beds of all the strangers? My mother, who was a strict woman, had warned me vehemently against the machinations of the Irish priests, and I, in truth, had been disposed to ridicule her. Could it be that there were such machinations? Was it possible that my trousers might be refused me till I had taken mass? Or that force would be put upon me in some other shape, perhaps equally disagreeable?
Regardless of that and other horrors, or rather, I should perhaps say, determined to face manfully whatever horrors the night or morning might bring upon me, I began to prepare for bed. There was something pleasant in the romance of sleeping at Pat Kirwan’s house in Ballymoy, instead of in my own room in Keppel Street, Russell Square. So I chuckled inwardly at Pat Kirwan’s idea of an hotel, and unpacked my things.
There was a little table covered with a clean cloth, on which I espied a small comb. I moved the comb carefully without touching it, and brought the table up to my bedside. I put out my brushes and clean linen for the morning, said my prayers, defying Father Giles and his machinations, and jumped into bed. The bed certainly was good, and the sheets were very pleasant. In five minutes I was fast asleep.
How long I had slept when I was awakened, I never knew.

===Chinese===

「真的咧，老爷，这床干净得很，干爽得很，打大风暴那晚起夜夜都有人睡。」姑娘和和气气地说。接着她又跟我说起贾尔斯神父的事来；只是她正俯身翻折被褥，讲的话我一句也没捉住。「摸摸看，」她说，「干爽得很呢。」
我真去摸了：被单又干又净，床虽很小，看去倒还舒服。我便对她口气软了些，吩咐她明早八点叫醒我。
「真的咧，老爷，贾尔斯神父会亲自来叫您的。」姑娘说。
我求她们务必吩咐贾尔斯神父莫做这种事。姑娘却一口咬定他准来，说完便走了。莫非在这个野蛮地方，教区神父的职责竟是挨个到所有外乡人床前巡视，也许还带着晨祷，或别的什么可恶的天主教仪式？我母亲是个严谨的人，曾疾言厉色警告我提防爱尔兰神父们的诡计；说实话，我原本还倾向于笑话她。难道真有这样的诡计？难道可能不给裤子穿，除非我先望了弥撒？或者要以别的什么形式对我用强——也许同样叫人不痛快？
顾不得这些以及其他种种可怕，或者说得确切些——我打定主意，无论夜里或清晨降临何种恐怖，都要硬汉般迎上去——我开始收拾睡下。睡在巴利莫伊帕特·柯万的屋子里，而不是拉塞尔广场凯佩尔街我自己房间里，这里面自有一种罗曼的趣味。于是我暗自嘲笑帕特·柯万的旅馆观，一面打开行装。
有一张小桌，铺着干净桌布，上面我发现一把小梳子。我小心翼翼、不碰着它地把它挪开，把桌子挪到床边。我摆好早晨用的刷子和干净衬衣，做了祷告——权当回敬贾尔斯神父和他的诡计——跳上了床。床确实好，被单非常舒服。五分钟我就睡熟了。
被吵醒时睡了多少时候，我始终不知道。

===Original===

But it was at some hour in the dead of night, when I was disturbed by footsteps in my room, and on jumping up, I saw a tall, stout, elderly man standing with his back towards me, in the middle of the room, brushing his clothes with the utmost care. His coat was still on his back, and his pantaloons on his legs; but he was most assiduous in his attention to every part of his body which he could reach.
I sat upright, gazing at him, as I thought then, for ten minutes﻿—we will say that I did so perhaps for forty seconds﻿—and of one thing I became perfectly certain﻿—namely, that the clothes-brush was my own! Whether, according to Irish hotel law, a gentleman would be justified in entering a stranger’s room at midnight for the sake of brushing his clothes, I could not say; but I felt quite sure that in such a case, he would be bound at least to use the hotel brush or his own. There was a manifest trespass in regard to my property.
“Sir,” said I, speaking very sharply, with the idea of startling him, “what are you doing here in this chamber?”
“ ’Deed, then, and I’m sorry I’ve waked ye, my boy,” said the stout gentleman.
“Will you have the goodness, Sir, to tell me what you are doing here?”
“Bedad, then, just at this moment it’s brushing my clothes, I am. It was badly they wanted it.”
“I dare say they did. And you were doing it with my clothes-brush.”
“And that’s thrue too. And if a man hasn’t a clothes-brush of his own, what else can he do but use somebody else’s?”
“I think it’s a great liberty, Sir,” said I.
“And I think it’s a little one. It’s only in the size of it we differ. But I beg your pardon. There is your brush. I hope it will be none the worse.”
Then he put down the brush, seated himself on one of the two chairs which the room contained, and slowly proceeded to pull off his shoes, looking me full in the face all the while.
“What are you going to do, Sir?” said I, getting a little further out from under the clothes, and leaning over the table.
“I am going to bed,” said the gentleman.
“Going to bed! where?”
“Here,” said the gentleman; and he still went on untying the knot of his shoestring.
It had always been a theory with me, in regard not only to my own country, but to all others, that civilisation displays itself never more clearly than when it ordains that every man shall have a bed for himself.

===Chinese===

那是深夜某一时辰，我在睡梦中被房里的脚步声搅醒，一跃而起，看见一个高大的壮实老者背对着我站在屋子中央，正一板一眼地刷他的衣服。外套还穿在身上，裤子还套在腿上；可但凡他手够得着的身上每一处，他都刷得极其尽心。
我坐直了身子盯着他——当时自觉盯了十分钟——咱们就算盯了四十秒吧——而有一件事我已完全确定：那把衣刷是我自己的！按照爱尔兰的旅馆法，一位绅士深夜闯进外乡人房间刷衣服算不算正当，我说不上；可我确信，这种情形下，他至少也该用旅馆的刷子或他自己的。这明摆着侵犯了我的财产。
「先生，」我厉声说道，想惊他一跳，「你在我屋里做什么？」
「真是的，吵醒了你，对不住，小伙子。」那位壮实的老先生说。
「劳驾，先生，能不能告诉我，你在这里做什么？」
「老天爷，这会儿么，我正刷我的衣裳呢。它们实在该刷了。」
「我谅必是的。你用的还是我的衣刷。」
「这也是实话。一个人自己没有衣刷，除了用别人的，还有什么法子？」
「我看这太放肆了，先生。」我说。
「我看这算小事一桩。咱们俩不过是大小上看法不同。不过请原谅。刷子还你。希望它没受什么损。」
说罢他放下刷子，在屋里仅有的两把椅子上坐了一把，慢慢地动手脱鞋，一面直直地望着我的脸。
「你要干什么，先生？」我说着，从被窝里往外多探出些身子，伏在桌上。
「我要睡觉了。」那位先生说。
「睡觉！在哪儿？」
「就在这儿。」那位先生说；手上还在解鞋带的结。
我一向有个理论——不仅关于我的国家，也关于一切国家——文明最明白的显示，莫过于它规定人人各有一张床。

===Original===

In older days Englishmen of good position﻿—men supposed to be gentlemen﻿—would sleep together and think nothing of it, as ladies, I am told, will still do. And in outlandish regions, up to this time, the same practice prevails. In parts of Spain you will be told that one bed offers sufficient accommodation for two men, and in Spanish America the traveller is considered to be fastidious who thinks that one on each side of him is oppressive. Among the poorer classes with ourselves this grand touchstone of civilisation has not yet made itself felt. For aught I know there might be no such touchstone in Connaught at all. There clearly seemed to be none such at Ballymoy.
“You can’t go to bed here,” said I, sitting bolt upright on the couch.
“You’ll find you are wrong there, my friend,” said the elderly gentleman. “But make yourself aisy, I won’t do you the least harm in life, and I sleep as quiet as a mouse.”
It was quite clear to me that time had come for action. I certainly would not let this gentleman get into my bed. I had been the first comer, and was for the night, at least, the proprietor of this room. Whatever might be the custom of this country in these wild regions, there could be no special law in the land justifying the landlord in such treatment of me as this.
“You won’t sleep here, Sir,” said I, jumping out of the bed, over the table, on to the floor, and confronting the stranger just as he had succeeded in divesting himself of his second shoe. “You won’t sleep here tonight, and so you may as well go away.”
With that I picked up his two shoes, took them to the door, and chucked them out. I heard them go rattling down the stairs, and I was glad that they made so much noise. He would see that I was quite in earnest.
“You must follow your shoes,” said I, “and the sooner the better.”
