I had not even yet seen the man very plainly, and even now, at this time, I hardly did so, though I went close up to him and put my hand upon his shoulder. The light was very imperfect, coming from one small farthing candle, which was nearly burnt out in the socket. And I, myself, was confused, ill at ease, and for the moment unobservant. I knew that the man was older than myself, but I had not recognised him as being old enough to demand or enjoy personal protection by reason of his age. He was tall, and big, and burly﻿—as he appeared to me then.

===Chinese===

早年间，有身份的英国人——公认的绅士们——会同榻而眠且不以为意；听说女士们至今还这样。在偏荒之地，这种做法至今盛行。在西班牙某些地方，人家会告诉你一张床尽够安置两个男人；在西属美洲，旅行者若觉得两边各睡一人太挤，便算娇气。在我们自己国家的贫苦阶层中，这块文明的伟大试金石尚未见效。就我所知，康诺特也许压根没有这样的试金石。巴利莫伊分明就没有。
「你不能在这儿睡。」我说，在床上笔直坐起。
「这儿你会发现自己错了，我的朋友，」老先生说。「不过你放一百个心，我一辈子不会伤你一根毫毛，我睡起来安静得像只老鼠。」
我看得很清楚，动手的时候到了。我断断不能让这位先生钻进我的床。我是先来的，至少这一夜，我是这间屋子的主人。这荒僻地方风俗再怎样，国法里也决不会有哪一条，允许店主这样对待我。
「你不能睡在这儿，先生，」我说着跳下床，越过桌子落到地板上，正好在那陌生人褪下第二只鞋时同他照面。「你今夜不能睡在这儿，所以还是走吧。」
说着，我拾起他那两只鞋，拿到门口，扔了出去。我听见鞋子一路咯噔咯噔滚下楼梯，很高兴它们动静这么大。他会看出我是十分认真的。
「你也得跟着鞋走，」我说，「越快越好。」
到那时我还没看清这人的模样，甚至此刻也算不上看清，虽然我已走近他，把手搭上了他的肩膀。光很暗，只有一支快燃到窝里的法寻小蜡烛。我自己又昏乱、又不安，一时顾不上细看。我知道这人比我年长，却没认出他已老到该凭年纪享受人身庇护的程度。他高大、魁伟、敦实——那是他当时给我的印象。

===Original===

Hitherto, till his shoes had been chucked away, he had maintained imperturbable good-humour. When he heard the shoes clattering downstairs, it seemed that he did not like it, and he began to talk fast and in an angry voice. I would not argue with him, and I did not understand him, but still keeping my hand on the collar of his coat, I insisted that he should not sleep there. Go away out of that chamber he should.
“But it’s my own,” he said, shouting the words a dozen times. “It’s my own room. It’s my own room.”
So this was Pat Kirwan himself﻿—drunk probably, or mad.
“It may be your own,” said I; “but you’ve let it to me for tonight, and you shan’t sleep here;” so saying I backed him towards the door, and in so doing I trod upon his unguarded toe.
“Bother you, thin, for a pigheaded Englishman!” said he. “You’ve kilt me entirely now. So take your hands off my neck, will ye, before you have me throttled outright?”
I was sorry to have trod on his toe, but I stuck to him all the same. I had him near the door now, and I was determined to put him out into the passage. His face was very round and very red, and I thought that he must be drunk; and since I had found out that it was Pat Kirwan the landlord, I was more angry with the man than ever.
“You shan’t sleep here, so you might as well go,” I said, as I backed him away towards the door. This had not been closed since the shoes had been thrown out, and with something of a struggle between the doorposts, I got him out. I remembered nothing whatever as to the suddenness of the stairs. I had been fast asleep since I came up them, and hardly even as yet knew exactly where I was. So, when I got him through the aperture of the door, I gave him a push, as was most natural, I think, for me to do. Down he went backwards﻿—down the stairs, all in a heap, and I could hear that in his fall he had stumbled against Mrs. Kirwan, who was coming up, doubtless to ascertain the cause of all the trouble above her head.
A hope crossed my mind that the wife might be of assistance to her husband in this time of his trouble. The man had fallen very heavily, I knew, and had fallen backwards. And I remembered then how steep the stairs were. Heaven and earth! Suppose that he were killed﻿—or even seriously injured in his own house. What, in such case as that, would my life be worth in that wild country?

===Chinese===

直到鞋子被扔出去之前，他一直保持着不动声色的和气。听见鞋子在楼下哐当作响，他似乎不乐意了，说起话来又快又带怒气。我不同他争辩，也听不太懂他的话，只是一只手仍揪着他外套的领子，坚持不许他睡在那里。他必须滚出那间屋子。
「可这是我自己的，」他嚷道，这句话嚷了十几遍。「是我自己的屋子。是我自己的屋子。」
原来这位就是帕特·柯万本人——多半喝醉了，或是疯了。
「也许是你自己的，」我说，「可你今晚租给了我，就不许你睡这儿。」说着，我把他往门口逼，一不留神踩了他光着的脚趾。
「你这头犟驴英国人，真讨厌！」他说。「你这回干脆把我弄死算了。把手从我脖子上拿开，行不行？免得干脆把我掐死。」
踩了他的脚趾，我是过意不去的，但我照样不松手。这时我已把他逼到门边，打定主意要把他撵出门厅去。他的脸又圆又红，我想他准是喝醉了；既然发现他就是店主帕特·柯万，我对这人的火气更大了。
「你不许睡在这儿，所以还是走的好。」我一边说，一边把他往门口逼。自打鞋子扔出去，门就再没关上；在两扇门柱之间扭了一阵，我总算把他弄了出去。那楼梯来得如何突然，我全然不记得。上楼之后我一直沉睡，连自己身在何处都还不大清楚。于是，把他挤出门口的那道缝之后，我推了他一把——我想，这在我是最自然不过的了。他仰面倒了下去——一路滚下楼梯，摔作一堆；我听得出来，他跌落时还撞上了正上楼来的柯万太太——她无疑是上来查究头顶上这场祸事的根由的。
我心中闪过一个念头：但愿这婆娘能在她丈夫落难时帮衬一把。我知道那人摔得很重，而且是仰面摔的。这时我才想起那楼梯有多陡。天哪地啊！倘若他摔死了——或者干脆在他自己家里摔成重伤——到了那步田地，在这蛮荒地方，我这条命还值几个钱？

===Original===

Then I began to regret that I had been so hot. It might be that I had murdered a man on my first entrance into Connaught!
For a moment or two I could not make up my mind what I would first do. I was aware that both the landlady and the servant were occupied with the body of the ejected occupier of my chamber, and I was aware also that I had nothing on but my nightshirt. I returned, therefore, within the door, but could not bring myself to shut myself in and return to bed without making some enquiry as to the man’s fate. I put my head out, therefore, and did make enquiry.
“I hope he is not much hurt by his fall,” I said.
“Ochone, ochone! murdher, murdher! Spake, Father Giles, dear, for the love of God!” Such and many such exclamations I heard from the women at the bottom of the stairs.
“I hope he is not much hurt,” I said again, putting my head out from the doorway; “but he shouldn’t have forced himself into my room.”
“His room, the omadhaun!﻿—the born idiot!” said the landlady.
“Faix, Ma’am, and Father Giles is a dead man,” said the girl, who was kneeling over the prostrate body in the passage below.
I heard her say Father Giles as plain as possible, and then I became aware that the man whom I had thrust out was not the landlord, but the priest of the parish! My heart became sick within me as I thought of the troubles around me. And I was sick also with fear lest the man who had fallen should be seriously hurt. But why﻿—why﻿—why had he forced his way into my room? How was it to be expected that I should have remembered that the stairs of the accursed house came flush up to the door of the chamber?
“He shall be hanged if there’s law in Ireland,” said a voice down below; and as far as I could see it might be that I should be hung. When I heard that last voice I began to think that I had in truth killed a man, and a cold sweat broke out all over me, and I stood for awhile shivering where I was. Then I remembered that it behoved me as a man to go down among my enemies below, and to see what had really happened, to learn whom I had hurt﻿—let the consequences to myself be what they might. So I quickly put on some of my clothes﻿—a pair of trousers, a loose coat, and a pair of slippers, and I descended the stairs.

===Chinese===

于是我后悔自己太冲动了。说不定我初进康诺特，就害死了一条人命！
有一两分钟，我拿不定主意先做什么。我知道老板娘和女仆都在楼下忙着料理我屋里那位被逐者的身子，也知道我自己只穿着一件睡衣。我便退回门内，可又不肯把自己关起来回床上去，总得先问问那人的死活。于是我又探出头去，问了。
「但愿他摔得不重。」我说。
「哎呀，哎呀！杀人啦，杀人啦！说话呀，亲爱的贾尔斯神父，看在上帝份上！」楼梯脚下，妇人们发出这一声声和诸如此类的呼喊。
「但愿他摔得不重，」我又从门口探出头说，「可他不该硬闯我的屋子。」
「他的屋子！这傻蛋！——天生的痴子！」老板娘骂道。
「真的，太太，贾尔斯神父死啦。」楼下门厅里跪在那不省人事的身子旁的姑娘说。
「贾尔斯神父」四个字我听得清清楚楚，于是我明白过来：我撵出去的那人不是店主，而是本堂神父！想到四下里的祸事，我心里一阵发呕。我又怕得发晕，唯恐摔下去那人伤重。可是为什么——为什么——为什么他要硬闯我的屋子？这该死的房子的楼梯齐着屋门就到头，这叫我如何想得起来？
「只要爱尔兰还有王法，就得绞死他。」楼下一个声音说；照我看，被绞死的很可能就是我。听到最后那个声音，我开始当真以为自己杀了人，浑身冒出冷汗，站在原地抖了一阵。随后我想起，作为一个男子汉，我该下楼到我的敌人们中间去，看看究竟出了什么事，弄清我伤了谁——不管我自己后果如何。于是我匆匆穿上几件衣裳——一条裤子、一件宽外套、一双拖鞋，走下了楼梯。

===Original===

By this time they had taken the priest into the whisky-perfumed chamber below, and although the hour was late, there were already six or seven persons with him. Among them was the real Pat Kirwan himself, who had not been so particular about his costume as I had.
Father Giles﻿—for indeed it was Father Giles, the priest of the parish﻿—had been placed in an old armchair, and his head was resting against Mrs. Kirwan’s body. I could tell from the moans which he emitted that there was still, at any rate, hope of life.
Pat Kirwan, who did not quite understand what had happened, and who was still half asleep, and as I afterwards learned, half tipsy, was standing over him wagging his head. The girl was also standing by, with an old woman and two men who had made their way in through the kitchen.
“Have you sent for a doctor?” said I.
“Oh, you born blagghuard!” said the woman. “You thief of the world! That the like of you should ever have darkened my door!”
“You can’t repent it more than I do, Mrs. Kirwan; but hadn’t you better send for the doctor?”
“Faix, and for the police too, you may be shure of that, young man. To go and chuck him out of the room like that﻿—his own room too, and he a priest and an ould man﻿—he that had given up the half of it, though I axed him not to do so, for a sthranger as nobody knowed nothing about.”
The truth was coming out by degrees. Not only was the man I had put out Father Giles, but he was also the proper occupier of the room. At any rate somebody ought to have told me all this before they put me to sleep in the same bed with the priest.
I made my way round to the injured man, and put my hand upon his shoulder, thinking that perhaps I might be able to ascertain the extent of the injury. But the angry woman, together with the girl, drove me away, heaping on me terms of reproach, and threatening me with the gallows at Galway.
I was very anxious that a doctor should be brought as soon as possible; and as it seemed that nothing was being done, I offered to go and search for one. But I was given to understand that I should not be allowed to leave the house until the police had come. I had therefore to remain there for half-an-hour, or nearly so, till a sergeant, with two other policemen, really did come. During this time I was in a most wretched frame of mind. I knew no one at Ballymoy or in the neighbourhood.

===Chinese===

这时他们已把神父抬进楼下那间威士忌味儿的屋里；时辰虽晚，他身边已围了六七个人。其中就有帕特·柯万本人——他在衣着上可不像我那么讲究。
贾尔斯神父——的确是贾尔斯神父，本堂神父——被安在一把旧扶手椅里，头靠在柯万太太身上。听他发出的呻吟，至少还有活的指望。
帕特·柯万还不很明白出了什么事，人还半睡，而且——我后来才知道——半醉，正站在他跟前晃着脑袋。姑娘也在旁边站着，同她一起的还有一个老妪和两个从厨房挤进来的男人。
「去请医生了吗？」我说。
「哦，你这天生的恶棍！」那女人骂道。「你这世界的贼！像你这样的东西，居然进过我家的门！」
「您再悔，也悔不过我，柯万太太；可您是不是最好去请医生？」
「真的，还要请警察呢，这个你放心，年轻人。跑去就把人家那样往外扔——还是他自己的屋子，他又是个神父、一个老人——他把半间屋都让了出来，我求都求不住，就为一个谁也不知底细的外乡人。」
真相一点点水落石出。我撵出去的那人不仅是贾尔斯神父，还是这屋子的正主。至少，在安排我同神父睡同一间屋之前，总该有人把这些告诉我。
我绕到伤者跟前，把手搭上他的肩，想着也许能探出伤势轻重。可那怒气冲冲的女人带着姑娘把我轰开了，劈头盖脸一顿骂，还拿戈尔韦的绞架吓唬我。
我急盼着尽快请来医生；眼见没人张罗，我便自告奋勇去找。可我得到的答复是：警察来之前，休想离开这屋子。我只得在那里等了半个钟头上下，直到一位警士果真带着两名警察来了。这段时间里，我的心境凄惶极了。巴利莫伊本地也好，四邻也好，我一个人也不认得。

===Original===

From the manner in which I was addressed, and also threatened by Mrs. Kirwan and by those who came in and out of the room, I was aware that I should encounter the most intense hostility. I had heard of Irish murders, and heard also of the love of the people for their priests, and I really began to doubt whether my life might not be in danger.
During this time, while I was thus waiting, Father Giles himself recovered his consciousness. He had been stunned by the fall, but his mind came back to him, though by no means all at once; and while I was left in the room with him he hardly seemed to remember all the events of the past hour.
I was able to discover from what was said that he had been for some days past, or, as it afterwards turned out, for the last month, the tenant of the room, and that when I arrived he had been drinking tea with Mrs. Kirwan. The only other public bedroom in the hotel was occupied, and he had with great kindness given the landlady permission to put the Saxon stranger into his chamber. All this came out by degrees, and I could see how the idea of my base and cruel ingratitude rankled in the heart of Mrs. Kirwan. It was in vain that I expostulated and explained, and submitted myself humbly to everything that was said around me.
“But, Ma’am,” I said, “if I had only been told that it was the reverend gentleman’s bed!”
“Bed, indeed! To hear the blagghuard talk you’d think it was axing Father Giles to sleep along with the likes of him we were. And there’s two beds in the room as dacent as any Christian iver stretched in.”
It was a new light to me. And yet I had known over night, before I undressed, that there were two bedsteads in the room! I had seen them, and had quite forgotten the fact in my confusion when I was woken. I had been very stupid, certainly. I felt that now. But I had truly believed that that big man was going to get into my little bed. It was terrible as I thought of it now. The good-natured priest, for the sake of accommodating a stranger, had consented to give up half of his room, and had been repaid for his kindness by being﻿—perhaps murdered! And yet, though just then I hated myself cordially, I could not quite bring myself to look at the matter as they looked at it. There were excuses to be made, if only I could get anyone to listen to them.
“He was using my brush﻿—my clothes-brush﻿—indeed he was,” I said.

===Chinese===

从柯万太太和那些进出屋子的人对我说话的口气，还有恫吓的口气里，我知道我将遭遇最深切的敌意。我听人讲过爱尔兰的凶杀，也听人讲过民众对神父的爱戴，我真开始疑心自己性命难保了。
我这样等候的当口，贾尔斯神父自己醒了过来。那一摔把他摔懵了，但神志慢慢回了笼，只是回得绝不算利索；屋里只剩我和他时，方才一个钟头的事，他仿佛记不全了。
从人们的话里，我弄明白了：他早先是这屋子的房客——后来才知道，租了整整一个月；我到店时，他正同柯万太太喝茶。旅馆里仅有的另一间客房已住了人，是他大发善心，许可老板娘把撒克逊外乡人安置进他的屋子。这一切渐渐摆明，我看得出「我」的卑劣而残忍的忘恩负义，在柯万太太心里扎得有多深。我又辩又解，又对周围的一切话低眉顺眼地领受，全都是白费。
「可是，太太，」我说，「哪怕只告诉我一声，那是这位可敬神父的床呢！」
「床，说得倒好！听这恶棍的口气，倒像我们求着贾尔斯神父同他这号人睡一头似的。屋里明明两张床，哪一张都体体面面，哪个基督徒都睡得。」
这话对我是一片新光明。可是昨夜脱衣之前，我分明知道屋里有两张床架！我亲眼见过，只是被叫醒时一阵慌乱，把这事忘了个干净。我实在蠢，这没得说。现在我有体会了。可我当时真信那么大个子男人要钻进我那张小床。如今想来，实在可怕。那位好心的神父，为安顿一个外乡人，甘愿让出半间屋，而他的善心得的报偿是——兴许被谋害了！然而，虽然那一刻我打心底恨自己，却始终没法完全照他们的眼光看这件事。辩解的话不是没有，只可惜没人肯听。
「他当时正用我的刷子——我的衣刷——真的。」我说。

===Original===

“Not but what he’d be welcome; but it made me think he was an intruder.”
“And wasn’t it too much honour for the likes of ye?” said one of the women, with infinite scorn in the tone of her voice.
“I did use the gentleman’s clothes-brush, certainly,” said the priest. They were the first collected words he had spoken, and I felt very grateful to him for them. It seemed to me that a man who could condescend to remember that he had used a clothes-brush could not really be hurt to death, even though he had been pushed down such very steep stairs as those belonging to Pat Kirwan’s hotel.
“And I’m sure you were very welcome, Sir,” said I. “It wasn’t that I minded the clothes-brush. It wasn’t, indeed; only I thought﻿—indeed, I did think that there was only one bed. And they had put me into the room, and had not said anything about anybody else. And what was I to think when I woke up in the middle of the night?”
“Faix, and you’ll have enough to think of in Galway gaol, for that’s where you’re going to,” said one of the bystanders.
I can hardly explain the bitterness that was displayed against me. No violence was absolutely shown to me, but I could not move without eliciting a manifest determination that I was not to be allowed to stir out of the room. Red angry eyes were glowering at me, and every word I spoke called down some expression of scorn and ill-will. I was beginning to feel glad that the police were coming, thinking that I needed protection. I was thoroughly ashamed of what I had done, and yet I could not discover that I had been very wrong at any particular moment. Let any man ask himself the question, what he would do, if he supposed that a stout old gentleman had entered his room at an inn and insisted on getting into his bed? It was not my fault that there had been no proper landing-place at the top of the stairs.
Two sub-constables had been in the room for some time before the sergeant came, and with the sergeant arrived also the doctor, and another priest﻿—Father Columb he was called﻿—who, as I afterwards learned, was curate or coadjutor to Father Giles. By this time there was quite a crowd in the house, although it was past one o’clock, and it seemed that all Ballymoy knew that its priest had been foully misused.

===Chinese===

「倒不是舍不得他用；只是这让我以为他是个闯进来的外人。」
「对你这号人来说，这还不得算天大的体面？」一个女人说，话音里透着无限的轻蔑。
「我确实用了这位先生的衣刷。」神父说。这是他说的第一句成句的话，我为此非常感激他。我想，一个能把『用过人家的衣刷』这样的小事放在心上的人，总不至于真的摔死了——哪怕他被推下的是帕特·柯万旅馆里那样陡的楼梯。
「您用着当然完全欢迎，先生，」我说，「倒不是心疼那把衣刷。真的不是；只是我以为——我确实以为屋里只有一张床。他们把我领进屋子，对旁人只字未提。半夜里醒了，教我怎么想？」
「真的，够你想的，在戈尔韦监牢里——你就是要去那儿。」旁边一个人说。
人们对我的怨毒，我几乎难以描摹。倒没有真的对我动手，可我稍一动弹，就惹来一片明明白白的决心：不许我离开这间屋子。愤怒的红眼睛都朝我瞪着，我每说一句话，都招来一阵轻蔑与恶意的抢白。我开始觉得警察来是好事，心想我需要保护。我对自己的所作所为羞愧万分，却又想不出自己在哪个具体关头大错特错。任凭哪位扪心自问：设若他以为一位壮实的老先生闯进旅馆他的房间、执意要上他的床，他会怎么办？楼梯顶上没有像样的平台，这总不是我的错。
警士到来之前，两名普通警员已在屋里守了些时候；同警士一起到的还有医生，以及另一位神父——人称哥伦布神父（Father Columb），我后来才知道，他是贾尔斯神父的副手或助理。这时屋里已相当拥挤，虽然已过半夜一点；看来全巴利莫伊都知道本堂神父遭了毒手。

===Original===

It was manifest to me that there was something in the Roman Catholic religion which made the priests very dear to the people; for I doubt whether in any village in England, had such an accident happened to the rector, all the people would have roused themselves at midnight to wreak their vengeance on the assailant. For vengeance they were now beginning to clamour, and even before the sergeant of police had come, the two sub-constables were standing over me; and I felt that they were protecting me from the people in order that they might give me up﻿—to the gallows!
I did not like the Ballymoy doctor at all﻿—then, or even at a later period of my visit to that town. On his arrival he made his way up to the priest through the crowd, and would not satisfy their affection or my anxiety by declaring at once that there was no danger. Instead of doing so he insisted on the terrible nature of the outrage and the brutality shown by the assailant. And at every hard word he said, Mrs. Kirwan would urge him on.
“That’s thrue for you, doctor!” “ ’Deed, and you may say that, doctor; two as good beds as ever Christian stretched in!” “ ’Deed, and it was just Father Giles’s own room, as you may say, since the big storm fetched the roof off his riverence’s house below there.”
Thus gradually I was learning the whole history. The roof had been blown off Father Giles’s own house, and therefore he had gone to lodge at the inn! He had been willing to share his lodging with a stranger, and this had been his reward!
“I hope, doctor, that the gentleman is not much hurt,” said I, very meekly.
“Do you suppose a gentleman like that, Sir, can be thrown down a long flight of stairs without being hurt?” said the doctor, in an angry voice. “It is no thanks to you, Sir, that his neck has not been sacrificed.”
Then there arose a hum of indignation, and the two policemen standing over me bustled about a little, coming very close to me, as though they thought they should have something to do to protect me from being torn to pieces.
I bethought me that it was my special duty in such a crisis to show a spirit, if it were only for the honour of my Saxon blood among the Celts. So I spoke up again, as loud as I could well speak.
“No one in this room is more distressed at what has occurred than I am. I am most anxious to know, for the gentleman’s sake, whether he has been seriously hurt?”

===Chinese===

我看得分明，天主教里自有一种东西，使神父在民众心中无比亲近；因为我很怀疑，在英国随便哪个村子，教区牧师若遭了这样的意外，全村人会不肯半夜爬起来找肇事者报仇。此刻他们已开始叫嚷着要报仇了；警士还没到，两名警员就一左一右看住我；我觉得他们保护我不受民众伤害，是为了把我交出去——交上绞架！
这位巴利莫伊医生，我一点也不喜欢——当时不喜欢，后来旅居该镇期间也不喜欢。他一到，便从人群中挤到神父跟前，却不肯立刻宣布并无危险，让大家的情和我这颗心都得到安顿。非但如此，他还大肆渲染这桩暴行的可怕性质和凶手的残忍。他每说一句狠话，柯万太太便在一旁添柴。
「医生，这话不假！」「可不是嘛，医生，您说得好；两张好床，基督徒睡过的数它好！」「真真就是贾尔斯神父自己的屋子，可以说，打大风暴把他老人家下头那座房的屋顶掀跑以后就是了。」
就这样，我一点点得知了全部原委。贾尔斯神父自家的屋顶被风掀了，这才寄宿到旅馆！他甘愿同一个外乡人分住一屋，得的报偿竟是这般！
「医生，但愿这位先生伤得不重。」我说，语气极谦卑。
「先生，你以为那样一位先生，从长长一段楼梯上摔下来，能不受伤吗？」医生怒声说。「他的脖子没断，先生，可不领你的情。」
接着响起一片愤怒的嗡嗡声；看守我的两名警察忙乱了一阵，紧贴到我身边，仿佛觉得要动手护住我、免得我被撕成碎片似的。
我寻思，值此危局，摆一摆气概是我的本分——哪怕只为着凯尔特人中撒克逊血统的体面。于是我再次开口，嗓门放到最大。
「这屋里没有人比我更为此事痛心。为了这位先生，我急切地想知道：他伤得重不重？」

===Original===

“Very seriously hurt indeed,” said the doctor; “very seriously hurt. The vertebrae may have been injured for aught I know at present.”
“Arrah, blazes, man,” said a voice, which I learned afterwards had belonged to an officer of the revenue corps of men which was then stationed at Ballymoy, a gentleman with whom I became afterwards familiarly acquainted; Tom Macdermot was his name, Captain Tom Macdermot, and he came from the county of Leitrim﻿—“Arrah, blazes, man; do ye think a gentleman’s to fall sthrait headlong backwards down such a ladder as that, and not find it inconvanient? Only that he’s the priest, and has had his own luck, sorrow a neck belonging to him there would be this minute.”
“Be aisy, Tom,” said Father Giles himself; and I was delighted to hear him speak. Then there was a pause for a moment. “Tell the gentleman I aint so bad at all,” said the priest; and from that moment I felt an affection to him which never afterwards waned.
They got him upstairs back into the room from which he had been evicted, and I was carried off to the police-station, where I positively spent the night. What a night it was! I had come direct from London, sleeping on my road but once in Dublin, and now I found myself accommodated with a stretcher in the police barracks at Ballymoy! And the worst of it was that I had business to do at Ballymoy which required that I should hold up my head and make much of myself. The few words which had been spoken by the priest had comforted me and had enabled me to think again of my own position. Why was I locked up? No magistrate had committed me. It was really a question whether I had done anything illegal. As that man whom Father Giles called Tom had very properly explained, if people will have ladders instead of staircases in their houses, how is anybody to put an intruder out of the room without risk of breaking the intruder’s neck? And as to the fact﻿—now an undoubted fact﻿—that Father Giles was no intruder, the fault in that lay with the Kirwans, who had told me nothing of the truth. The boards of the stretcher in the police-station were very hard, in spite of the blankets with which I had been furnished; and as I lay there I began to remind myself that there certainly must be law in county Galway. So I called to the attendant policeman and asked him by whose authority I was locked up.

===Chinese===

「伤得非常重，」医生说，「非常重。据我目前所知，脊椎骨恐怕已受了伤。」
「嗬，见鬼，老兄，」一个声音说——我后来得知，那声音属于当时驻在巴利莫伊的税务队里的一位军官，此人我后来熟识了；他名叫汤姆·麦克德莫特（Tom Macdermot），汤姆·麦克德莫特上尉，利特里姆郡（Leitrim）人——「嗬，见鬼，老兄；你以为一位绅士直挺挺仰面从那么一架梯子上摔下去，还能不觉得碍事么？幸亏他是神父，自有他的福气，要不然，这会儿他脖子上可就一根好骨头都不剩喽。」
「轻点儿，汤姆。」贾尔斯神父自己说道；听见他开口，我满心欢喜。随后静了片刻。「告诉那位先生，我一点儿也不碍事。」神父说；从那一刻起，我对他生出了一份情谊，此后从未衰减。
他们把他抬上楼，送回他被逐出的那间屋子；我则被押去警察所，切切实实在那里过了一夜。那是怎样的一夜！我从伦敦（London）直接赶来，一路只在都柏林睡过一觉，如今却落得在巴利莫伊警察营房里享用一张帆布床！最糟的是，我在巴利莫伊还有公事要办，那公事需要我昂着头、拿足身份。神父说的那几句话安慰了我，使我重新能够盘算自己的处境。凭什么关我？没有一个治安官下过拘押令。我究竟做没做违法的事，实在大成问题。正如贾尔斯神父唤作汤姆的那人非常在理地解释的：谁叫人家里装梯子不装楼梯，别人要把闯进屋的人撵出去，能不冒摔断他脖子的风险么？至于说贾尔斯神父并非外人——这一点如今铁定无疑——那过错也在柯万夫妇，是他们半点实情也没告诉我。警察所里帆布床的木板硬得很，虽说也给我配了毯子；躺在那里，我开始提醒自己：戈尔韦郡总该有王法。于是我唤来看守的警察，问他凭什么权力关押我。

===Original===

“Ah, thin, don’t bother,” said the policeman; “shure, and you’ve given throuble enough this night!” The dawn was at that moment breaking, so I turned myself on the stretcher, and resolved that I would put a bold face on it all when the day should come.
The first person I saw in the morning was Captain Tom, who came into the room where I was lying, followed by a little boy with my portmanteau. The sub-inspector of police who ruled over the men at Ballymoy lived, as I afterwards learned, at Oranmore, so that I had not, at this conjuncture, the honour of seeing him. Captain Tom assured me that he was an excellent fellow, and rode to hounds like a bird. As in those days I rode to hounds myself﻿—as nearly like a bird as I was able﻿—I was glad to have such an account of my head-gaoler. The sub-constables seemed to do just what Captain Tom told them, and there was, no doubt, a very good understanding between the police force and the revenue officer.
“Well, now, I’ll tell you what you must do, Mr. Green,” said the captain.
“In the first place,” said I, “I must protest that I’m now locked up here illegally.”
“Oh, bother; now don’t make yourself unaisy.”
“That’s all very well, Captain﻿—. I beg your pardon, Sir, but I didn’t catch any name plainly except the Christian name.”
“My name is Macdermot﻿—Tom Macdermot. They call me captain﻿—but that’s neither here nor there.”
“I suppose, Captain Macdermot, the police here cannot lock up anybody they please, without a warrant?”
“And where would you have been if they hadn’t locked you up? I’m blessed if they wouldn’t have had you into the Lough before this time.”
There might be something in that, and I therefore resolved to forgive the personal indignity which I had suffered, if I could secure something like just treatment for the future. Captain Tom had already told me that Father Giles was doing pretty well.
“He’s as sthrong as a horse, you see, or, sorrow a doubt, he’d be a dead man this minute. The back of his neck is as black as your hat with the bruises, and it’s the same way with him all down his loins. A man like that, you know, not just as young as he was once, falls mortial heavy. But he’s as jolly as a four-year old,” said Captain Tom, “and you’re to go and ate your breakfast with him, in his bedroom, so that you may see with your own eyes that there are two beds there.”

===Chinese===

「嗐，别烦人了，」警察说，「真的，你这晚上惹的麻烦够多啦！」这时天正破晓，我在帆布床上翻了个身，打定主意：天亮之后，一切都要厚着脸皮硬顶过去。
早晨我见到的第一个人是汤姆上尉。他走进我躺着的那间屋，身后跟着一个提我旅行箱的小男孩。管着巴利莫伊这些警察的副督察，我后来得知，住在奥兰莫尔（Oranmore），所以这一节骨眼上，我无福见他了。汤姆上尉向我保证，那是顶好的人，骑马逐猎轻捷如飞。那些年我自己也猎狐——也尽我所能地接近飞鸟的水平——听到我这位典狱长如此人品，很是欣慰。那些警员仿佛事事都听汤姆上尉的，警队同这位税务官之间，无疑交情极好。
「好了，格林先生，我告诉你你该怎么办。」上尉说。
「首先，」我说，「我必须抗议：我现在被非法关押在这里。」
「嗐，得了；别自找不自在。」
「这话不错，——上尉。对不起，先生，除了教名，您贵姓我实在没听真切。」
「我姓麦克德莫特——汤姆·麦克德莫特。他们叫我上尉——不过这无关紧要。」
「麦克德莫特上尉，我想，此地警察总不能无法院拘票，随意关押任何人吧？」
「他们若不关你，你还能在哪儿？老天保佑，不然这会儿早把你扔进湖里去了。」
这话兴许有几分道理，于是我决意宽恕我所蒙受的人身羞辱，只要往后的待遇能大致公道。汤姆上尉早已告诉我，贾尔斯神父恢复得不错。
「他壮得像匹马，你瞧，要不然，毫无疑问，这会儿他早死透了。他后颈乌青得跟你的帽子一样，腰眼往下也处处如此。那样的人，你知道，不比当年年轻了，摔下去重得很。可他快活得像匹四岁口的小马，」汤姆上尉说，「你这就去他卧室同他一起用早餐，好亲眼看看那里头明明是两张床。」

===Original===

“I remembered it afterwards quite well,” said I.
“ ’Deed, and Father Giles got such a kick of laughter this morning, when he came to understand that you thought he was going to get into bed alongside of you, that he strained himself all over again, and I thought he’d have frightened the house, yelling with the pain. But anyway you’ve to go over and see him. So now you’d better get yourself dressed.”
This announcement was certainly very pleasant. Against Father Giles, of course, I had no feeling of bitterness. He had behaved well throughout, and I was quite alive to the fact that the light of his countenance would afford me a better aegis against the ill-will of the people of Ballymoy, than anything the law would do for me. So I dressed myself in the barrack-room, while Captain Tom waited without, and then I sallied out under his guidance to make a second visit to Pat Kirwan’s hotel. I was amused to see that the police, though by no means subject to Captain Tom’s orders, let me go without the least difficulty, and that the boy was allowed to carry my portmanteau away with him.
“Oh, it’s all right,” said Captain Tom when I alluded to this. “You’re not down in the sheet. You were only there for protection, you know.”
Nevertheless, I had been taken there by force, and had been locked up by force. If, however, they were disposed to forget all that, so was I. I did not return to the barracks again; and when, after that, the policemen whom I had known met me in the street, they always accosted me as though I were an old friend; hoping my honour had found a better bed than when they last saw me. They had not looked at me with any friendship in their eyes when they had stood over me in Pat Kirwan’s parlour.
This was my first view of Ballymoy, and of the “hotel” by daylight. I now saw that Mrs. Pat Kirwan kept a grocery establishment, and that the three-cornered house which had so astonished me was very small. Had I seen it before I entered it, I should hardly have dared to look there for a night’s lodging. As it was, I stayed there for a fortnight, and was by no means uncomfortable. Knots of men and women were now standing in groups round the door, and, indeed, the lower end of the street was almost crowded.

===Chinese===

「后来我想起来，记得清清楚楚。」我说。
「真的，贾尔斯神父今早明白过来、知道你当他要钻到你被窝里时，爆发出那一场大笑，笑得重新扭伤了筋，疼得直叫唤，我以为他要吓坏全家。可不管怎样，你总得过去看看他。这就去把衣裳穿好吧。」
这个宣布自然十分可喜。对贾尔斯神父，我当然毫无怨气。他自始至终行事体面；而且我很明白，他的一个笑脸，比法律能给我的任何东西，都是抵挡巴利莫伊民众恶意的更好盾牌。我便在营房里穿好衣裳，汤姆上尉在外等候；随后我在他引领下再度出发，二进帕特·柯万的旅馆。我饶有兴味地看到：警察虽绝不受汤姆上尉节制，却放我走得不费半点周折；那小男孩也获准提着我的旅行箱跟了去。
「嗐，没事的，」我提起这事时汤姆上尉说，「簿子上没记你的名。你不过是去受保护的，明白么。」
话虽如此，我确是被武力押去、武力关押的。不过他们既肯尽数忘却，我也肯。我再没回警察营房；此后我认识的那些警察在街上遇见我，总像老朋友一样同我招呼，祝我老爷寻到了比上回见面时更好的铺位。在帕特·柯万家客厅里看守我时，他们眼里可没有半点友好的意思。
这是我第一次在白天看巴利莫伊，看这家「旅馆」。我这才发现帕特·柯万太太还兼开着一爿杂货铺，那座曾叫我惊诧不已的三角屋其实很小。若是进门前先看上一眼，我断不敢指望在那里过夜。而实际上，我在那里住了两个星期，还相当舒服。男男女女正三五成群围在门口；确实，街那头几乎挤满了人。

===Original===

“They’re all here,” whispered Captain Tom, “because they’ve heard how Father Giles has been murdered during the night by a terrible Saxon; and there isn’t a man or woman among them who doesn’t know that you are the man who did it.”
“But they know also, I suppose,” said I, “that Father Giles is alive.”
“Bedad, yes, they know that, or I wouldn’t be in your skin, my boy. But come along. We mustn’t keep the priest waiting for his breakfast.”
I could see that they all looked at me, and there were some of them, especially among the women, whose looks I did not even yet like. They spoke among each other in Gaelic, and I could perceive that they were talking of me.
“Can’t you understand, then,” said Captain Tom, speaking to them aloud, just as he entered the house, “that father Giles, the Lord be praised, is as well as ever he was in his life? Shure it was only an accident.”
“An accident done on purpose, Captain Tom,” said one person.
“What is it to you how it was done, Mick Healy? If Father Giles is satisfied, isn’t that enough for the likes of you? Get out of that, and let the gentleman pass.” Then Captain Tom pushed Mick away roughly, and the others let us enter the house. “Only they wouldn’t do it unless somebody gave them the wink, they’d pull you in pieces this moment for a dandy of punch﻿—they would, indeed.”
Perhaps Captain Tom exaggerated the prevailing feeling, thinking thereby to raise the value of his own service in protecting me; but I was quite alive to the fact that I had done a most dangerous deed, and had a most narrow escape.
I found Father Giles sitting up in his bed, while Mrs. Kirwan was rubbing his shoulder diligently with an embrocation of arnica. The girl was standing by with a basin half full of the same, and I could see that the priest’s neck and shoulders were as red as a raw beefsteak. He winced grievously under the rubbing, but he bore it like a man.
“And here comes the hero,” said Father Giles. “Now stop a minute or two, Mrs. Kirwan, while we have a mouthful of breakfast, for I’ll go bail that Mr. Green is hungry after his night’s rest. I hope you got a better bed, Mr. Green, than the one I found you in when I was unfortunate enough to waken you last night. There it is, all ready for you still,” said he; “and if you accept of it tonight, take my advice and don’t let a trifle stand in the way of your dhraims.”

===Chinese===

「他们全在这儿，」汤姆上尉低声说，「因为他们听说贾尔斯神父夜里叫一个可怕的撒克逊人谋害了；他们里头没有一个人不知道，干这事的就是你。」
「可我想，他们也知道，」我说，「贾尔斯神父还活着。」
「老天爷，是，这他们知道；要不然，小子，你那身皮我可不想要。走吧。不能让神父等早餐。」
我看得见他们个个都在打量我，其中有些人——尤其是女人——的目光，我到这时也不喜欢。他们彼此说着盖尔语，我察觉得出谈的是我。
「你们就不能明白么，」汤姆上尉进屋前高声对他们说，「贾尔斯神父，感谢上帝，好得同他一辈子任何好时候一样？真的，不过是一场意外。」
「一场存心造成的意外，汤姆上尉。」有人说。
「怎么办的，与你什么相干，米克·希利（Mick Healy）？贾尔斯神父都满意了，对你这号人还不够么？闪开，让先生过去。」说着汤姆上尉粗粗地把米克推开，旁人便放我们进屋。「要不是总有人给他们递眼色，这会儿他们准把你撕成碎块，换一盅潘趣酒喝——真真会的。」
也许汤姆上尉把这股群情夸大了，想借此抬高他保护我的功劳；可我很清醒：我干下的是一桩顶危险的事，逃过的是顶险的一劫。
我见到贾尔斯神父时，他正靠坐在床上，柯万太太正拿山金车药酒卖力地揉他的肩膀。姑娘端着半盆同样的药酒站在一旁；我看得见神父的脖颈和两肩红得像一块生牛排。揉一下他便疼得抽一下，可他硬汉似的忍着。
「瞧，好汉来了。」贾尔斯神父说。「先停一两分钟吧，柯万太太，让我们垫口早餐——我敢打赌，格林先生睡了一夜，早饿了。但愿你找的铺位比昨夜我倒霉吵醒你时那张好，格林先生。瞧，那张还在给你留着呢，」他说，「你今夜若肯赏脸，听我一句劝：别让鸡毛蒜皮绊了你的睡梦。」

===Original===

“I hope, thin, the gintleman will contrive to suit hisself elsewhere,” said Mrs. Kirwan.
“He’ll be very welcome to take up his quarters here if he likes,” said the priest. “And why not? But, bedad, Sir, you’d better be a little more careful the next time you see a stranger using your clothes-brush. They are not so strict here in their ideas of *meum* and *tuum* as they are perhaps in England; and if you had broken my neck for so small an offence, I don’t know but what they’d have stretched your own.”
We then had breakfast together, Father Giles, Captain Tom, and I; and a very good breakfast we had. By degrees even Mrs. Kirwan was induced to look favourably at me, and before the day was over I found myself to be regarded as a friend in the establishment. And as a friend I certainly was regarded by Father Giles﻿—then, and for many a long day afterwards. And many times when he has, in years since that, but years nevertheless which are now long back, come over and visited me in my English home, he has told the story of the manner in which we first became acquainted. “When you find a gentleman asleep,” he would say, “always ask his leave before you take a liberty with his clothes-brush.”

===Chinese===

「那，我看这位先生还是想想法子，别处将就将就吧。」柯万太太说。
「他若愿意住这儿，我们竭诚欢迎，」神父说。「有什么不好呢？不过，老天在上，先生，下回再见外乡人用你的衣刷，你可得小心些。这里的人对『你的』『我的』，不像你们英国也许那样严究；你若为这么点小过摔断了我的脖子，我不敢说他们就不会吊断你的脖子。」
随后我们共进了早餐——贾尔斯神父、汤姆上尉和我；那是一顿很好的早餐。渐渐地，连柯万太太也肯对我另眼相看了；不到天黑，我发觉自己已被这店里当作朋友。而贾尔斯神父确也拿我当朋友——当时如此，此后漫长的岁月里也如此。多年以后——如今也算久远的年代了——他多次渡海到我英国的家里做客，总要讲起我们初识的这段经过。「见一位绅士睡着时，」他总说，「动他的衣刷之前，务必先讨他一句许可。」

## Lotta Schmidt / 洛塔·施密特
===Original===

As all the world knows, the old fortifications of Vienna have been pulled down﻿—the fortifications which used to surround the centre or kernel of the city; and the vast spaces thus thrown open and forming a broad ring in the middle of the town have not as yet been completely filled up with those new buildings and gardens which are to be there, and which, when there, will join the outside city and the inside city together, so as to make them into one homogeneous whole.
The work, however, is going on, and if the war which has come and passed has not swallowed everything appertaining to Austria into its maw, the ugly remnants of destruction will be soon carted away, and the old glacis will be made bright with broad pavements, and gilded railings, and well-built lofty mansions, and gardens beautiful with shrubs, and beautiful with turf also, if Austrian patience can make turf to grow beneath an Austrian sky.
On an evening of September, when there was still something left of daylight, at eight o’clock, two girls were walking together in the Burgplatz, or large open space which lies between the city palace of the emperor and the gate which passes thence from the old town out to the new town. Here at present stand two bronze equestrian statues, one of the Archduke Charles, and the other of Prince Eugene. And they were standing there also, both of them, when these two girls were walking round them; but that of the prince had not as yet been uncovered for the public.
There was coming a great gala day in the city, Emperors and empresses, archdukes and grand-dukes, with their archduchesses and grand-duchesses, and princes and ministers, were to be there, and the new statue of Prince Eugene was to be submitted to the art-critics of the world. There was very much thought at Vienna of the statue in those days. Well; since that, the statue has been submitted to the art-critics, and henceforward it will be thought of as little as any other huge bronze figure of a prince on horseback. A very ponderous prince is poised in an impossible position, on an enormous dray horse. But yet the thing is grand, and Vienna is so far a finer city in that it possesses the new equestrian statue of Prince Eugene.
“There will be such a crowd, Lotta,” said the elder of the two girls, “that I will not attempt it. Besides, we shall have plenty of time for seeing it afterwards.”

===Chinese===

众所周知，维也纳（Vienna）的老城墙已经拆了——那道从前环抱着城中心、即城市核心的工事；由此敞出的一大片空地，在城市正中形成一道宽阔的环带，如今还没有被那些规划中的新楼与花园填满；待它们建成，将把外城与内城连成一体，合成一个浑然的整体。
不过工程正在进行；只要那场来了又去的战争不曾把奥地利的一切都吞进肚里，破败的残土很快就会运走，老城郭将用宽阔的步道、镀金的栏杆、造得堂皇的高楼大厦装点得焕然明亮，还有美丽的花园——灌木美丽，草坪也要美丽，只要奥地利的耐心能叫草皮在奥地利的天空底下长起来。
九月的一个傍晚，天光还剩着一些，八点钟，两个姑娘正并肩走在城堡广场（Burgplatz）上——那是位于皇帝城宫与老城通往新城的大门之间的一片开阔地。如今那里立着两座青铜骑马像，一座是卡尔大公，一座是欧根亲王。这两个姑娘绕着它们走的时候，两座像也都立在那里；只是亲王那一座，当时还没有对公众揭幕。
城里要来一个大节庆的日子了。皇帝与皇后们，大公与大公们，连同大公夫人们，还有亲王与大臣们，都要到场，欧根亲王的新像将提交给全世界的艺术批评家品评。那些日子，维也纳对这座雕像想得极多。后来呢，雕像果然提交给了艺术批评家们，从此以后，它会同任何一尊骑在马上的巨型青铜亲王像一样，再没多少人惦记。一位极沉重的亲王，以一个不可能的姿势，跨在一匹巨大的驮马背上。可这东西终究气派，维也纳有了欧根亲王的新骑马像，也就此多了一分体面。
「人一定挤得很，洛塔，」两个姑娘中年长的那个说，「我不去凑这个热闹。再说，往后有的是工夫看它。」

===Original===

“Oh, yes,” said the younger girl, whose name was Lotta Schmidt; “of course we shall all have enough of the old prince for the rest of our lives; but I should like to see the grand people sitting up there on the benches; and there will be something nice in seeing the canopy drawn up. I think I will come. Herr Crippel has said that he would bring me, and get me a place.”
“I thought, Lotta, you had determined to have nothing more to say to Herr Crippel.”
“I don’t know what you mean by that. I like Herr Crippel very much, and he plays beautifully. Surely a girl may know a man old enough to be her father without having him thrown in her teeth as her lover.”
“Not when the man old enough to be her father has asked her to be his wife twenty times, as Herr Crippel has asked you. Herr Crippel would not give up his holiday afternoon to you if he thought it was to be for nothing.”
“There I think you are wrong, Marie. I believe Herr Crippel likes to have me with him simply because every gentleman likes to have a lady on such a day as that. Of course it is better than being alone. I don’t suppose he will say a word to me except to tell me who the people are, and to give me a glass of beer when it is over.”
It may be as well to explain at once, before we go any further, that Herr Crippel was a player on the violin, and that he led the musicians in the orchestra of the great beer-hall in the Volksgarten. Let it not be thought that because Herr Crippel exercised his art in a beer-hall therefore he was a musician of no account. No one will think so who has once gone to a Vienna beer-hall, and listened to such music as is there provided for the visitors.
The two girls, Marie Weber and Lotta Schmidt, belonged to an establishment in which gloves were sold in the Graben, and now, having completed their work for the day﻿—and indeed their work for the week, for it was Saturday evening﻿—had come out for such recreation as the evening might afford them. And on behalf of these two girls, as to one of whom at least I am much interested, I must beg my English readers to remember that manners and customs differ much in Vienna from those which prevail in London.

===Chinese===

「哦，去，」年幼的那个说，她名叫洛塔·施密特（Lotta Schmidt）；「往后一辈子，这老亲王我们自然看得够够的；可我想看看那些大人物坐在高台上的样子；还有华盖拉起来的时候，也有趣。我想我会去。克里佩尔先生说了，他带我去，替我占位子。」
「我还当，洛塔，你拿定了主意，再不理克里佩尔先生了呢。」
「我不懂你这话什么意思。我很喜欢克里佩尔先生，他演奏得美极了。一个姑娘认识一个年纪做得她父亲的男人，难道就得被人拿他当情人嚼舌根吗？」
「可这年纪做得她父亲的男人，已经求她做妻子求了二十回，克里佩尔先生就是这样求你的。克里佩尔先生若是想透了白费工夫，他也不会把歇工的下午整个儿搭给你。」
「这我可说你错了，玛丽。我看克里佩尔先生乐意带着我，不过是因为那样的日子里，哪位先生都乐意身边有位女士罢了。总比一个人强。我料想他除了指给我看那些人物都是谁、散场时给我杯啤酒，一句多余的话也不会说。」
趁早说明一句为好，免得往下走岔：克里佩尔先生（Herr Crippel）是拉小提琴的，在人民公园（Volksgarten）大啤酒馆的乐池里当乐队首席。请别以为克里佩尔先生在啤酒馆里卖艺，就算不得什么音乐家。谁只要进过一回维也纳的啤酒馆、听过那里待客的音乐，就不会这样想。
这两个姑娘，玛丽·韦伯（Marie Weber）和洛塔·施密特，同在格拉本街一家卖手套的铺子里做事；此刻做完了当天的活——其实是一周的活，因为是礼拜六傍晚——便出来寻这傍晚能给他们什么消遣。为了这两个姑娘——其中至少有一位，我是顶关心的——我必须请我的英国读者记着：维也纳的风俗习惯，同伦敦（London）通行的，差得很远。

===Original===

Were I to tell of two London shop girls going out into the streets after their day’s work, to see what friends and what amusement the fortune of the evening might send to them, I should be supposed to be speaking of young women as to whom it would be better that I should be silent; but these girls in Vienna were doing simply that which all their friends would expect and wish them to do. That they should have some amusement to soften the rigours of long days of work was recognised to be necessary; and music, beer, dancing, with the conversation of young men, are thought in Vienna to be the natural amusements of young women, and in Vienna are believed to be innocent.
The Viennese girls are almost always attractive in their appearance, without often coming up to our English ideas of prettiness. Sometimes they do fully come up to our English idea of beauty. They are generally dark, tall, light in figure, with bright eyes, which are however very unlike the bright eyes of Italy, and which constantly remind the traveller that his feet are carrying him eastward in Europe. But perhaps the peculiar characteristic in their faces which most strikes a stranger is a certain look of almost fierce independence, as though they had recognised the necessity, and also acquired the power, of standing alone, and of protecting themselves. I know no young women by whom the assistance of a man’s arm seems to be so seldom required as the young women of Vienna. They almost invariably dress well, generally preferring black, or colours that are very dark; and they wear hats that are, I believe, of Hungarian origin, very graceful in form, but which are peculiarly calculated to add something to that assumed savageness of independence of which I have spoken.
Both the girls who were walking in the Burgplatz were of the kind that I have attempted to describe. Marie Weber was older, and not so tall, and less attractive than her friend; but as her position in life was fixed, and as she was engaged to marry a cutter of diamonds, I will not endeavour to interest the reader specially in her personal appearance. Lotta Schmidt was essentially a Viennese pretty girl of the special Viennese type. She was tall and slender, but still had none of that appearance of feminine weakness which is so common among us with girls who are tall and slim.

===Chinese===

我若讲两个伦敦女店工下了工上街去，看晚间的运气给他们送来什么朋友、什么消遣，人家准以为我说的是那种顶好闭口不提的年轻女人；可维也纳的这两个姑娘做的，不过是亲朋都盼着她们做、乐意她们做的事。劳苦的漫长日子之外总该有些消遣缓缓乏劲，这是公认的必需；而音乐、啤酒、跳舞，加上同小伙子们说说话，在维也纳人看来就是年轻女子的正经消遣，而且维也纳人相信这是清白的。
维也纳的姑娘模样几乎总是讨人喜欢的，虽然往往够不上我们英国人心里的「俊」。有时她们也全然够得上我们英国人说的「美」。她们多半深色头发、高挑身材、体态轻盈，一双亮眼睛——可那亮眼睛同意大利的亮眼睛又大不一样，时时提醒旅人：他的脚步正把他带向欧洲的东边。不过她们脸上最教陌生人注目的特别之处，怕是那股近乎剽悍的独立之气，仿佛她们既认清了独自站立、自己保护自己的必要，也练出了这份本事。依我看，哪里的年轻女子也不像维也纳的年轻女子这样少用得着男人搀一把。她们几乎个个穿戴齐整，多半爱穿黑的或极深的颜色；头上戴的帽子，我想是匈牙利样式的，形态极飘逸，偏偏又最能给我说到的那份装出来的剽悍独立再添几分。
在城堡广场上散步的这两个姑娘，都属于我试图描写的这一类。玛丽·韦伯年长些，个子矮些，人不及她朋友惹眼；但她的人生地位已定，聘了一位钻石切割匠，我在此就不必特意费读者的心在她的品貌上了。洛塔·施密特则是不折不扣的维也纳美人，正是维也纳型的。她高挑纤瘦，却没有我们这里高瘦姑娘常有的那副女子家的单薄相。

===Original===

She walked as though she had plenty both of strength and courage for all purposes of life without the assistance of any extraneous aid. Her hair was jet-black, and very plentiful, and was worn in long curls which were brought round from the back of her head over her shoulders. Her eyes were blue﻿—dark blue﻿—and were clear and deep rather than bright. Her nose was well formed, but somewhat prominent, and made you think at the first glance of the tribes of Israel. But yet no observer of the physiognomy of races would believe for half a moment that Lotta Schmidt was a Jewess. Indeed, the type of form which I am endeavouring to describe is in truth as far removed from the Jewish type as it is from the Italian; and it has no connection whatever with that which we ordinarily conceive to be the German type. But, overriding everything in her personal appearance, in her form, countenance, and gait, was that singular fierceness of independence, as though she were constantly asserting that she would never submit herself to the inconvenience of feminine softness. And yet Lotta Schmidt was a simple girl, with a girl’s heart, looking forward to find all that she was to have of human happiness in the love of some man, and expecting and hoping to do her duty as a married woman and the mother of a family. Nor would she have been at all coy in saying as much had the subject of her life’s prospects become matter of conversation in any company; no more than one lad would be coy in saying that he hoped to be a doctor, or another in declaring a wish for the army.
When the two girls had walked twice round the hoarding within which stood all those tons of bronze which were intended to represent Prince Eugene, they crossed over the centre of the Burgplatz, passed under the other equestrian statue, and came to the gate leading into the Volksgarten. There, just at the entrance, they were overtaken by a man with a fiddle-case under his arm, who raised his hat to them, and then shook hands with both of them.
“Ladies,” he said, “are you coming in to hear a little music? We will do our best.”
“Herr Crippel always does well,” said Marie Weber. “There is never any doubt when one comes to hear him.”
“Marie, why do you flatter him?” said Lotta.
“I do not say half to his face that you said just now behind his back,” said Marie.
“And what did she say of me behind my back?” said Herr Crippel.

===Chinese===

她走路的样子，仿佛人生种种用途，她的力气和胆量都尽够，无须任何外力相助。她的头发乌黑浓密，梳成长卷，从脑后拢过来披在肩上。她的眼睛是蓝的——深蓝——清澈深沉而不流于明亮。她鼻子端正，却略嫌突出，第一眼教你想起以色列的众支派。可任何一个留心种族面貌的人，也决不会有一刻疑心洛塔·施密特是犹太女子。其实，我努力描写的这个形体类型，同犹太型相去之远，不亚于同意大利型；同我们寻常认作的日耳曼型，更毫无干系。然而压倒她周身一切——她的身段、容貌、步态——的，是那股特异的剽悍独立之气，仿佛她时刻在申明：她决不受女子家温柔的累。然而洛塔·施密特又是个单纯的姑娘，怀着一颗姑娘的心，指望人生全部的幸福就在某个男人的爱里，并且一心指望、盼着做个贤妻、做个良母。她的人生前程若在哪个体面场合成了话题，她也不讳言这一点——不比一个小伙子讳言自己想当医生，或另一个宣称想从军更害臊。
两个姑娘绕着围板走了两圈——板里立着那好几吨青铜，都是用来铸欧根亲王的——随后穿过城堡广场中央，从另一座骑马像底下走过，来到通往人民公园的大门。就在门口，一个腋下夹着琴匣的男人赶上了她们；他举了举帽，同两个姑娘握了手。
「两位女士，」他说，「进来听点音乐吗？我们尽力演奏好。」
「克里佩尔先生向来演奏得好，」玛丽·韦伯说。「来听他的，从不用犯嘀咕。」
「玛丽，你干吗奉承他？」洛塔说。
「我当面说的，还不及你刚才背后说的一半呢。」玛丽说。
「她背后说我什么来着？」克里佩尔先生问。

===Original===

He smiled as he asked the question, or attempted to smile, but it was easy to see that he was too much in earnest. He blushed up to his eyes, and there was a slight trembling motion in his hands as he stood with one of them pressed upon the other.
As Marie did not answer at the moment, Lotta replied for her.
“I will tell you what I said behind your back. I said that Herr Crippel had the firmest hand upon a bow, and the surest fingers among the strings, in all Vienna﻿—when his mind was not woolgathering. Marie, is not that true?”
“I do not remember anything about the woolgathering,” said Marie.
“I hope I shall not be woolgathering tonight; but I shall doubtless;﻿—I shall doubtless﻿—for I shall be thinking of your judgment. Shall I get you seats at once? There; you are just before me. You see I am not coward enough to fly from my critics,” and he placed them to sit at a little marble table, not far from the front of the low orchestra in the foremost place in which he would have to take his stand.
“Many thanks, Herr Crippel,” said Lotta. “I will make sure of a third chair, as a friend is coming.”
“Oh, a friend!” said he; and he looked sad, and all his sprightliness was gone.
“Marie’s friend,” said Lotta, laughing. “Do not you know Carl Stobel?”
Then the musician became bright and happy again. “I would have got two more chairs if you would have let me; one for the fraulein’s sake, and one for his own. And I will come down presently, and you shall present me, if you will be so very kind.”
Marie Weber smiled and thanked him, and declared that she should be very proud;﻿—and the leader of the band went up into his place.
“I wish he had not placed us here,” said Lotta.
“And why not?”
“Because Fritz is coming.”
“No!”
“But he is.”
“And why did you not tell me?”
“Because I did not wish to be speaking of him. Of course you understand why I did not tell you. I would rather it should seem that he came of his own account﻿—with Carl. Ha, ha!” Carl Stobel was the diamond-cutter to whom Marie Weber was betrothed. “I should not have told you now﻿—only that I am disarranged by what Herr Crippel has done.”
“Had we not better go﻿—or at least move our seats? We can make any excuse afterwards.”
“No,” said Lotta. “I will not seem to run away from him. I have nothing to be ashamed of. If I choose to keep company with Fritz Planken, that should be nothing to Herr Crippel.”

===Chinese===

他问这话时笑了笑，或者说想笑一笑，可一眼便看得出他过分认真了。他红脸一直红到眼边，站在那里一只手压着另一只手，手上有微微的颤动。
玛丽一时没有答话，洛塔便替她接了。
「我把背后说的告诉你吧。我说，全维也纳，弓子握得最稳、琴弦上指头最有准头的，数克里佩尔先生——只要他心思不走神。玛丽，这话不对吗？」
「走神不走神的，我可不记得了。」玛丽说。
「但愿今晚我不走神；只怕多半要走——多半要走——因为我总要想念你们的评判。这就替你们占座？好，你们正好赶在前头。你们看，我还不至于胆小得躲开我的批评家。」说着他把她们安顿在一张小理石桌边坐下，离乐池前沿不远——那是他等会儿要登台站定的最前排。
「多谢，克里佩尔先生，」洛塔说。「我再占一把椅子，有位朋友要来。」
「哦，一位朋友！」他说；他神色一黯，那点活泼劲儿全没了。
「玛丽的朋友，」洛塔笑着说。「卡尔·施托贝尔你还不认得？」
音乐家随即又欢喜起来。「你们早说，我就多搬两把椅子了；一把为小姐，一把为他本人。回头我就下来，你们给我引见，肯不肯赏这个脸？」
玛丽·韦伯笑着谢了他，说那才是她的光荣呢——乐队首席便上了他的台。
「我倒愿意他没把我们安在这儿。」洛塔说。
「怎么？」
「因为弗里茨要来。」
「不会吧！」
「他要来。」
「那你怎么不告诉我？」
「因为我不愿意提起他。你不明白我为什么不说吗？我情愿显得是他自己要来的——同卡尔一道。哈，哈！」卡尔·施托贝尔（Carl Stobel）就是玛丽·韦伯聘的那位钻石切割匠。「我这会儿原也不说——只是克里佩尔先生这一来，把我的安排全搅了。」
「咱们要不要走——或者至少挪挪座？过后找个由头就是了。」
「不，」洛塔说。「我不要显得躲他。我又没什么见不得人的。我乐意同弗里茨·普兰肯做伴，关克里佩尔先生什么事。」

===Original===

“But you might have told him.”
“No; I could not tell him. And I am not sure Fritz is coming either. He said he would come with Carl if he had time. Never mind; let us be happy now. If a bad time comes by-and-by, we must make the best of it.”
Then the music began, and, suddenly, as the first note of a fiddle was heard, every voice in the great beer-hall of the Volksgarten became silent. Men sat smoking, with their long beer-glasses before them, and women sat knitting, with their long beer-glasses also before them, but not a word was spoken. The waiters went about with silent feet, but even orders for beer were not given, and money was not received. Herr Crippel did his best, working with his wand as carefully﻿—and I may say as accurately﻿—as a leader in a fashionable opera-house in London or Paris. But every now and then, in the course of the piece, he would place his fiddle to his shoulder and join in the performance. There was hardly one there in the hall, man or woman, boy or girl, who did not know, from personal knowledge and judgment, that Herr Crippel was doing his work very well.
“Excellent, was it not?” said Marie.
“Yes; he is a musician. Is it not a pity he should be so bald?” said Lotta.
“He is not so very bald,” said Marie.
“I should not mind his being bald so much, if he did not try to cover his old head with the side hairs. If he would cut off those loose straggling locks, and declare himself to be bald at once, he would be ever so much better. He would look to be fifty then. He looks sixty now.”
“What matters his age? He is forty-five, just; for I know. And he is a good man.”
“What has his goodness to do with it?”
“A great deal. His old mother wants for nothing, and he makes two hundred florins a month. He has two shares in the summer theatre. I know it.”
“Bah! what is all that when he will plaster his hair over his old bald head?”
“Lotta, I am ashamed of you.” But at this moment the further expression of Marie’s anger was stopped by the entrance of the diamond-cutter; and as he was alone, both the girls received him very pleasantly.

===Chinese===

「可你本可以告诉他。」
「不；我不能告诉他。再说弗里茨来不来，我也拿不准。他说若有工夫，同卡尔一道来。别管了；咱们先痛快一会儿。往后坏时辰来了，再想办法对付。」
音乐开始了；提琴第一个音符一响，人民公园大啤酒馆里千百个嗓门顿时全静了下来。男人们坐着抽烟，面前摆着长长的啤酒杯；女人们坐着织毛线，面前也摆着长长的啤酒杯；可谁也不说一个字。侍者们蹑着脚走动，连叫啤酒都不点了，钱也不收了。克里佩尔先生尽了全力，指挥棒挥得一丝不苟——我可以说，同伦敦或巴黎（Paris）一流歌剧院的指挥一样有准头。可一曲之中，他时时把提琴架上肩头，亲自加入演奏。馆里的男男女女、大大小小，几乎个个凭亲身的见识，都晓得克里佩尔先生干得非常出色。
「好极了，是不是？」玛丽说。
「是的；他是音乐家。可惜他秃得那么厉害。」洛塔说。
「也没秃得那么厉害。」玛丽说。
「他若不拿边上的头发去盖那颗老脑袋，秃就秃些我也不在乎。他若肯把那几绺披散的长毛铰掉，痛痛快快认了自己秃，那还强得多。那样他看着像五十岁。现在看着像六十。」
「年纪有什么要紧？他刚四十五，我知道的。而且他是个好人。」
「他好不好的，有什么相干？」
「相干大了。他的老母亲什么都不缺；他每月挣两百盾。夏日剧院里他还有两份股。我知道的。」
「呸！他偏要把头发抹在那颗秃脑袋上，说这些顶什么用？」
「洛塔，我都替你害臊。」可玛丽这一腔怒话没得往下说——钻石切割匠进门了；他既是一个人来的，两个姑娘都欢欢喜喜迎接他。

===Original===

We must give Lotta her due, and declare that, as things had gone, she would much prefer now that Fritz should stay away, though Fritz Planken was as handsome a young fellow as there was in Vienna, and one who dressed with the best taste, and danced so that no one could surpass him, and could speak French, and was confidential clerk at one of the largest hotels in Vienna, and was a young man acknowledged to be of much general importance﻿—and had, moreover, in plain language, declared his love for Lotta Schmidt. But Lotta would not willingly give unnecessary pain to Herr Crippel, and she was generously glad when Carl Stobel, the diamond-cutter, came by himself. Then there was a second and third piece played, and after that Herr Crippel came down, according to promise, and was presented to Marie’s lover.
“Ladies,” said he, “I hope I have not gathered wool.”
“You have surpassed yourself,” said Lotta.
“At woolgathering?” said Herr Crippel.
“At sending us out of this world into another,” said Lotta.
“Ah! go into no other world but this,” said Herr Crippel, “lest I should not be able to follow you.” And then he went away again to his post.
Before another piece had been commenced, Lotta saw Fritz Planken enter the door. He stood for a moment gazing round the hall, with his cane in his hand and his hat on his head, looking for the party which he intended to join. Lotta did not say a word, nor would she turn her eyes towards him. She would not recognise him if it were possible to avoid it. But he soon saw her, and came up to the table at which they were sitting. When Lotta was getting the third chair for Marie’s lover, Herr Crippel, in his gallantry, had brought a fourth, and now Fritz occupied the chair which the musician had placed there. Lotta, as she perceived this, was sorry that it should be so. She could not even dare to look up to see what effect this new arrival would have upon the leader of the band.
The newcomer was certainly a handsome young man, such a one as inflicts unutterable agonies on the hearts of the Herr Crippels of the world. His boots shone like mirrors, and fitted his feet like gloves. There was something in the make and set of his trousers which Herr Crippel, looking at them, as he could not help looking at them, was quite unable to understand.

===Chinese===

我们得替洛塔说句公道话：照眼下的情形，她其实巴不得弗里茨别来——虽然弗里茨·普兰肯（Fritz Planken）是维也纳数得着的美少年，穿戴的品味数一数二，舞跳得无人能出其右，还会说法语，在维也纳最大的一家旅馆当机要账房，是公认前程远大的青年——而且，明说了吧，他已经向洛塔·施密特表过了爱情。可洛塔不愿平白教克里佩尔先生难受，所以钻石切割匠卡尔·施托贝尔独自来时，她由衷地高兴。随后又奏了第二支、第三支曲子；奏罢，克里佩尔先生依着前约走下台来，被引见给玛丽的未婚夫。
「女士们，」他说，「我但愿刚才没走神。」
「您超出自己平常的水准了。」洛塔说。
「走神走得超水准？」克里佩尔先生说。
「是把我们从这个世界送进了另一个世界。」洛塔说。
「啊！除了这个世界，哪个世界也别去，」克里佩尔先生说，「免得我跟不上你们。」说罢他又回他的岗位去了。
下一支曲子还没开奏，洛塔望见弗里茨·普兰肯进了门。他手拄手杖、头戴帽子，站了片刻，环视整个大厅，寻找他要入伙的那一桌。洛塔一言不发，也不把眼睛转向他。能不认他，她就不认。可他很快就望见了她，径直朝她们坐的桌子走来。洛塔方才给玛丽的未婚夫搬第三把椅子时，克里佩尔先生献殷勤，又搬来了第四把；此刻弗里茨坐的，正是音乐家安放的那把。洛塔一觉察这个，心里就懊恼。她连抬头都不敢，看乐队首席见了这新来的是个什么神色。
新来的确是位美少年，正是那种教天下克里佩尔先生们心头受着说不出的煎熬的人物。他的靴子亮得像镜子，合脚得像手套。他裤子的裁剪与熨贴，克里佩尔先生瞧着——他忍不住要瞧——怎么也不明白是怎么做出来的。

===Original===

Even twenty years ago, Herr Crippel’s trousers, as Herr Crippel very well knew, had never looked like that. And Fritz Planken wore a blue frock coat with silk lining to the breast, which seemed to have come from some tailor among the gods. And he had on primrose gloves, and round his neck a bright pink satin handkerchief joined by a ring, which gave a richness of colouring to the whole thing which nearly killed Herr Crippel, because he could not but acknowledge that the colouring was good. And then the hat! And when the hat was taken off for a moment, then the hair﻿—perfectly black, and silky as a raven’s wing, just waving with one curl! And when Fritz put up his hand, and ran his fingers through his locks, their richness and plenty and beauty were conspicuous to all beholders. Herr Crippel, as he saw it, involuntarily dashed his hand up to his own pate, and scratched his straggling, lanky hairs from off his head.
“You are coming to Sperl’s tomorrow, of course?” said Fritz to Lotta. Now Sperl’s is a great establishment for dancing in the Leopoldstadt, which is always open of a Sunday evening, and which Lotta Schmidt was in the habit of attending with much regularity. It was here she had become acquainted with Fritz. And certainly to dance with Fritz was to dance indeed! Lotta, too, was a beautiful dancer. To a Viennese such as Lotta Schmidt, dancing is a thing of serious importance. It was a misfortune to her to have to dance with a bad dancer, as it is to a great whist-player among us to sit down with a bad partner. Oh, what she had suffered more than once when Herr Crippel had induced her to stand up with him!
“Yes; I shall go. Marie, you will go?”
“I do not know,” said Marie.
“You will make her go, Carl; will you not?” said Lotta.
“She promised me yesterday, as I understood,” said Carl.
“Of course we will all be there,” said Fritz, somewhat grandly; “and I will give a supper for four.”
Then the music began again, and the eyes of all of them became fixed upon Herr Crippel. It was unfortunate that they should have been placed so fully before him as it was impossible that he should avoid seeing them. As he stood up with his violin to his shoulder, his eyes were fixed on Fritz Planken and Fritz Planken’s boots, and coat, and hat, and hair. And as he drew his bow over the strings he was thinking of his own boots and of his own hair.

===Chinese===

即便二十年前，克里佩尔先生的裤子——这层他自己知道得很清楚——也从来没那副模样。弗里茨·普兰肯还穿一件蓝色长礼服，胸前衬着绸里，仿佛出自某位天神裁缝之手。他戴柠檬黄手套，颈上一条鲜粉红缎巾，用指环扣着；这一身的颜色，富丽得几乎要了克里佩尔先生的命——因为他不能不承认，这配色就是好。还有那顶帽子！帽子摘下来片刻，还有那头发——纯黑，亮得像乌鸦的翅膀，正正好卷起一波！弗里茨抬手，手指插进发间一拢，那份丰厚、茂美，众人都看得见。克里佩尔先生看着，不由自主把手往自己头顶上一拍，把他那几绺披散稀拉的长发从头上搔开。
「明天你当然来斯佩尔？」弗里茨对洛塔说。斯佩尔（Sperl's）是利奥波德城（Leopoldstadt）一家大舞场，礼拜日晚上照例开放，洛塔·施密特向来是常去不移的。她也就是在这里认识弗里茨的。同弗里茨跳舞，那才真是跳舞！洛塔自己也是位美妙的舞伴。对洛塔·施密特这样的维也纳人，跳舞是件郑重的大事。同蹩脚的舞伴下场，于她是桩不幸，好比我们这儿一位打惠斯特牌的高手偏偏对上了蹩脚的搭档。唉，克里佩尔先生几次三番劝她下场那阵子，她受过多少罪！
「去的。我去。玛丽，你去吗？」
「说不准。」玛丽说。
「你会让她去的，卡尔；对不对？」洛塔说。
「照我昨天听她说的，她答应了。」卡尔说。
「咱们自然都到，」弗里茨说，口气颇阔气；「我请四位的宵夜。」
随后音乐又起，他们的眼睛都落到了克里佩尔先生身上。不幸他们坐的位置正对着他，他想不看他们也办不到。他提琴架肩站着，眼睛盯住弗里茨·普兰肯，和他那靴子、外套、帽子和头发。弓子拉着弦，心里想的却是自己的靴子、自己的头发。

===Original===

Fritz was sitting, leaning forward in his chair, so that he could look up into Lotta’s face, and he was playing with a little amber-headed cane, and every now and then he whispered a word. Herr Crippel could hardly play a note. In very truth he was woolgathering. His hand became unsteady, and every instrument was more or less astray.
“Your old friend is making a mess of it tonight,” said Fritz to Lotta. “I hope he has not taken a glass too much of schnapps.”
“He never does anything of the kind,” said Lotta, angrily. “He never did such a thing in his life.”
“He is playing awfully bad,” said Fritz.
“I never heard him play better in my life than he has played tonight,” said Lotta.
“His hand is tired. He is getting old,” said Fritz. Then Lotta moved her chair and drew herself back, and was determined that Marie and Carl should see that she was angry with her young lover. In the meantime the piece of music had been finished, and the audience had shown their sense of the performer’s inferiority by withdrawing those plaudits which they were so ready to give when they were pleased.
After this some other musician led for awhile, and then Herr Crippel had to come forward to play a solo. And on this occasion the violin was not to be his instrument. He was a great favourite among the lovers of music in Vienna, not only because he was good at the fiddle and because with his bow in his hand he could keep a band of musicians together, but also as a player on the zither. It was not often nowadays that he would take his zither to the music-hall in the Volksgarten; for he would say that he had given up that instrument; that he now played it only in private; that it was not fit for a large hall, as a single voice, the scraping of a foot, would destroy its music. And Herr Crippel was a man who had his fancies and his fantasies, and would not always yield to entreaty. But occasionally he would send his zither down to the public hall; and in the programme for this evening there had been put forth that Herr Crippel’s zither would be there and that Herr Crippel would perform. And now the zither was brought forward, and a chair was put for the zitherist, and Herr Crippel stood for a moment behind his chair and bowed. Lotta glanced up at him, and could see that he was very pale. She could even see that the perspiration stood upon his brow.

===Chinese===

弗里茨坐在椅子里，身子前倾，好仰看洛塔的脸；他手里耍着一支琥珀头的小手杖，不时凑近说一句悄悄话。克里佩尔先生几乎拉不成一个音了。说真的，他是走神了。他的手发飘，每件乐器都或多或少跟着跑调。
「你那位老朋友今晚可砸锅了，」弗里茨对洛塔说。「别是果子烧酒多喝了一杯吧。」
「他从来不干那种事，」洛塔怒道。「他平生没干过那种事。」
「他演奏得糟透了。」弗里茨说。
「我平生没听他演奏得比今晚更好过。」洛塔说。
「他手累了。他上了年纪了。」弗里茨说。洛塔随即挪了挪椅子，把身子往后一撤，决意让玛丽和卡尔看出她在生这位年轻情郎的气。这时那支曲子奏完了；听众觉出演奏者失了水准，便把方才那副随时奉送的热烈喝彩收了回去。
此后换了别的乐师领了一阵，随后克里佩尔先生又得上前独奏。这一回，提琴可不作他的乐器了。他在维也纳的爱乐者中间素得人心，不光因为提琴拉得好、弓子在手能压得住一队乐师，还因为他是弹齐特尔琴的妙手。如今他不常把齐特尔琴带进人民公园的音乐厅了；他说他已经撂下那件乐器了，如今只在私下弹；它上不得大场面，一个人的嗓门、一只鞋底蹭地，就能毁了它的音乐。克里佩尔先生又是个有脾气有癖性的人，不总是肯依人恳求。可他偶尔还是把齐特尔琴送到公开的厅里去；今晚的节目单上便登了，说克里佩尔先生的齐特尔琴将到场，克里佩尔先生将亲自演奏。此刻琴搬上来了，给琴师放了一把椅子；克里佩尔先生在椅后站了片刻，鞠了一躬。洛塔抬眼望他，看得出他脸色极白。她甚至看得出，汗珠子正站在他的额头上。

===Original===

She knew that he was trembling, and that he would have given almost his zither itself to be quit of his promised performance for that night. But she knew also that he would make the attempt.
“What! the zither?” said Fritz. “He will break down as sure as he is a living man.”
“Let us hope not,” said Carl Stobel.
“I love to hear him play the zither better than anything,” said Lotta.
“It used to be very good,” said Fritz; “but everybody says he has lost his touch. When a man has the slightest feeling of nervousness he is done for the zither.”
“H﻿—sh; let him have his chance at any rate,” said Marie.
Reader, did you ever hear the zither? When played, as it is sometimes played in Vienna, it combines all the softest notes of the human voice. It sings to you of love and then wails to you of disappointed love, till it fills you with a melancholy from which there is no escaping﻿—from which you never wish to escape. It speaks to you as no other instrument ever speaks, and reveals to you with wonderful eloquence the sadness in which it delights. It produces a luxury of anguish, a fullness of the satisfaction of imaginary woe, a realisation of the mysterious delights of romance, which no words can ever thoroughly supply. While the notes are living, while the music is still in the air, the ear comes to covet greedily every atom of tone which the instrument will produce, so that the slightest extraneous sound becomes an offence. The notes sink and sink so low and low, with their soft sad wail of delicious woe, that the listener dreads that something will be lost in the struggle of listening. There seems to come some lethargy on his sense of hearing, which he fears will shut out from his brain the last, lowest, sweetest strain, the very pearl of the music, for which he has been watching with all the intensity of prolonged desire. And then the zither is silent, and there remains a fond memory together with a deep regret.
Herr Crippel seated himself on his stool and looked once or twice round about upon the room almost with dismay. Then he struck his zither, uncertainly, weakly, and commenced the prelude of his piece. But Lotta thought that she had never heard so sweet a sound. When he paused after a few strokes there was a noise of applause in the room, of applause intended to encourage by commemorating past triumphs.

===Chinese===

她知道他在发抖，知道他几乎肯搭上他那把齐特尔琴，只求免去当晚许下的演出。可她也知道，他还是要上场。
「怎么！齐特尔琴？」弗里茨说。「他准得砸，像他是活人一样准。」
「但愿不会。」卡尔·施托贝尔说。
「我爱听他弹齐特尔琴，胜过一切。」洛塔说。
「从前是很好，」弗里茨说；「可人人都说他指头不行了。弹齐特尔的人，心里稍有一点儿慌，就完了。」
「嘘——让他试试再说。」玛丽说。
读者，你可曾听过齐特尔琴？弹得好的时候——维也纳有时就弹得那样好——它兼有人声里一切最柔的音。它对你唱爱情，又对你哭诉失恋，直教人满心一种逃不掉的忧郁——一种人从不想逃的忧郁。它对你说话，是任何别的乐器都不曾有过的说法；它用惊人的口才，向你吐露它所钟爱的那种哀愁。它酿出一种苦恼里的奢侈，一种想象之悲的饱满的满足，一种神秘浪漫之乐的真切实现——这些，言语是永远供不全的。音符还活着、乐声还悬在空气里的时候，耳朵便贪婪地渴求这乐器要吐出的每一个音的原子，于是顶细的一点杂响都成了冒犯。那乐音一沉再沉、一低再低，带着柔婉凄恻的、美妙的哀声，听的人唯恐在倾耳的挣扎里失落了什么。听觉上仿佛罩来一阵麻痹，人生怕这麻痹要把那最后一缕、最低也最甜的乐音——音乐的明珠，他凝神久候的那一颗——关在脑子外面。然后齐特尔琴静了，留下一点眷恋的记忆，和一腔深深的怅惘。
克里佩尔先生在琴凳上坐下，一两次惶惶地四下望了望大厅。然后他拨响齐特尔琴——迟疑地、虚弱地——起了他那支曲子的前奏。可在洛塔听来，她从没听过这样甜的琴音。他拨了几声便停了停，厅里响起一片喝彩，那是追念往日的辉煌、有意鼓劲的喝彩。

The musician looked again away from his music to his audience, and his eyes caught the eyes of the girl he loved; and his gaze fell also upon the face of the handsome, well-dressed, young Adonis who was by her side.
He, Herr Crippel the musician, could never make himself look like that; he could make no slightest approach to that outward triumph. But then, he could play the zither, and Fritz Planken could only play with his cane! He would do what he could! He would play his best! He had once almost resolved to get up and declare that he was too tired that evening to do justice to his instrument. But there was an insolence of success about his rival’s hat and trousers which spirited him on to the fight. He struck his zither again, and they who understood him and his zither knew that he was in earnest.
The old men who had listened to him for the last twenty years declared that he had never played as he played on that night. At first he was somewhat bolder, somewhat louder than was his wont; as though he were resolved to go out of his accustomed track; but, after awhile, he gave that up; that was simply the effect of nervousness, and was continued only while the timidity remained present with him. But he soon forgot everything but his zither and his desire to do it justice. The attention of all present soon became so close that you might have heard a pin fall. Even Fritz sat perfectly still, with his mouth open, and forgot to play with his cane. Lotta’s eyes were quickly full of tears, and before long they were rolling down her cheeks. Herr Crippel, though he did not know that he looked at her, was aware that it was so. Then came upon them all there an ecstasy of delicious sadness. As I have said before, every ear was struggling that no softest sound might escape unheard. And then at last the zither was silent, and no one could have marked the moment when it had ceased to sing.
For a few moments there was perfect silence in the room, and the musician still kept his seat with his face turned upon his instrument. He knew well that he had succeeded, that his triumph had been complete, and every moment that the applause was suspended was an added jewel to his crown.

乐师的目光又从琴上移向听众，正撞上他爱的那姑娘的眼睛；也落在她身旁那位衣冠楚楚的美少年阿多尼斯脸上。
他，音乐家克里佩尔，永远打扮不出那副模样；那外表的得意，他连一丝一毫也挨不上边。可是——他弹得齐特尔琴，弗里茨·普兰肯只会耍手杖！他要尽他的力！他要弹他的绝技！方才他几乎打定主意起身宣布：今晚太乏，对不住他这乐器。可他那对手的帽子和裤子上那股得势的骄气，偏偏激他应战。他又拨响齐特尔琴，懂他、也懂他齐特尔琴的人，都知道他是动真格的了。
二十年来听他演奏的老听众们说，他从没弹得像今晚这样过。起初他比素常更放、更响，仿佛决意走出惯常的路子；可过了一阵，那股劲儿撂下了——那不过是心慌的缘故，怯意还在身上时就那样。但他很快忘了一切，只记得他的齐特尔琴，和不负此琴的心愿。满场听众的注意凝到了这样的地步：一根针落地也听得见。连弗里茨也端坐不动，张着嘴，忘了耍他的手杖。洛塔的眼睛很快噙满了泪，不多时便顺着腮滚下来。克里佩尔先生虽不知道自己望着她，却晓得是这样。随后，一种美妙的哀愁的迷醉罩住了满场的人。如我先前所说，每一只耳朵都在奋力挣扎，不肯放走一丝最轻的乐音。终于，齐特尔琴静了；它是哪个瞬间停止歌唱的，谁也说不出。
厅里静了片刻，乐师仍坐在凳上，脸对着他的琴。他清楚自己成功了，成功得圆满；喝彩每迟一刻，他王冠上的宝石便又添一颗。

“To be sure I did.”

Fritz, as he walked home by himself, was in doubt as to the course which it would be his duty as a man to pursue in reference to the lady whom he loved.

===Original===

He had distinctly heard that lady ask an old admirer of hers to go to Sperl’s and dance with her; and yet, within ten minutes afterwards, she had peremptorily commanded him not to dance with another girl! Now, Fritz Planken had a very good opinion of himself, as he was well entitled to have, and was quite aware that other pretty girls besides Lotta Schmidt were within his reach. He did not receive two hundred florins a month, as did Herr Crippel, but then he was five-and-twenty instead of five-and-forty; and, in the matter of money, too, he was doing pretty well. He did love Lotta Schmidt. It would not be easy for him to part with her. But she, too, loved him, as he told himself, and she would hardly push matters to extremities. At any rate, he would not submit to a threat. He would dance with Adela Bruhl, at Sperl’s. He thought, at least, that when the time should come he would find it well to dance with her.
Sperl’s dancing saloon, in the Tabor Strasse, is a great institution at Vienna. It is open always of a Sunday evening, and dancing there commences at ten, and is continued till two or three o’clock in the morning. There are two large rooms, in one of which the dancers dance, and in the other the dancers and visitors who do not dance, eat, and drink, and smoke continually. But the most wonderful part of Sperl’s establishment is this, that there is nothing there to offend anyone. Girls dance and men smoke, and there is eating and drinking, and everybody is as well behaved as though there was a protecting phalanx of dowagers sitting round the walls of the saloon. There are no dowagers, though there may probably be a policeman somewhere about the place. To a stranger it is very remarkable that there is so little of what we call flirting;﻿—almost none of it. It would seem that to the girls dancing is so much a matter of business, that here at Sperl’s they can think of nothing else. To mind their steps, and at the same time their dresses, lest they should be trod upon, to keep full pace with the music, to make all the proper turns at every proper time, and to have the foot fall on the floor at the exact instant; all this is enough, without further excitement. You will see a girl dancing with a man as though the man were a chair, or a stick, or some necessary piece of furniture.

他亲耳听得那位姑娘邀她的一位老仰慕者上斯佩尔陪她跳舞；不出十分钟，她又斩钉截铁不许他同另一位姑娘跳！好个弗里茨·普兰肯，他对自己一向估价很高——这也怪不得他——而且很明白，除了洛塔·施密特，够得上他一顾的漂亮姑娘还多的是。他挣不到克里佩尔先生那每月两百盾；可他二十五，不是四十五；论钱，他混得也颇不坏。他确实爱洛塔·施密特。要撒手，不是容易的事。可她也爱他——他这样对自己说——总不至于真把事情做绝。无论如何，威胁他是受不了的。他偏要同阿黛拉·布吕尔跳，就在斯佩尔。至少他心想，到时候他会觉得同她跳一跳才好。
塔博尔街（Tabor Strasse）的斯佩尔舞厅，是维也纳的一大去处。礼拜日晚上照例开放，十点起舞，跳到凌晨两三点。有两个大间：一间跳舞，另一间里，跳舞的和不跳舞的宾客连吃带喝、抽烟不断。而斯佩尔这地方最妙的一桩是：那里没有任何教人看不惯的事。姑娘们跳舞，男人们抽烟，又吃又喝，人人规规矩矩，倒像厅墙四周坐了一圈护法的诰命夫人似的。其实一位诰命夫人也没有，至多什么地方藏着个警察。在生人看来顶稀奇的是：那里几乎见不到我们所谓的「打情骂俏」——几乎一点也没有。在斯佩尔的姑娘们，跳舞简直是桩正经营生，旁的一概无暇去想。顾着自己的舞步，同时顾着自己的裙子，怕被人踩了；合着音乐的节拍；该转身处按点转身；落脚分毫不差踩在拍子上——光这些就够人忙的，无须再添刺激。你会看见姑娘同一个男人跳，就仿佛那男人是把椅子、一根棍子、一件必不可少的家具似的。

===Original===

She condescends to use his services, but as soon as the dance is over she sends him away. She hardly speaks a word to him, if a word! She has come there to dance, and not to talk; unless, indeed, like Marie Weber and Lotta Schmidt, she has a recognised lover there of her very own.
At about half-past ten Marie and Lotta entered the saloon, and paid their kreutzers and sat themselves down on seats in the further saloon, from which through open archways they could see the dancers. Neither Carl nor Fritz had come as yet, and the girls were quite content to wait. It was to be presumed that they would be there before the men, and they both understood that the real dancing was not commenced early in the evening. It might be all very well for such as Adela Bruhl to dance with anyone who came at ten o’clock, but Lotta Schmidt would not care to amuse herself after that fashion. As to Marie, she was to be married after another week, and of course she would dance with no one but Carl Stobel.
“Look at her,” said Lotta, pointing with her foot to a fair girl, very pretty, but with hair somewhat untidy, who at this moment was waltzing in the other room. “That lad is a waiter from the Minden hotel. I know him. She would dance with anyone.”
“I suppose she likes dancing, and there is no harm in the boy,” said Marie.
“No, there is no harm, and if she likes it I do not begrudge it her. See what red hands she has.”
“She is of that complexion,” said Marie.
“Yes, she is of that complexion all over; look at her face. At any rate she might have better shoes on. Did you ever see anybody so untidy?”
“She is very pretty,” said Marie.
“Yes, she is pretty. There is no doubt she is pretty. She is not a native here. Her people are from Munich. Do you know, Marie, I think girls are always thought more of in other countries than in their own.”
Soon after this Carl and Fritz came in together, and Fritz, as he passed across the end of the first saloon, spoke a word or two to Adela. Lotta saw this, but determined that she would take no offence at so small a matter. Fritz need not have stopped to speak, but his doing so might be all very well. At any rate, if she did quarrel with him she would quarrel on a plain, intelligible ground. Within two minutes Carl and Marie were dancing, and Fritz had asked Lotta to stand up. “I will wait a little,” said she, “I never like to begin much before eleven.”

她屈尊用他一用，曲子一完便打发他走。她连一句话也难得同他说——若有半句的话！她是来跳舞的，不是来聊天的；除非她也像玛丽·韦伯和洛塔·施密特那样，在那里有自己名正言顺的未婚夫。
十点半光景，玛丽和洛塔进了舞厅，付了克罗伊策铜币，在里间坐下来；透过敞开的拱门，望得见舞着的人。卡尔和弗里茨都还没来，两个姑娘安然等着。她们料定会比男人们先到；两人心里都有数：正经的跳舞，晚间早不了。像阿黛拉·布吕尔那样十点钟谁来就跟谁跳的，自去跳好了；洛塔·施密特可不肯那样打发自己。至于玛丽，再过一礼拜她就要出阁，自然除卡尔·施托贝尔外谁也不跳。
「瞧她，」洛塔抬脚指了指一个浅色头发的姑娘，人很俊，只是头发略乱，此刻正在那间里旋着华尔兹。「那小子是明登旅馆的侍者。我认得。她跟谁都肯跳。」
「我猜她是爱跳，那小子又没坏处。」玛丽说。
「没坏处，她爱跳我也不眼红。瞧她那双手，多红。」
「她是那个肤色。」玛丽说。
「是，她浑身都是那个肤色；瞧她的脸。且不管肤色，她总可以穿双像样些的鞋。你见过这么邋遢的人吗？」
「她很俊。」玛丽说。
「是，俊。她俊是没有疑问的。她不是本地人。她家是慕尼黑（Munich）来的。玛丽，你知道吗，姑娘在外国，总比在本国更被人高看。」
随后不久，卡尔同弗里茨一道进来；弗里茨穿过头一间厅的尽头时，同阿黛拉搭了一两句话。洛塔看见了，可她拿定主意，这点小事不与她计较。弗里茨本可以不停步说话的；不过停了也就停了。真的要吵，她也要拣个明白晓畅的由头吵。不出两分钟，卡尔同玛丽下了场，弗里茨也请洛塔起身。「我再等等，」她说，「我从来不爱在十一点前多跳。」

“As you please,” said Fritz; and he sat down in the chair which Marie had occupied. Then he played with his cane, and as he did so his eyes followed the steps of Adela Bruhl.
“She dances very well,” said Lotta.
“H﻿—m﻿—m, yes.” Fritz did not choose to bestow any strong praise on Adela’s dancing.
“Yes, Fritz, she does dance well﻿—very well, indeed. And she is never tired. If you ask me whether I like her style, I cannot quite say that I do. It is not what we do here﻿—not exactly.”
“She has lived in Vienna since she was a child.”
“It is in the blood then, I suppose. Look at her fair hair, all blowing about. She is not like one of us.”
“Oh no, she is not.”
“That she is very pretty, I quite admit,” said Lotta. “Those soft gray eyes are delicious. Is it not a pity she has no eyebrows?”
“But she has eyebrows.”
“Ah! you have been closer than I, and you have seen them. I have never danced with her, and I cannot see them. Of course they are there﻿—more or less.”
After a while the dancing ceased, and Adela Bruhl came up into the supper-room, passing the seats on which Fritz and Lotta were sitting.
“Are you not going to dance, Fritz?” she said, with a smile, as she passed them.
“Go, go,” said Lotta; “why do you not go? She has invited you.”
“No; she has not invited me. She spoke to us both.”
“She did not speak to me, for my name is not Fritz. I do not see how you can help going, when she asked you so prettily.”
“I shall be in plenty of time presently. Will you dance now, Lotta? They are going to begin a waltz, and we will have a quadrille afterwards.”
“No, Herr Planken, I will not dance just now.”
“Herr Planken, is it? You want to quarrel with me then, Lotta.”
“I do not want to be one of two. I will not be one of two. Adela Bruhl is very pretty, and I advise you to go to her. I was told only yesterday her father can give her fifteen hundred florins of fortune! For me﻿—I have no father.”
“But you may have a husband tomorrow.”
“Yes, that is true, and a good one. Oh, such a good one!”
“What do you mean by that?”
“You go and dance with Adela Bruhl, and you shall see what I mean.”
Fritz had some idea in his own mind, more or less clearly developed, that his fate, as regarded Lotta Schmidt, now lay in his own hands. He undoubtedly desired to have Lotta for his own. He would have married her there and then﻿—at that moment, had it been possible.

「随你，」弗里茨说；他在玛丽坐过的椅子上坐下了。随后他耍起手杖，眼睛却跟着阿黛拉·布吕尔的舞步。

「嗯——嗯，是。」弗里茨不肯把重话的夸赞加在阿黛拉的舞艺上。
「是的，弗里茨，她跳得是好——实在好。而且她不累。你若问我喜欢不喜欢她那个路数，我说不上喜欢。不是我们这里跳的样子——不全是。」
「她从小就住在维也纳。」
「那就是血里带来的了。瞧她那头浅色头发，四处飘。她不像我们一路人。」

「她很俊，我完全承认，」洛塔说。「那双温柔的灰眼睛，招人爱。可惜没有眉毛，多煞风景。」

「啊！你比我挨得近，你看清楚了。我没同她跳过，看不见。自然是有——多多少少有。」

「你不跳吗，弗里茨？」她走过时含笑说。
「去呀，去呀，」洛塔说；「怎么不去？人家请你了。」
「没有；她没请我。她同咱们俩打招呼。」
「她没同我打招呼，我不叫弗里茨。人家请得这样客气，你怎么好不去。」
「回头有的是工夫。这就跳吗，洛塔？要起华尔兹了，跳完华尔兹咱们再跳一场四对舞。」
「不，普兰肯先生，我这就先不跳。」
「『普兰肯先生』都出来了？这是要同我吵架，洛塔。」

「可你明天就能有个丈夫。」
「是，这话不假，还是个好丈夫。哦，多好的一个！」
「你这话什么意思？」

弗里茨心里多少有点数，清楚又模糊地觉得：他对洛塔·施密特的命数，如今全攥在他自己手里。他无疑是要洛塔做他的人的。他当时当地就会娶她——那会儿就行，只要办得到。

He had quite made up his mind that he preferred her much to Adela Bruhl, though Adela Bruhl had fifteen hundred florins. But he did not like to endure tyranny, even from Lotta, and he did not know how to escape the tyranny otherwise than by dancing with Adela. He paused a moment, swinging his cane, endeavouring to think how he might best assert his manhood and yet not offend the girl he loved. But he found that to assert his manhood was now his first duty.
“Well, Lotta,” he said, “since you are so cross with me, I will ask Adela to dance.” And in two minutes he was spinning round the room with Adela Bruhl in his arms.
“Certainly she dances very well,” said Lotta, smiling, to Marie, who had now come back to her seat.
“Very well,” said Marie, who was out of breath.
“And so does he.”
“Beautifully,” said Marie.
“Is it not a pity that I should have lost such a partner forever?”
“Lotta!”
“It is true. Look here, Marie, there is my hand upon it. I will never dance with him again﻿—never﻿—never﻿—never. Why was he so hard upon Herr Crippel last night?”
“Was he hard upon Herr Crippel?”
“He said that Herr Crippel was too old to play the zither; too old! Some people are too young to understand. I shall go home, I shall not stay to sup with you tonight.”
“Lotta, you must stay for supper.”
“I will not sup at his table. I have quarrelled with him. It is all over. Fritz Planken is as free as the air for me.”
“Lotta, do not say anything in a hurry. At any rate do not do anything in a hurry.”
“I do not mean to do anything at all. It is simply this﻿—I do not care very much for Fritz, after all. I don’t think I ever did. It is all very well to wear your clothes nicely, but if that is all, what does it come to? If he could play the zither, now!”
“There are other things except playing the zither. They say he is a good bookkeeper.”
“I don’t like bookkeeping. He has to be at his hotel from eight in the morning till eleven at night.”
“You know best.”
“I am not so sure of that. I wish I did know best. But I never saw such a girl as you are. How you change! It was only yesterday you scolded me because I did not wish to be the wife of your dear friend Crippel.”
“Herr Crippel is a very good man.”
“You go away with your good man! You have got a good man of your own. He is standing there waiting for you, like a gander on one leg. He wants you to dance; go away.”

===Chinese===

他完全打定了主意：阿黛拉·布吕尔纵有一千五百盾，也远不及洛塔。可他不愿受辖制，哪怕辖制他的是洛塔；而他懂得，要摆脱辖制，除了同阿黛拉跳一场，再没别的法子。他顿了顿，转着手杖，苦苦思量怎样既张起他男子汉的气概、又不开罪他心爱的姑娘。可他到底觉得，此刻头一件要紧的，还是张起他的男子汉气概。
「好吧，洛塔，」他说，「你既然这样同我使性子，我就去请阿黛拉跳。」不出两分钟，他已搂着阿黛拉·布吕尔满场旋转了。
「她跳得确实好。」洛塔笑着对玛丽说；玛丽这时也回到座上。
「好得很。」玛丽说，气还没匀。
「他跳得也好。」
「美极了。」玛丽说。
「可惜这样一位舞伴，从此叫我丢了。」
「洛塔！」
「是真的。你听着，玛丽，我把手放在这儿作证：我从此再不同他跳——再也不——再也不——再也不。他昨晚干吗那样刻薄克里佩尔先生？」
「他刻薄克里佩尔先生了吗？」
「他说克里佩尔先生弹齐特尔琴年纪太老了；太老了！有些人啊，是年纪太轻，懂不了事。我要回家了，今晚不同你们吃宵夜了。」
「洛塔，宵夜你一定得留下。」
「我不上他的桌吃东西。我们吵翻了。完了。弗里茨·普兰肯于我，就像空气一样自由。」
「洛塔，急话别说，急事更别做。」
「我什么都不打算做。就是这么回事——弗里茨这个人，我到底不怎么在乎。我想我从没在乎过。衣裳穿得好看自然是好；可若光剩了这一样，又算得什么？他若会弹齐特尔琴，倒也罢了！」
「除了弹齐特尔琴，还有别的呢。都说他账目是把好手。」
「我不喜欢账房。他一天从早八点到夜里十一点都得钉在旅馆里。」
「你最知道。」
「这我可不敢说。我倒愿意我最知道。可我从没见过你这号姑娘，变来变去！昨天你还数落我，怪我不肯做你那位好朋友克里佩尔的太太。」
「克里佩尔先生是个顶好的人。」
「带着你的好人走吧！你自己的好人已经到手了。他正站在那边等你呢，活像单腿站的一只公鹅。他要你跳舞呢；去吧。」
