> I think that literature needs no introduction, and, judging of you by the character which you have made for yourself in its paths, I do not doubt but you will feel as I do. I shall therefore write to you without reserve. I am a lady not possessing that modesty which should make me hold a low opinion of my own talents, and equally free from that feeling of self-belittlement which induces so many to speak humbly while they think proudly of their own acquirements. Though I am still young, I have written much for the press, and I believe I may boast that I have sometimes done so successfully. Hitherto I have kept back my name, but I hope soon to be allowed to see it on the title page of a book which shall not shame me.
> My object in troubling you is to announce the fact, agreeable enough to myself, that I have just completed a novel in three volumes, and to suggest to you that it should make its first appearance to the world in the pages of the magazine under your control. I will frankly tell you that I am not myself fond of this mode of publication; but Messrs. X., Y., Z. of Paternoster Row, with whom you are doubtless acquainted, have assured me that such will be the better course. In these matters one is still terribly subject to the tyranny of the publishers, who surely of all cormorants are the most greedy, and of all tyrants are the most arrogant. Though I have never seen you, I know you too well to suspect for a moment that my words will ever be repeated to my respectable friends in the Row.
> Shall I wait upon you with my MS.﻿—or will you call for it? Or perhaps it may be better that I should send it to you. Young ladies should not run about﻿—even after editors; and it might be so probable that I should not find you at home. Messrs. X., Y., and Z. have read the MS.﻿—or more probably the young man whom they keep for the purpose has done so﻿—and the nod of approval has been vouchsafed. Perhaps this may suffice; but if a second examination be needful, the work is at your service.
> Yours faithfully, and in hopes of friendly relations,
> Josephine de Montmorenci.
> I am English, though my unfortunate name will sound French in your ears.

===Chinese===

> 我想，文学是无须介绍信的；照您自己在这条路上挣下的声名来看您，我不疑心您会同我一样感到这一点。所以我写信给您，就不留余地了。我是一位不具备那种谦逊的女士——那种本该叫我把自己才分看低的谦逊；我也同样没有那份自我贬抑之心——多少人嘴上说得谦卑、心里却为自己的造诣骄傲，我却没有。我年纪还轻，却已为报刊写过许多东西；我相信我可以夸口：有几次还写得成功。至今我一直隐着我的名字；可我不久就盼着获准在某一本书的扉页上看见它——一本不至于叫我蒙羞的书。
> 我劳动您的目的，是通报一件于我自己相当可喜的事实：我刚写成了一部三卷本的小说；并想向您进一言：它不妨首度问世于您掌管的那份杂志。我坦白告诉您，我自己并不喜欢这种发表的路数；可是帕特诺斯特街（Paternoster Row）的 X、Y、Z 几位先生——您想必同他们相熟——向我担保，这样走更好。这些事上，人还受着出版商可怕的专制：论贪，鸬鹚里数他们最贪；论横，暴君里数他们最横。我虽从未见过您，却把您知道得太清楚了，绝不疑心我的话会传到那街上我那些可敬的朋友们耳朵里去。
> 我该带着稿子登门拜见呢——还是您来取？或者，由我寄给您，也许更好。年轻女子不该四处奔跑——哪怕是追编辑；何况我多半会扑空，撞不上您在家。X、Y、Z 几位先生已读过稿子——多半是他们养来专干这个的年轻人读的——首肯的头也点过了。这也许就够了；可若需再验看一次，此稿听凭尊便。
> 您忠实的、盼结善缘的，
> 约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西（Josephine de Montmorenci）
> 我是英国人，虽然我这倒霉的名字在您耳朵里听着像法国人。

===Original===

For facility in the telling of our story we will call this especial editor Mr. Brown. Mr. Brown’s first feeling on reading the letter was decidedly averse to the writer. But such is always the feeling of editors to would-be contributors, though contributions are the very food on which an editor must live. But Mr. Brown was an unmarried man, who loved the rustle of feminine apparel, who delighted in the brightness of a woman’s eye when it would be bright for him, and was not indifferent to the touch of a woman’s hand. As editors go, or went then, he knew his business, and was not wont to deluge his pages with weak feminine ware in return for smiles and flattering speeches﻿—as editors have done before now; but still he liked an adventure, and was perhaps afflicted by some slight flaw of judgment, in consequence of which the words of pretty women found with him something of preponderating favour. Who is there that will think evil of him because it was so?
He read the letter a second time, and did not send that curt, heartrending answer which is so common to editors﻿—“The editor’s compliments and thanks, but his stock of novels is at present so great that he cannot hope to find room for the work which has been so kindly suggested.”
Of King-Charles Street, Brown could not remember that he had ever heard, and he looked it out at once in the Directory. There was a King-Charles Street in Camden Town, at No. 19 of which street it was stated that a Mr. Puffle resided. But this told him nothing. Josephine de Montmorenci might reside with Mrs. Puffle in Camden Town, and yet write a good novel﻿—or be a very pretty girl. And there was a something in the tone of the letter which made him think that the writer was no ordinary person. She wrote with confidence. She asked no favour. And then she declared that Messrs. X., Y., Z., with whom Mr. Brown was intimate, had read and approved her novel. Before he answered the note he would call in the Row and ask a question or two.
He did call, and saw Mr. Z. Mr. Z. remembered well that the MS. had been in their house. He rather thought that X., who was out of town, had seen Miss Montmorenci﻿—perhaps on more than one occasion. The novel had been read, and﻿—well, Mr. Z. would not quite say approved; but it had been thought that there was a good deal in it. “I think I remember X.

===Chinese===

为叙述方便，我们管这位特别的编辑叫布朗先生（Mr. Brown）。布朗先生读罢此信的第一个感觉，是分明地厌恶写信人。可编辑对投稿人向来的感觉本就如此——尽管投稿恰是编辑赖以为生的食粮。可布朗先生是个未婚男人，爱听女人衣装的窸窣，爱看女人的眼睛为他而亮，女人手的轻触他也并非无动于衷。就编辑而论，他懂他的行当，不惯于拿软绵绵的女性劣货去灌满他的版面，换几句笑靥同恭维——从前的编辑倒是有这样干的；可他到底喜欢一桩艳遇，也许还害着判断力上的一点小毛病：漂亮女人的话，在他这里总占着几分过重的分量。谁会为这个就把他往坏里想呢？
他把信又读了一遍，没有发出编辑们最常发的那种简短伤心的回音——「编辑敬谢并致意；惟小说存稿眼下过多，无力为如此好意惠示之大作觅得篇幅。」
国王查理街，布朗想不起曾听说过；他当即查了姓名地址录。卡姆登镇有一条国王查理街，街上的十九号，登记着一位帕弗尔先生（Mr. Puffle）住着。可这告诉不了他什么。约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西尽可以同帕弗尔太太一起住在卡姆登镇，也尽可以写出一部好小说——或者本人是个很标致的姑娘。况且信的腔调里有种什么，叫他觉得写信人不是寻常人物。她写得自信。她不求情。随后她又声明：同布朗先生相熟的 X、Y、Z 几位先生已读过并赞许了她的小说。回信之前，他要先去那街上问一两句话。
他去了，见到的是 Z 先生。Z 先生记得那部稿子到过他们家里。他倒有点想得起，出门在外的 X 见过蒙莫朗西小姐——也许不止一回。小说读过了，而且——嗯，Z 先生不肯就说赞许；可他们觉得里头颇有东西。「我想我记得 X 对我说过，她是个出格标致的年轻女人，」Z 说——「她身上有点神秘。我没亲眼见她，可我拿准那里头有神秘。」布朗先生打定了主意：无论如何要看看那部稿子。

telling me that she was an uncommon pretty young woman,” said Z.﻿—“and there is some mystery about her. I didn’t see her myself, but I am sure there was a mystery.” Mr. Brown made up his mind that he would, at any rate, see the MS.
He felt disposed to go at once to Camden Town, but still had fears that in doing so he might seem to make himself too common. There are so many things of which an editor is required to think! It is almost essential that they who are ambitious of serving under him should believe that he is enveloped in MSS. from morning to night﻿—that he cannot call an hour his own﻿—that he is always bringing out that periodical of his in a frenzy of mental exertion﻿—that he is to be approached only with difficulty﻿—and that a call from him is a visit from a god. Mr. Brown was a Jupiter, willing enough on occasions to go a little out of his way after some literary Leda, or even on behalf of a Danae desirous of a price for her compositions;﻿—but he was obliged to acknowledge to himself that the occasion had not as yet arisen. So he wrote to the young lady as follows:﻿—

> The Editor presents his compliments to Miss de Montmorenci, and will be very happy to see her MS. Perhaps she will send it to the above address. The Editor has seen Mr. Z., of Paternoster Row, who speaks highly of the work. A novel, however, may be very clever and yet hardly suit a magazine. Should it be accepted by the *Olympus*, some time must elapse before it appears. The Editor would be very happy to see Miss de Montmorenci if it would suit her to call any Friday between the hours of two and three.

When the note was written Mr. Brown felt that it was cold;﻿—but then it behoves an editor to be cold. A gushing editor would ruin any publication within six months. Young women are very nice; pretty young women are especially nice; and of all pretty young women, clever young women who write novels are perhaps as nice as any;﻿—but to an editor they are dangerous. Mr. Brown was at this time about forty, and had had his experiences. The letter was cold, but he was afraid to make it warmer. It was sent;﻿—and when he received the following answer, it may fairly be said that his editorial hair stood on end:

===Chinese===

他想去卡姆登镇，马上就去；可又怕这样一来，显得自贬身份。编辑要操心的事真多！凡想在他手下效力的人，几乎非信这个不可：他从早到晚埋在稿子里——一个钟头也归不得他自己——他那份期刊永远在心神狂奋中赶出来——接近他千难万难——他肯登门，便是天神下凡。布朗先生是位朱庇特，遇到机会，也肯为哪位文学的勒达稍稍绕一绕路，甚至肯为一位盼着稿子卖个好价的达那厄出把力；——可他不得不对自己承认：这样的机会至今还不曾有过。于是他给那位年轻女士写了如下的信：——

> 编辑向德·蒙莫朗西小姐致意，乐于一见其稿。请寄至上址为盼。编辑已见过帕特诺斯特街的 Z 先生，其于该作颇致嘉许。惟小说虽佳，未必尽合杂志之用。倘蒙《奥林波斯》（Olympus）采用，刊出亦需时日。德·蒙莫朗西小姐如蒙拨冗，任何周五二至三时莅临，编辑甚愿一见。

信写完，布朗先生觉得它冷；——可编辑本该冷。一位热情泛滥的编辑，不出六个月就能毁掉任何刊物。年轻女子很好；漂亮的年轻女子尤其好；漂亮年轻女子里，会写小说的聪明女子也许顶好；——可对编辑，她们危险。布朗先生这时约四十岁，阅历是有的。信冷；他不敢叫它暖。信发了；随后他接到下面这封回信，可以说，他编辑的头发根根倒竖：

===Original===

> Dear Mr. Brown,
> I hate you and your compliments. That sort of communication means nothing, and I won’t send you my MS. unless you are more in earnest about it. I know the way in which rolls of paper are shoved into pigeonholes and left there till they are musty, while the writers’ hearts are being broken. My heart may be broken some day, but not in that way.
> I won’t come to you between two and three on Friday. It sounds a great deal too like a doctor’s appointment, and I don’t think much of you if you are only at your work one hour in the week. Indeed, I won’t go to you at all. If an interview is necessary you can come here. But I don’t know that it will be necessary.
> Old X. is a fool and knows nothing about it. My own approval is to me very much more than his. I don’t suppose he’d know the inside of a book if he saw it. I have given the very best that is in me to my work, and I know that it is good. Even should you say that it is not I shall not believe you. But I don’t think you will say so, because I believe you to be in truth a clever fellow in spite of your “compliments” and your “two and three o’clock on a Friday.”
> If you want to see my MS., say so with some earnestness, and it shall be conveyed to you. And please to say how much I shall be paid for it, for I am as poor as Job. And name a date. I won’t be put off with your “some time must elapse.” It shall see the light, or, at least, a part of it, within six months. That is my intention. And don’t talk nonsense to me about clever novels not suiting magazines﻿—unless you mean that as an excuse for publishing so many stupid ones as you do.
> You will see that I am frank; but I really do mean what I say. I want it to come out in the *Olympus*; and if we can I shall be so happy to come to terms with you.
> Yours as I find you,
> Josephine de Montmorenci.
> Thursday﻿—King-Charles Street.

> 亲爱的布朗先生：

> 约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西
> 周四——国王查理街

===Original===

This was an epistle to startle an editor as coming from a young lady; but yet there was something in it that seemed to imply strength. Before answering it Mr. Brown did a thing which he must be presumed to have done as man and not as editor. He walked off to King-Charles Street in Camden Town, and looked at the house. It was a nice little street, very quiet, quite genteel, completely made up with what we vaguely call gentlemen’s houses, with two windows to each drawing-room, and with a balcony to some of them, the prettiest balcony in the street belonging to No. 19, near the park, and equally removed from poverty and splendour. Brown walked down the street, on the opposite side, towards the park, and looked up at the house. He intended to walk at once homewards, across the park, to his own little home in St. John’s Wood Road; but when he had passed half a street away from the Puffle residence, he turned to have another look, and retraced his steps. As he passed the door it was opened, and there appeared upon the steps﻿—one of the prettiest little women he had ever seen in his life. She was dressed for walking, with that jaunty, broad, open bonnet which women then wore, and seemed, as some women do seem, to be an amalgam of softness, prettiness, archness, fun, and tenderness﻿—and she carried a tiny blue parasol. She was fair, gray-eyed, dimpled, all alive, and dressed so nicely and yet simply, that Mr. Brown was carried away for the moment by a feeling that he would like to publish her novel, let it be what it might. And he heard her speak. “Charles,” she said, “you shan’t smoke.” Our editor could, of course, only pass on, and had not an opportunity of even seeing Charles. At the corner of the street he turned round and saw them walking the other way. Josephine was leaning on Charles’s arm. She had, however, distinctly avowed herself to be a young lady﻿—in other words, an unmarried woman. There was, no doubt, a mystery, and Mr. Brown felt it to be incumbent on him to fathom it. His next letter was as follows:﻿—

===Chinese===

这样一封书翰，出自年轻女士之手，够编辑吃惊的；可里头又有一种什么，透着力气。回信之前，布朗先生做了一件事——必得算他做人、不是做编辑做的。他步行到卡姆登镇的国王查理街，去看那所房子。那是条漂亮的小街，极清静，十足体面，两边盖满了我们含含糊糊称作「绅士住宅」的房子，每家起居室两扇窗，有几家带阳台；全街顶俊的阳台，属于近公园的那座十九号，离穷奢两头一样远。布朗沿街对面朝公园走去，抬头望那所房子。他本打算穿过公园直接回圣约翰林路他自己那个小家；可走出半条街，又回身再看一眼，倒折了回去。他经过门口时，门正开着，台阶上出现了——他平生见过的顶俊俏的小妇人之一。她一身出门的装束，戴那时女子戴的那种轻快阔大的软帽，仿佛——有些女人就是那样——集温柔、俊俏、俏皮、风趣、娇嫩于一身——手里拿一柄小小的蓝阳伞。她浅色头发，灰眼睛，带酒窝，浑身是活气，衣裳穿得那样好看又那样素净，布朗先生一时间竟被一种心情裹挟：但愿能出她的小说，管它写得怎样！他还听见她说话。「查尔斯，」她说，「不许你抽烟。」我们这位编辑当然只能走过去，连查尔斯的一面也没得见。在街角他回头望，见他们朝另一头走去。约瑟芬倚着查尔斯的胳膊。可她分明自己声明过是年轻小姐——换句话说，未婚女子。这里头无疑有神秘；布朗先生觉得，揭开它是他分内的事。他的下一封信如下：——

===Original===

> My dear Miss de Montmorenci,
> I am sorry that you should hate me and my compliments. I had intended to be as civil and as nice as possible. I am quite in earnest, and you had better send the MS. As to all the questions you ask, I cannot answer them to any purpose till I have read the story﻿—which I will promise to do without subjecting it to the pigeonholes. If you do not like Friday, you shall come on Monday, or Tuesday, or Wednesday, or Thursday, or Saturday, or even on Sunday, if you wish it;﻿—and at any hour, only let it be fixed.
> Yours faithfully,
> Jonathan Brown.
> Friday.

===Chinese===

> 亲爱的德·蒙莫朗西小姐：
> 您恨我同我的致意，我很难过。我本意是要尽量客气、尽量和善。我是十二分有诚意的；您还是把稿子送来好。您问的那些，我没有读故事以前，一概答不到点子上——读我一定读，而且担保不经鸽子洞的手。您不喜欢周五，那就周一，或周二，或周三，或周四，或周六，甚至周日也行，只要您愿意；——钟点也随您，只要定下来。
> 您忠实的，
> 乔纳森·布朗（Jonathan Brown）
> 周五

===Original===

In the course of the next week the novel came, with another short note, to which was attached no ordinary beginning or ending. “I send my treasure, and, remember, I will have it back in a week if you do not intend to keep it. I have not £5 left in the world, and I owe my milliner ever so much, and money at the stables where I get a horse. And I am determined to go to Dieppe in July. All must come out of my novel. So do be a good man. If you are I will see you.” Herein she declared plainly her own conviction that she had so far moved the editor by her correspondence﻿—for she knew nothing, of course, of that ramble of his through King-Charles Street﻿—as to have raised in his bosom a desire to see her. Indeed, she made no secret of such conviction. “Do as I wish,” she said plainly, “and I will gratify you by a personal interview.” But the interview was not to be granted till the novel had been accepted and the terms fixed﻿—such terms, too, as it would be very improbable that any editor could accord.
“Not so Black as he’s Painted;”﻿—that was the name of the novel which it now became the duty of Mr. Brown to read. When he got it home, he found that the writing was much worse than that of the letters. It was small, and crowded, and carried through without those technical demarcations which are so comfortable to printers, and so essential to readers. The erasures were numerous, and bits of the story were written, as it were, here and there. It was a manuscript to which Mr. Brown would not have given a second glance, had there not been an adventure behind it. The very sending of such a manuscript to any editor would have been an impertinence, if it were sent by any but a pretty woman. Mr. Brown, however, toiled over it, and did read it﻿—read it, or at least enough of it to make him know what it was. The verdict which Mr. Z. had given was quite true. No one could have called the story stupid. No mentor experienced in such matters would have ventured on such evidence to tell the aspirant that she had mistaken her walk in life, and had better sit at home and darn her stockings. Out of those heaps of ambitious manuscripts which are daily subjected to professional readers such verdicts may safely be given in regard to four-fifths﻿—either that the aspirant should darn her stockings, or that he should prune his fruit trees.

===Chinese===

下个礼拜里，小说寄到了，另附一张短简，开头结尾都不落俗套。「我把宝贝奉上；记住，您若不打算留下，一礼拜内就得还我。我在这世上剩不到五镑了；欠女帽铺一屁股账；马房里赊着马的账。我拿定主意七月去迪耶普。这一切都得从我的小说里出。所以，做个好人吧。您做了好人，我就见您。」她在这里明白宣告了自己的信念：她凭通信已把这编辑打动到这般地步——国王查理街那一趟溜达她自然一无所知——已经在他胸中唤起了见她的欲望。说真的，这信念她也不讳饰。「照我的意思办，」她明明白白说，「我便赏您一面。」只是这见面要等小说被接受、条款被议定之后才给——而且定的还得是这样一种条款：哪个编辑多半也给不出。
《他不像传说的那么黑》——这便是如今落到布朗先生头上、责成他一读的那部小说的名字。拿到家里，他发现稿子的字迹比信里的坏得多。字小而挤，一气写到底，全没有那些于排字工这样舒服、于读者这样必不可少的分段记号。涂改极多，故事的片段东一段西一段，仿佛随手写下的。若不是背后有一桩艳遇，这样的稿子布朗先生原不会看第二眼。这样的稿子寄给任何编辑都是冒失——除非寄的是个漂亮女人。布朗先生却埋头苦干，当真读了——读了它，至少读到足以知道它是件什么。Z 先生下的断语一点不差。谁也不能说这故事蠢。再老练的明师也不敢凭这样的证据，告诉这投稿人她入错了行，最好坐在家里补袜子。每日送到职业读稿人面前的雄心稿堆里，五分之四尽可放心地那样断——不是叫她补袜子，就是叫他修果树。

===Original===

It is equally so with the works of one sex as with those of the other. The necessity of saying so is very painful, and the actual stocking, or the fruit tree itself, is not often named. The cowardly professional reader indeed, unable to endure those thorns in the flesh of which poor Thackeray spoke so feelingly, when hard-pressed for definite answers, generally lies. He has been asked to be candid, but he cannot bring himself to undertake a duty so onerous, so odious, and one as to which he sees so little reason that he personally should perform it. But in regard to these aspirations﻿—to which have been given so much labour, which have produced so many hopes, offsprings which are so dear to the poor parents﻿—the decision at least is easy. And there are others in regard to which a hopeful reader finds no difficulty﻿—as to which he feels assured that he is about to produce to the world the fruit of some newfound genius. But there are doubtful cases which worry the poor judge till he knows not how to trust his own judgment. At this page he says, “Yes, certainly;” at the next he shakes his head as he sits alone amidst his papers. Then he is dead against the aspirant. Again there is improvement, and he asks himself﻿—where is he to find anything that is better? As our editor read Josephine’s novel﻿—he had learned to call her Josephine in that silent speech in which most of us indulge, and which is so necessary to an editor﻿—he was divided between Yes and No throughout the whole story. Once or twice he found himself wiping his eyes, and then it was all “yes” with him. Then he found the pages ran with a cruel heaviness, which seemed to demand decisive editorial severity. A whole novel, too, is so great a piece of business! There would be such difficulty were he to accept it! How much must he cut out! How many of his own hours must he devote to the repairing of mutilated sentences, and the remodelling of indistinct scenes! In regard to a small piece an editor, when moved that way, can afford to be good-natured. He can give to it the hour or so of his own work which it may require. And if after all it be nothing﻿—or, as will happen sometimes, much worse than nothing﻿—the evil is of short duration. In admitting such a thing he has done an injury﻿—but the injury is small. It passes in the crowd, and is forgotten. The best Homer that ever edited must sometimes nod.

===Chinese===

两性的作品在这一点上一样。不得不说这话，很难堪；所以那实在的袜子、或果树本身，倒不常被点破。怯懦的职业读稿人，受不住可怜的萨克雷说得那样恳切的那些肉中刺，被逼着要明确答复时，多半撒谎。人家求他坦白；可这样一桩繁重、可憎的差事，他又看不出凭什么该由他本人来尽，便尽不到底。可对着这些心血——化了这么多劳力、生出这么多指望的心血，穷人家里顶亲爱的儿女——决断至少是容易的。另有一些稿子，满怀希望的读稿人也毫无难处——他自觉笃定，就要给世间捧出某位新发现的天才之果。可有那疑难的案子，磨得这可怜的裁判不知该不该信自己的判断。这一页他说「是，当然」；下一页，他独坐稿纸中间，又摇头。于是他又死命反对投稿人。随后又见长进，他问自己——叫他上哪儿找更好的去？我们这位编辑读约瑟芬的小说时——他在我们多半都沉溺的那种无声的自语里，已学会叫她约瑟芬了；这无声的自语，于编辑是这样必需——从头到尾在是与不是之间摇摆。有一两回他发觉自己在擦眼睛；那时于他全是「是」了。随后他又觉出稿页流得滞重难受，简直该祭出编辑的雷霆。何况一部整本的小说是多大一桩工程！接受它该有多难！得删掉多少！得搭上他自己多少钟点，去修补残句、重整糊涂的场面！小块的东西，编辑动了心，还阔气得起、好心得起。它要的个把钟头他自己的工，他出得起。到底它若一文不值——或者，有时竟比一文不值还糟——祸害也短。收了这样的东西他伤了刊物——可伤得小。混在人堆里就过去了，就忘了。顶好的荷马做编辑，也免不了打盹。

===Original===

But a whole novel! A piece of work that would last him perhaps for twelve months! No editor can afford to nod for so long a period.
But then this tale, this novel of “Not so Black as he’s Painted,” this story of a human devil, for whose crimes no doubt some Byronic apology was made with great elaboration by the sensational Josephine, was not exactly bad. Our editor had wept over it. Some tenderhearted Medora, who on behalf of her hyena-in-love had gone through miseries enough to kill half a regiment of heroines, had dimmed the judge’s eyes with tears. What stronger proof of excellence can an editor have? But then there were those long pages of metaphysical twaddle, sure to elicit scorn and neglect from old and young. They, at any rate, must be cut out. But in the cutting of them out a very mincemeat would be made of the story. And yet Josephine de Montmorenci, with her impudent little letters, had already made herself so attractive! What was our editor to do?
He knew well the difficulty that would be before him should he once dare to accept, and then undertake to alter. She would be as a tigress to him﻿—as a tigress fighting for her young. That work of altering is so ungracious, so precarious, so incapable of success in its performance! The long-winded, far-fetched, high-stilted, unintelligible sentence which you elide with so much confidence in your judgment, has been the very apple of your author’s eye. In it she has intended to convey to the world the fruits of her best meditation for the last twelve months. Thinking much over many things in her solitude, she has at last invented a truth, and there it lies. That wise men may adopt it, and candid women admire it, is the hope, the solace, and at last almost the certainty of her existence. She repeats the words to herself, and finds that they will form a choice quotation to be used in coming books. It is for the sake of that one newly-invented truth﻿—so she tells herself, though not quite truly﻿—that she desires publication. You come﻿—and with a dash of your pen you annihilate the precious gem! Is it in human nature that you should be forgiven? Mr. Brown had had his experiences, and understood all this well. Nevertheless he loved dearly to please a pretty woman.

===Chinese===

可一整部小说！一件也许要缠他十二个月的工程！哪个编辑也打不起这么长的盹。
可这部小说——这部《他不像传说的那么黑》，这个写人间魔鬼的故事——那魔鬼的罪孽，煽情的约瑟芬无疑费尽笔墨替它做了番拜伦式的开脱——又并非当真坏。我们这位编辑为它落过泪。哪位心软的梅多拉，为着她那恋爱中的鬣狗，受尽了够害死半个团女主人公的苦难，把裁判的眼睛都哭雾了。编辑还能有什么更强的好证明？可接着便是那一页页玄学的废话，老读者少读者准要嗤之以鼻、弃之不顾。那些，无论如何，非删不可。可一删，故事就成了一盘碎肉。而约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西，凭她那些无礼的小简，已经把自己弄得这样迷人！我们这位编辑怎么办？
他心里清楚：一旦他胆敢接受、再动手改，等着他的是什么。她会对他变作一头母虎——一头护崽的母虎。改稿这活计这样不讨好、这样没把握、这样做不成！你满心自信勾掉的那句冗长、牵强、踩着高跷、难解的句子，正是你那位作家的掌上明珠。她要在那句话里，向世间交出她十二个月最好的沉思结出的果子。她在幽居里对万事想了又想，末了发明出一条真理，它就躺在那里。智者会采纳它、坦诚的女人会叹赏它——这是她的希望、她的慰藉、末了几乎是她的命。她把那些字句对自己念了又念，发觉它们将来正好做新书里引用的隽语。正是为着那条新发明的真理——她对自己这样说，虽不尽实——她才想出版。你来了——笔一挥，把这颗珍贵的宝石勾销了！人情上还容你被人饶恕吗？布朗先生阅历俱全，这层他懂得透。可他偏又极爱讨好漂亮女人。

===Original===

And it must be acknowledged that the letters of Josephine were such as to make him sure that there might be an adventure if he chose to risk the pages of his magazine. The novel had taken him four long evenings to read, and at the end of the fourth he sat thinking of it for an hour. Fortune either favoured him or the reverse﻿—as the reader may choose to regard the question﻿—in this, that there was room for the story in his periodical if he chose to take it. He wanted a novel﻿—but then he did not want feminine metaphysics. He sat thinking of it, wondering in his mind how that little smiling, soft creature with the gray eyes, and the dimples, and the pretty walking-dress, could have written those interminable pages as to the questionable criminality of crime; whether a cardsharper might not be a hero; whether a murderer might not sacrifice his all, even the secret of his murder, for the woman he loved; whether devil might not be saint, and saint devil. At the end of the hour he got up from his chair, stretched himself, with his hands in his trousers-pockets, and said aloud, though alone, that he’d be d﻿—﻿— if he would. It was an act of great self-denial, a triumph of principle over passion.
But though he had thus decided, he was not minded to throw over altogether either Josephine or her novel. He might still, perhaps, do something for her if he could find her amenable to reason. Thinking kindly of her, very anxious to know her personally, and still desirous of seeing the adventure to the end, he wrote the following note to her that evening:﻿—

===Chinese===

还得承认，约瑟芬的信就是有这样一种力量，叫他相信：他若肯拿他杂志的版面冒一回险，便有一场艳遇。那部小说花了他四个漫长的夜晚；第四夜读完，他又坐着想了一个钟头。命运在此或偏袒他、或亏待他——这层随读者怎样看——那就是：他的刊物里若有心要这故事，登得下。他要一部小说——可他不要女性的玄学。他坐着想，心里纳闷：那个笑吟吟、软绵绵、灰眼睛、带酒窝、一身漂亮出门装的小人儿，怎么写得出那些没完没了的页子——写罪的罪性怎样可疑；赌棍算不算英雄；杀人犯会不会为所爱的女人舍出一切、连他杀人的秘密也舍出去；魔鬼会不会是圣徒、圣徒会不会是魔鬼。一个钟头想完，他从椅子上站起来，两手插进裤袋，伸了个懒腰，尽管四下无人，还是出了声：他要是肯才见鬼呢。这是绝大的一次克己，是原则对情欲的一场大胜。
可是他虽这样决了，却并不打算把约瑟芬或她的小说整个撂开。倘若她肯讲理，他也许仍能替她出点力。他心下善待她，急欲结识其人，又还想把这桩艳遇看到底，当晚给她写了下面这封短简：——

===Original===

> “I knew how it would be. I cannot give you an answer about your novel without seeing you. It so often happens that the answer can’t be Yes or No. You said something very cruel about dear old X., but after all he was quite right in his verdict about the book. There is a great deal in it; but it evidently was not written to suit the pages of a magazine. Will you come to me, or shall I come to you;﻿—or shall I send the MS. back, and so let there be an end of it? You must decide. If you direct that the latter course be taken, I will obey; but I shall do so with most sincere regret, both on account of your undoubted aptitude for literary work, and because I am very anxious to become acquainted with my fair correspondent. You see I can be as frank as you are yourself.
> Yours most faithfully,
> Jonathan Brown.
> My advice to you would be to give up the idea of publishing this tale in parts, and to make terms with X., Y., and Z.﻿—in endeavouring to do which I shall be most happy to be of service to you.

===Chinese===

> 「我料到会这样。不见您本人，您的大作我没法给答复。答复往往既不能是、也不能否。您说了老 X 几句顶狠的话；可到底，他对那部书的断语全对。里头很有东西；只是显然不是照杂志的页幅写的。您来我这里，还是我去您那里？——或者我把稿子退回，就此了结？您得决定。您若吩咐照后一条办，我遵命；但我将怀着至诚的惋惜照办——既为您文学工作上无可置疑的才具，也为着我极愿结识我这通信的美人。您看，我能同您一样坦白。
> 您最忠实的，
> 乔纳森·布朗
> 我对您的忠告是：打消分期刊登这故事的念头，同 X、Y、Z 去议价——议价之中，我极愿为您效劳。」

This note he posted on the following day, and when he returned home on the next night from his club, he found three replies from the divine, but irritable and energetic, Josephine. We will give them according to their chronology.
No. 1. “Monday Morning.﻿—Let me have my MS. back﻿—and pray, without any delay.﻿—J. de M.”
No. 2. “Monday, 2 o’clock.﻿—How can you have been so ill-natured﻿—and after keeping it twelve days?” His answer had been written within a week of the receipt of the parcel at his office, and he had acted with a rapidity which nothing but some tender passion would have instigated.﻿—“What you say about being clever, and yet not fit for a magazine, is rubbish. I know it is rubbish. I do not wish to see you. Why should I see a man who will do nothing to oblige me? If X., Y., Z. choose to buy it, at once, they shall have it. But I mean to be paid for it, and I think you have behaved very ill to me.﻿—Josephine.”
No. 3. “Monday Evening.﻿—My dear Mr. Brown﻿—Can you wonder that I should have lost my temper and almost my head? I have written twice before today, and hardly know what I said. I cannot understand you editing people. You are just like women;﻿—you will and you won’t. I am so unhappy. I had allowed myself to feel almost certain that you would take it, and have told that cross man at the stables he should have his money. Of course I can’t make you publish it;﻿—but how you can put in such yards of stupid stuff, all about nothing on earth, and then send back a novel which you say yourself is very clever, is what I can’t understand. I suppose it all goes by favour, and the people who write are your uncles, and aunts, and grandmothers, and ladyloves. I can’t make you do it, and therefore I suppose I must take your advice about those old hugger-muggers in Paternoster Row. But there are ever so many things you must arrange. I must have the money at once. And I won’t put up with just a few pounds. I have been at work upon that novel for more than two years, and I know that it is good. I hate to be grumbled at, and complained of, and spoken to as if a publisher were doing me the greatest favour in the world when he is just going to pick my brains to make money of them. I did see old X., or old Z., or old Y., and the snuffy old fellow told me that if I worked hard I might do something some day.

这封信他次日付邮；隔天夜里从俱乐部回家，他发现那位如神明却又易怒、精力充沛的约瑟芬来了三封回信。我们按先后录下。
第一封：「周一晨。——把稿子还我——务请即刻，不得耽搁。——约·德·蒙」
第二封：「周一，两点。——你怎么能这样恶作剧——还扣了它十二天？」他的复信是在稿子寄到办公室后一礼拜内写下的，行动之速，若无一腔柔情催逼，断办不到。——「你说的什么聪明、又不合杂志用，全是昏话。我知道是昏话。我不想见你。一个不肯替我出一点力的人，我见他做什么？X、Y、Z 若肯马上买，就让他们买。可我要的是钱；我觉得你待我坏透了。——约瑟芬」
第三封：「周一晚。——亲爱的布朗先生——我发了脾气、几乎发了昏，你还奇怪吗？今天我已写过两回信，自己都几乎不记得说了什么。我懂不了你们编辑这路人。你们同女人一模一样；——又肯又不肯。我这样不幸。我原几乎拿准你要它，都同马房里那个凶人说过他的钱有着落了。我自然没法逼你登它；——可是你们怎么登得下那样一码一码的蠢货，写的全是世上根本没有的东西，却把我一部你自己都说很聪明的小说退回来，这个我懂不了。我猜全是看人情：投稿的不是你们的叔叔、婶婶、祖母，就是相好。我没法叫你登；所以我想，只好听你的，去找帕特诺斯特街那伙老神棍。可有好些事你得替我办。钱我要立等。几镑钱打发我可不干。那部小说我写了两年多，我知道它好。我恨人家对我哼鼻子、挑眼儿，恨人家说话仿佛出版商赏了我天大的脸，其实他正要掏我的脑子去卖钱。老 X，还是老 Z，还是老 Y，我倒见过；那老头子鼻烟兮兮地对我说，我若苦干，将来兴许有成。我干得比他狠多了——他坐在那里挤人脑子，像老食尸鬼似的吮脑子里的汁。我想我还是见你一面好，为着钱那一类的事。周三两点我来，要不打发个人来。拖到周五我可不干；三点前我必须到家。这期间你不妨去一趟 X、Y、Z，把话带给我。——约·德·蒙」

===Original===

I have worked harder than ever he did﻿—sitting there and squeezing brains, and sucking the juice out of them like an old ghoul. I suppose I had better see you, because of money and all that. I’ll come, or else send someone, at about two on Wednesday. I can’t put it off till Friday, and I must be home by three. You might as well go to X., Y., Z., in the meantime, and let me know what they say.﻿—J. de M.”
There was an unparalleled impudence in all this which affronted, amazed, and yet in part delighted our editor. Josephine evidently regarded him as her humble slave, who had already received such favours as entitled her to demand from him any service which she might require of him. “You might as well go to X., Y., Z., and let me know what they say!” And then that direct accusation against him﻿—that all went by favour with him! “I think you have behaved very ill to me!” Why﻿—had he not gone out of his way, very much out of his way indeed, to do her a service? Was he not taking on her behalf an immense trouble for which he looked for no remuneration﻿—unless remuneration should come in that adventure of which she had but a dim foreboding? All this was unparalleled impudence. But then impudence from pretty women is only sauciness; and such sauciness is attractive. None but a very pretty woman who openly trusted in her prettiness would dare to write such letters, and the girl whom he had seen on the doorstep was very pretty. As to his going to X., Y., Z., before he had seen her, that was out of the question. That very respectable firm in the Row would certainly not give money for a novel without considerable caution, without much talking, and a regular understanding and bargain. As a matter of course, they would take time to consider. X., Y., Z. were not in a hurry to make money to pay a milliner or to satisfy a stable-keeper, and would have but little sympathy for such troubles;﻿—all which it would be Mr. Brown’s unpleasant duty to explain to Josephine de Montmorenci.
But though this would be unpleasant, still there might be pleasure. He could foresee that there would be a storm, with much pouting, some violent complaint, and perhaps a deluge of tears. But it would be for him to dry the tears and allay the storm. The young lady could do him no harm, and must at last be driven to admit that his kindness was disinterested.

===Chinese===

这一切里头有种独一无二的放肆，触犯了我们这位编辑，叫他惊，却也叫他暗中欢喜。约瑟芬分明拿他当她的卑贱奴隶，看作已经领过她那样的大恩，有资格差遣他办她要的任何差事。「这期间你不妨去一趟 X、Y、Z，把话带给我！」还有那句对他直截了当的控告——说他凡事都凭人情！「我觉得你待我坏透了！」——怎么？他不曾专门绕路——实实在在绕了远路——去给她出力吗？他不正在为她担一桩大麻烦、分文不取吗——除非报酬就出在那场她还懵懂的艳遇里？这都是独一无二的放肆。可漂亮女人的放肆只算娇嗔；而这娇嗔招人。只有十分漂亮、又公然信着自己漂亮的女人，才敢写这样的信；而他在门阶上见过的那姑娘，十分漂亮。至于说他先去见 X、Y、Z、再来见她——那想也别想。街上那家极可敬的商号，为一部小说掏钱，断不会不慎之又慎、不磨半天嘴皮、不定下正式的谅解同契约。他们照例要考虑时日。X、Y、Z 不急等钱付女帽铺、打发马房，对这类难处也少有同情——这一切，都得由布朗先生不痛快地向约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西讲解。
可这虽不痛快，里头也会有甜。他预见到会有一场风暴，撅嘴、狠话，也许还有泪水滂沱。可拭泪、息风，正是他的事。这位年轻女士害不了他什么；末了总得认下他的好意无私。

He waited, therefore, for the Wednesday, and was careful to be at the office of his magazine at two o’clock. In the ordinary way of his business the office would not have seen him on that day, but the matter had now been present in his mind so long, and had been so much considered, had assumed so large a proportion in his thoughts﻿—that he regarded not at all this extra trouble. With an air of indifference he told the lad who waited upon him as half clerk and half errand-boy, that he expected a lady; and then he sat down, as though to compose himself to his work. But no work was done. Letters were not even opened. His mind was full of Josephine de Montmorenci. If all the truth is to be told, it must be acknowledged that he did not even wear the clothes that were common to him when he sat in his editorial chair. He had prepared himself somewhat, and a new pair of gloves was in his hat. It might be that circumstances would require him to accompany Josephine at least a part of the way back to Camden Town.
At half-past two the lady was announced﻿—Miss de Montmorenci; and our editor, with palpitating heart, rose to welcome the very figure, the very same pretty walking-dress, the same little blue parasol, which he had seen upon the steps of the house in King-Charles Street. He could swear to the figure, and to the very step, although he could not as yet see the veiled face. And this was a joy to him; for, though he had not allowed himself to doubt much, he had doubted a little whether that graceful houri might or might not be his Josephine. Now she was there, present to him in his own castle, at his mercy as it were, so that he might dry her tears and bid her hope, or tell her that there was no hope so that she might still weep on, just as he pleased. It was not one of those cases in which want of bread and utter poverty are to be discussed. A horsekeeper’s bill and a visit to Dieppe were the melodramatic incidents of the tragedy, if tragedy it must be. Mr. Brown had in his time dealt with cases in which a starving mother or a dying father was the motive to which appeal was made. At worst there could be no more than a rose-water catastrophe; and it might be that triumph, and gratitude, and smiles would come. He rose from his chair, and, giving his hand gracefully to his visitor, led her to a seat.
“I am very glad to see you here, Miss de Montmorenci,” he said.

于是他等着礼拜三，两点钟准时到了他杂志的办公室。照他业务的常规，那天他本不会来；可这桩事在他心里盘桓得这样久、掂量得这样多、在他思虑里占了这样大的分量——这层额外的辛劳他全不在乎。他装出淡漠的神气，吩咐那兼充半书记半听差的少年说有位太太要来；随后坐下，仿佛定下心做工。可工一点没做。信连拆都没拆。他满脑子约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西。倘若要句句说实话，还得承认：他连坐编辑椅时惯穿的衣裳都没穿。他稍稍打点过自己，帽子里搁着一副新手套。说不定情势会要他至少陪约瑟芬走一截回卡姆登镇的路。
两点半，那位女士通报进来了——德·蒙莫朗西小姐；我们这位编辑心跳着起身迎接：正是那个身形，正是那身好看的出门装，正是那柄小小的蓝阳伞——他在国王查理街门阶上见过的一切。他认得出这身形、认得出这步态，虽然蒙着面纱的脸还看不见。这于他是一喜；因为虽说不容自己多疑，他到底疑过一丝：那窈窕的天仙，会不会就是他的约瑟芬。如今她到了，亲临他自己的城堡，简直是任他发落——他可以拭她的泪、叫她存指望，也可以告诉她毫无指望、由她哭下去，全凭他的高兴。这不是那类要讨论断炊同赤贫的案子。马房的账同迪耶普之行，是这出悲剧——倘若必须算悲剧——里耸人听闻的关目。布朗先生生平经手过的案子，有拿饿着的母亲、垂死的父亲作呼吁的引线的。往坏里说，也不过一场玫瑰水的劫难；说不定来的是得意、感激同微笑。他从椅子里起身，风雅地把手伸给来客，引她入座。
「德·蒙莫朗西小姐，在这里见到您，我很高兴。」他说。

Relationships are complex things, and, as we all know, give rise to most intricate questions. There should be more of stature than Mrs. Puffle possessed, with dark hair, and piercing eyes. The colour of the dress should be black, with perhaps yellow trimmings; and the hand should not be of pearly whiteness﻿—as Mrs. Puffle’s no doubt was, though the well-fitting little glove gave no absolute information on this subject. For such an adventure the appropriate colour of the skin would be﻿—we will not say sallow exactly﻿—but running a little that way. 亲戚关系是复杂的东西，我们都知道，生出的问题最是缠夹。容他思索的半霎里，布朗先生想：帕弗尔太太尽可以是德·蒙莫朗西小姐的嫂子；或者，至少半嫂。甚至也说不定，帕弗尔太太虽看着年轻，先前嫁过一位德·蒙莫朗西家的人。这些细节他如今都不去细解，只想从一桩事实上讨点安慰：帕弗尔无疑就是查尔斯。约瑟芬手下也许并没有查尔斯。随后他又明白过来：眼前这个浅色头发、笑吟吟、带酒窝的小东西，多半写不出那部满纸玄学的《他不像传说的那么黑》。约瑟芬必是更硬的材料做的。再说，论艳遇，小酒窝同蓝阳伞终究不称。身量该比帕弗尔太太的高些，黑头发，眼睛逼人。裙子的颜色该是黑的，兴许镶黄边；手也不该是珍珠般白——帕弗尔太太的必定是，虽说那只熨贴的小手套不供给确实的消息。这样一场艳遇，肤色的正色该是——不必说蜡黄——可总要往那边偏一偏。美要恰好让忧愁调一调；血来去之际，不该显成红晕，该显成浅黑肤色那种温润变换的线条。这一切布朗先生全懂。
「哦——原来您是帕弗尔太太，」布朗顿了顿——也许顿得不够——说。「您是查尔斯·帕弗尔的太太？」

「他烟还抽得那样凶吗，帕弗尔太太？」

「他自然抽烟。男人们都抽。这么说，他没结婚前总在抽了。我看男人们从来不把事情的真话告诉人；姑娘们可是什么都说的。」
「现在说说您妹妹的小说？」布朗先生问——他觉得自己把小妇人关于她丈夫的玄虚吊够了。
「是，正是。她急着要用钱！那书写得多聪明；——是不是？我没读过比它更聪明的。奥兰多在众贵族跟前自辩那一节，不是叫人喘不上气来吗？」这指的是一段写得极飘的文字——布朗先前盘算把故事登进《奥林波斯》时，已定下要删的。「她会伤心死的！您没有为她那样写信生她的气吧？」
「一点没有。我喜欢她的信。她写的是她心里真想的。」
「您真好！我对她说过，我拿得准您是好性子，因为您回信回得客气。您知道，那是她的一种试验。」
「哦——一种试验！」
「人好难接近。是不是？她要是光写一句『敬启者，兹奉上稿件一件』——您才不会看呢：——会吗？」
「我们什么都读，帕弗尔太太。」
「可轮到这些事的次序来得这样慢；是不是？所以波莉就想——」
「波莉——波莉怎么想？」
「我是说约瑟芬。我们叫她波莉，不过是小名。她那样巴望您马上就读！如今我们该怎么办？」布朗先生默坐了一会，想。她们为什么管约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西叫波莉？可稿子总归是事实，不管作者姓甚名谁。有一件事他拿定了：不见到写小说的那位女士本人，他一步也不挪。「您这就去帕特诺斯特街见那几位先生；好不好？」帕弗尔太太问，那副娇小恳求的神情，叫人顶难拒绝。
「我想必须先见见女作家本人。」布朗先生说。
「我不行吗？」帕弗尔太太问。「约瑟芬顶讲究。我是说，她顶顶不愿意谈她自己的写作、她自己的作品。」

===Original===

Brown thought of the tenor of the letters which he had received, and found that he could not reconcile with it this character which was given to him of Miss de Montmorenci. “She has an idea,” continued Mrs. Puffle, “that genius should not show itself publicly. Of course, she does not say that herself. And she does not think herself to be a genius;﻿—though I think it. And she is a genius. There are things in ‘Not so Black as he’s Painted’ which nobody but Polly could have written.”
Nevertheless Mr. Brown was firm. He explained that he could not possibly treat with Messrs. X., Y., and Z.﻿—if any treating should become possible﻿—without direct authority from the principal. He must have from Miss de Montmorenci’s mouth what might be the arrangements to which she would accede. If this could not be done he must wash his hands of the affair. He did not doubt, he said, but that Miss de Montmorenci might do quite as well with the publishers by herself, as she could with any aid from him. Perhaps it would be better that she should see Mr. X. herself. But if he, Brown, was to be honoured by any delegated authority, he must see the author. In saying this he implied that he had not the slightest desire to interfere further, and that he had no wish to press himself on the lady. Mrs. Puffle, with just a tear, and then a smile, and then a little coaxing twist of her lips, assured him that their only hope was in him. She would carry his message to Josephine, and he should have a further letter from that lady. “And you won’t tell Charles that I have been here,” said Mrs. Puffle as she took her leave.
“Certainly not. I won’t say a word of it.”
“It is so odd that you should have known him.”
“Don’t let him smoke too much, Mrs. Puffle.”
“I don’t intend. I’ve brought him down to one cigar and a pipe a day﻿—unless he smokes at the office.”
“They all do that;﻿—nearly the whole day.”
“What; at the Post Office!”
“That’s why I mention it. I don’t think they’re allowed at any of the other offices, but they do what they please there. I shall keep the MS. till I hear from Josephine herself.” Then Mrs. Puffle took her leave with many thanks, and a grateful pressure from her pretty little hand.
Two days after this there came the promised letter from Josephine.

===Chinese===

布朗先生想起他收到的那些信的口吻，发觉这副加给德·蒙莫朗西小姐的画像同它对不上。「她有个想法，」帕弗尔太太接着说，「以为天才不该抛头露面。当然，这话她自己不说。她也不把自己当作天才；——我可是这样想。她就是天才。《他不像传说的那么黑》里有些东西，除波莉没有人写得出来。」
布朗先生却不动摇。他解释：若还有商谈的可能，没有当事者直接的授权，他无论如何不能同 X、Y、Z 去商谈。德·蒙莫朗西小姐口头上能答应哪些安排，他必须亲耳听到。做不到这一层，他就只好洗手不管。他说他不疑心：德·蒙莫朗西小姐自己去同出版商办，会同靠他帮忙办得一样好；也许她亲自去见 X 先生更好。可他布朗若蒙授予什么代理之权，他就必须见作者。这番话里他暗示：他丝毫不想多管，也无意强求那位女士。帕弗尔太太掉了一滴泪，随即一笑，唇边又来了一点哄人的扭动，向他担保：他们唯一的指望全在他。她愿把话带给约瑟芬；那位女士还会再来信的。「您不会告诉查尔斯我来过吧。」帕弗尔太太告辞时说。
「当然不。我一个字也不说。」
「您竟认得他，多巧啊。」
「别让他烟抽太凶，帕弗尔太太。」
「我不会。我已经把他降到一天一支雪茄一斗烟了——除非他在办公处抽。」
「他们都抽；——差不多一整天。」
「什么；在邮政总局！」
「所以我才提。别的部我想都不许；他们那儿可是随意。稿子我先留着，等约瑟芬本人的信。」随后帕弗尔太太千恩万谢地告辞，那只俊俏小手感激地一握。
两天后，约瑟芬如约来了信。

===Original===

> Dear Mr. Brown,
> I cannot understand why you should not go to X., Y., and Z. without seeing me. I hardly ever see anybody; but, of course, you must come if you will. I got my sister to go because she is so gentle and nice, that I thought she could persuade anybody to do anything. She says that you know Mr. Puffle quite well, which seems to be so very odd. He doesn’t know that I ever write a word, and I didn’t think he had an acquaintance in the world whom I don’t know the name of. You’re quite wrong about one thing. They never smoke at the Post Office, and they wouldn’t be let to do it. If you choose to come, you must. I shall be at home any time on Friday morning﻿—that is, after half-past nine, when Charles goes away.
> Yours truly,
> J. de M.
> We began to talk about editors after dinner, just for fun; and Charles said that he didn’t know that he had ever seen one. Of course we didn’t say anything about the *Olympus*; but I don’t know why he should be so mysterious.

Then there was a second postscript, written down in a corner of the sheet of paper.

> I know you’ll be sorry you came.

===Chinese===

> 亲爱的布朗先生：
> 我不懂您为什么不见我就不能去 X、Y、Z 那里。我几乎谁也不见；可您一定要来，自然得来。我打发妹妹去，因为她那样温柔和气，我想她说什么人都会依。她说您同帕弗尔先生很熟，这瞧着真怪。他不知道我写过半个字；我原想世上他有个把我不知名姓的熟人也没有呢。有一件事您全错了。邮政总局里从不许抽烟，也不容他们抽。您愿意来就来吧。周五上午我随时在家——就是说，九点半以后，查尔斯走了以后。
> 您忠实的，
> 约·德·蒙
> 我们饭桌上当笑话说起编辑来；查尔斯说，他不记得见过编辑。我们自然没提《奥林波斯》；可我不懂他干吗那样神秘。

随后还有第二条附言，写在信纸的角落里。

> 我知道您来了要后悔的。

===Original===

Our editor was now quite determined that he would see the adventure to an end. He had at first thought that Josephine was keeping herself in the background merely that she might enhance the favour of a personal meeting when that favour should be accorded. A pretty woman believing herself to be a genius, and thinking that good things should ever be made scarce, might not improbably fall into such a foible. But now he was convinced that she would prefer to keep herself unseen if her doing so might be made compatible with her great object. Mr. Brown was not a man to intrude himself unnecessarily upon any woman unwilling to receive him; but in this case it was, so he thought, his duty to persevere. So he wrote a pretty little note to Miss Josephine saying that he would be with her at eleven o’clock on the day named.
Precisely at eleven o’clock he knocked at the door of the house in King-Charles Street, which was almost instantaneously opened for him by the fair hands of Mrs. Puffle herself. “H﻿—sh,” said Mrs. Puffle; “we don’t want the servants to know anything about it.” Mr. Brown, who cared nothing for the servants of the Puffle establishment, and who was becoming perhaps a little weary of the unravelled mystery of the affair, simply bowed and followed the lady into the parlour. “My sister is upstairs,” said Mrs. Puffle, “and we will go to her immediately.” Then she paused, as though she were still struggling with some difficulty;﻿—“I am so sorry to say that Polly is not well.﻿—But she means to see you,” Mrs. Puffle added, as she saw that the editor, over whom they had so far prevailed, made some sign as though he was about to retreat. “She never is very well,” said Mrs. Puffle, “and her work does tell upon her so much. Do you know, Mr. Brown, I think the mind sometimes eats up the body; that is, when it is called upon for such great efforts.” They were now upon the stairs, and Mr. Brown followed the little lady into her drawing-room.
There, almost hidden in the depths of a low armchair, sat a little wizened woman, not old indeed﻿—when Mr. Brown came to know her better, he found that she had as yet only counted five-and-twenty summers﻿—but with that look of mingled youth and age which is so painful to the beholder. Who has not seen it﻿—the face in which the eye and the brow are young and bright, but the mouth and the chin are old and haggard?

===Chinese===

我们这位编辑如今拿定了主意：这桩艳遇要看到底。他起初想，约瑟芬按兵不动，无非为着等真见面时、把见面的恩抬高几分。一个自信是天才的漂亮女人，又认定好东西永远该显得稀罕，染上这样的小毛病原不足奇。可如今他信了：只要同她的宏图两不相碍，她宁可一直不露面。布朗先生不是那种对不愿接待他的女人无端纠缠的人；可在这一案上——他这样想——坚持下去是他的本分。于是他给约瑟芬小姐写了封漂亮小简，说定于那个日子的十一点登门。
十一点整，他叩响国王查理街那所房子的门；开门的几乎是顷刻间，正是帕弗尔太太自己那双白手。「嘘，」帕弗尔太太说；「我们不愿叫仆人们知道。」布朗先生对帕弗尔家的仆人毫不在意，对这桩已被拆穿的神秘兴许也有些腻了，只欠了欠身，随太太进了客厅。「我妹妹在楼上，」帕弗尔太太说；「我们这就上去见她。」随后她顿住，仿佛还在同什么难处挣扎——「我很抱歉地说，波莉不大舒服。——可她是要见您的。」帕弗尔太太见这位已被她们降住的编辑露出一点要退的迹象，赶紧添道。「她一向就不大好，」帕弗尔太太说，「她的工作又那样磨她。您知道吗，布朗先生，我有时想，脑子会把身子吃掉；就是说，逼它出这样大力气的时候。」这时他们已在楼梯上；布朗先生随小太太进了她的起居室。
那里，几乎埋在一张矮圈椅的深处，坐着一个小干瘪的女人——并不老；后来布朗先生同她熟了，才知道她统共才过了二十五个夏天——却带着那副老少混杂的形容，看的人心里最难受。谁没见过——那样的脸：眼睛同额头还年轻明亮，嘴同下巴却已衰老枯槁？

===Original===

See such a one when she sleeps﻿—when the brightness of the eye is hidden, and all the countenance is full of pain and decay, and then the difference will be known to you between youth with that health which is generally given to it, and youth accompanied by premature decrepitude. “This is my sister-in-law,” said Mrs. Puffle, introducing the two correspondents to each other. The editor looked at the little woman who made some half attempt to rise, and thought that he could see in the brightness of the eye some symptoms of the sauciness which had appeared so very plainly in her letters. And there was a smile too about the mouth, though the lips were thin and the chin poor, which seemed to indicate that the owner of them did in some sort enjoy this unravelling of her riddle﻿—as though she were saying to herself, “What do you think now of the beautiful young woman who has made you write so many letters, and read so long a manuscript, and come all the way at this hour of the morning to Camden Town?” Mr. Brown shook hands with her, and muttered something to the effect that he was sorry not to see her in better health.
“No,” said Josephine de Montmorenci, “I am not very well. I never am. I told you that you had better put up with seeing my sister.”
We say no more than the truth of Mr. Brown in declaring that he was now more ready than ever to do whatever might be in his power to forward the views of this young authoress. If he was interested before when he believed her to be beautiful, he was doubly interested for her now when he knew her to be a cripple;﻿—for he had seen when she made that faint attempt to rise that her spine was twisted, and that, when she stood up, her head sank between her shoulders. “I am very glad to make your acquaintance,” he said, seating himself near her. “I should never have been satisfied without doing so.”
“It is so very good of you to come,” said Mrs. Puffle.
“Of course it is good of him,” said Josephine; “especially after the way we wrote to him. The truth is, Mr. Brown, we were at our wits’ end to catch you.”
This was an aspect of the affair which our editor certainly did not like. An attempt to deceive anybody else might have been pardonable; but deceit practised against himself was odious to him. Nevertheless, he did forgive it. The poor little creature before him had worked hard, and had done her best.

===Chinese===

看这样的人睡着——眼里那点明亮掩了，满脸是痛苦同衰败——你就会明白：寻常康健的青春，同未老先衰的青春，分别在哪里。「这位是我嫂子。」帕弗尔太太说，把两位通信人相互引见。编辑望着那作了半起不起的姿态的小妇人，心想他在那双眼睛的明亮里，看得出几分她信里表露得那样明白的娇纵。嘴边也有一丝笑——虽然嘴唇薄、下巴瘦——仿佛这一切的主人对拆穿自己的哑谜也自有几分受用——仿佛她正对自己说：「如今你怎样看那个漂亮的年轻女人？她叫你写了那么多信、读了那么长一部稿、清早这个时辰大老远赶到卡姆登镇来。」布朗先生同她握了手，含糊说了句抱恙相见的惋惜。
「是，」约瑟芬·德·蒙莫朗西说，「我不大好。从来不曾好过。我说过，您还是将就见我妹妹的好。」
我们替布朗先生说句实话：此刻他比先前更愿意出力成全这位年轻女作家的心愿了。先前当他信她美丽时，他关心；如今他知她残废，他加倍关心——因为她那半起的尝试里，他看见她的脊柱是扭曲的，站起身时，头便陷进两肩之间。「我很高兴结识您。」他说，在她近旁坐下。「不这样见一面，我总不能甘心。」
「您肯来，真好。」帕弗尔太太说。
「自然是他好，」约瑟芬说；「尤其是我们那样给他写信之后。实话对您说，布朗先生，我们为钓您上钩，已经没了法子。」
这可是我们这位编辑断断不喜的这桩事的一面。骗别人还情有可原；对他使的骗术，他深恶。可他到底饶了。眼前这可怜的小人儿苦干过，尽了她的力。

===Original===

To teach her to be less metaphysical in her writings, and more straightforward in her own practices, should be his care. There is something to a man inexpressibly sweet in the power of protecting the weak; and no one had ever seemed to be weaker than Josephine. “Miss de Montmorenci,” he said, “we will let bygones be bygones, and will say nothing about the letters. It is no doubt the fact that you did write the novel yourself?”
“Every word of it,” said Mrs. Puffle energetically.
“Oh, yes; I wrote it,” said Josephine.
“And you wish to have it published?”
“Indeed I do.”
“And you wish to get money for it?”
“That is the truest of all,” said Josephine.
“Oughtn’t one to be paid when one has worked so very hard?” said Mrs. Puffle.
“Certainly one ought to be paid if it can be proved that one’s work is worth buying,” replied the sage mentor of literature.
“But isn’t it worth buying?” demanded Mrs. Puffle.
“I must say that I think that publishers do buy some that are worse,” observed Josephine.
Mr. Brown with words of wisdom explained to them as well as he was able the real facts of the case. It might be that that manuscript, over which the poor invalid had laboured for so many painful hours, would prove to be an invaluable treasure of art, destined to give delight to thousands of readers, and to be, when printed, a source of large profits to publishers, booksellers, and author. Or, again, it might be that, with all its undoubted merits﻿—and that there were such merits Mr. Brown was eager in acknowledging﻿—the novel would fail to make any way with the public. “A publisher,”﻿—so said Mr. Brown﻿—“will hardly venture to pay you a sum of money down, when the risk of failure is so great.”
“But Polly has written ever so many things before,” said Mrs. Puffle.
“That counts for nothing,” said Miss de Montmorenci. “They were short pieces, and appeared without a name.”
“Were you paid for them?” asked Mr. Brown.
“I have never been paid a halfpenny for anything yet.”
“Isn’t that cruel,” said Mrs. Puffle, “to work, and work, and work, and never get the wages which ought to be paid for it?”
“Perhaps there may be a good time coming,” said our editor. “Let us see whether we can get Messrs. X., Y., and Z. to publish this at their own expense, and with your name attached to it. Then, Miss de Montmorenci﻿—”
“I suppose we had better tell him all,” said Josephine.

===Chinese===

教她写东西少些玄虚、做人多些直道，该是他的操心。护佑弱者，于男人有一种说不出地甜的力量；而从不曾有人比约瑟芬显得更弱。「德·蒙莫朗西小姐，」他说，「既往不咎，信的事一字不提。小说确乎是您亲笔写的？」
「一字一句都是。」帕弗尔太太抢着说。
「哦，是；我写的。」约瑟芬说。
「您想出版它？」
「真想。」
「您想为它得钱？」
「这是顶真的心愿。」约瑟芬说。
「人家苦干了这样久，难道不该得钱吗？」帕弗尔太太说。
「倘能证明这劳作值得买，自然该得。」文学的贤明师说。
「可它难道不值得买？」帕弗尔太太质问。
「我得说，出版商买过的坏东西也有的是。」约瑟芬说。
布朗先生以明智之言，尽力向她们讲解了事情的实际。也许，那部可怜病人熬过那么多苦时辰的稿子，当真是艺术的无价宝，注定给千万读者以欢愉，印出来还是出版商、书商同作者的大利薮。又也许，它虽有种种不容疑的长处——有这些长处，布朗先生热心承认——却打不开公众的路。「出版商，」——布朗先生这样说——「失败的风险这样大，很难肯付您一笔现钱。」
「可波莉从前写过许许多多东西。」帕弗尔太太说。
「那算不得什么，」德·蒙莫朗西小姐说。「都是短篇，登出来也没署名。」
「得过稿费吗？」布朗先生问。
「至今半个便士也没得过。」
「这多狠心，」帕弗尔太太说，「做了工、做了工、做了工，永远拿不到该给的工钱。」
「好日子也许在后头，」我们这位编辑说。「且看我们能不能叫 X、Y、Z 自担费用出版它，把您的名字署上。到那时，德·蒙莫朗西小姐——」
「我看咱们还是全告诉他吧。」约瑟芬说。

===Original===

“Oh, yes; tell everything. I am sure he won’t be angry; he is so good-natured,” said Mrs. Puffle.
Mr. Brown looked first at one, and then at the other, feeling himself to be rather uncomfortable. What was there that remained to be told? He was good-natured, but he did not like being told of that virtue. “The name you have heard is not my name,” said the lady who had written the novel.
“Oh, indeed! I have heard Mrs. Puffle call you﻿—Polly.”
“My name is﻿—Maryanne.”
“It is a very good name,” said Mr. Brown﻿—“so good that I cannot quite understand why you should go out of your way to assume another.”
“It is Maryanne﻿—Puffle.”
“Oh;﻿—Puffle!” said Mr. Brown.
“And a very good name, too,” said Mrs. Puffle.
“I haven’t a word to say against it,” said Mr. Brown. “I wish I could say quite as much as to that other name﻿—Josephine de Montmorenci.”
“But Maryanne Puffle would be quite unendurable on a title page,” said the owner of the unfortunate appellation.
“I don’t see it,” said Mr. Brown doggedly.
“Ever so many have done the same,” said Mrs. Puffle. “There’s Boz.”
“Calling yourself Boz isn’t like calling yourself Josephine de Montmorenci,” said the editor, who could forgive the loss of beauty, but not the assumed grandeur of the name.
“And Currer Bell, and Jacob Omnium, and Barry Cornwall,” said poor Polly Puffle, pleading hard for her falsehood.
“And Michelangelo Titmarsh! That was quite the same sort of thing,” said Mrs. Puffle.
Our editor tried to explain to them that the sin of which he now complained did not consist in the intention﻿—foolish as that had been﻿—of putting such a name as Josephine de Montmorenci on the title page, but in having corresponded with him﻿—with him who had been so willing to be a friend﻿—under a false name. “I really think you ought to have told me sooner,” he said.

===Original===

I Hope
We hardly feel certain that we are justified in giving the following little story to the public as an Editor’s Tale, because at the time to which it refers, and during the circumstances with which it deals, no editorial power was, in fact, within our grasp. As the reader will perceive, the ambition and the hopes, and something of a promise of the privileges, were there; but the absolute chair was not mounted for us. The great **we** was not, in truth, ours to use. And, indeed, the interval between the thing we then so cordially desired, and the thing as it has since come to exist, was one of so many years, that there can be no right on our part to connect the two periods. We shall, therefore, tell our story, as might any ordinary individual, in the first person singular, and speak of such sparks of editorship as did fly up around us as having created but a dim coruscation, and as having been quite insufficient to justify the delicious plural.
---
It is now just thirty years ago since we determined to establish the *Panjandrum Magazine*. The “we” here spoken of is not an editorial we, but a small set of human beings who shall be personally introduced to the reader. The name was intended to be delightfully meaningless, but we all thought that it was euphonious, graphic, also﻿—and sententious, even though it conveyed no definite idea. That question of a name had occupied us a good deal, and had almost split us into parties. I﻿—for I will now speak of myself as I﻿—I had wished to call it by the name of a very respectable young publisher who was then commencing business, and by whom we intended that the trade part of our enterprise should be undertaken. *Colburn’s* was an old affair in those days, and I doubt whether *Bentley’s* was not already in existence. *Blackwood’s* and *Fraser’s* were at the top of the tree, and, as I think, the *Metropolitan* was the only magazine then in much vogue not called by the name of this or that enterprising publisher. But some of our colleagues would not hear of this, and were ambitious of a title that should describe our future energies and excellences. I think we should have been called the *Pandrastic*, but that the one lady who joined our party absolutely declined the name. At one moment we had almost carried *Panurge*.

===Chinese===

一、希望
把下面这篇小故事当作「编辑的故事」公之于众，我们实在拿不准是否问心有理：因为它所讲述的那个年代、它所处置的那些境况里，编辑的权柄其实并不在我们手中。读者会看到，野心与希望是有的，特权也隐隐许了愿；可那把交椅终究没替我们摆上。那个堂皇的「我们」，说实在的，尚不归我们使用。再说，当年我们满心热望的那个东西，同它后来实际长成的那个东西，中间隔了那样多的年头，我们实在无权把两段时光焊接在一起。因此，我们将像随便哪个普通人那样，用第一人称单数来讲这个故事；至于当年在我们周身迸起的那几点编辑事业的火星，我们只说它们闪过一片幽微的光，全然配不上那个美妙的复数。
我们决定创办《潘詹德鲁姆杂志》（Panjandrum Magazine），至今恰好三十年。这里的「我们」不是编辑的我们，而是一小群人——他们都将一一同读者见面。这名字原就打算取得妙在无意义；可我们全都觉得它音韵悦耳、形象生动，而且——哪怕它不传达任何明确的观念——还颇为铿锵有格言味。起名的事占去了我们不少工夫，几乎把我们分裂成了党派。我——因为从现在起我要照「我」来说我自己——原想用它当时正起步营业的一位极可敬的年轻出版商的名字来命名；我们打算把我们这桩事业的生意一摊，就托付给他。《柯尔本》那时已是老字号；我疑心《本特利》那时也已经出世。《布莱克伍德》与《弗雷泽》正高踞树顶；而据我记忆，当时风行一时的杂志里，不冠某位进取出版商之名的，只有《大都会》一家。可同人中几位说什么也不肯，一心想要一个能描画我们未来的干劲与造诣的名号。我想我们本会叫《潘德拉斯蒂克》的，若非入伙的唯一那位女士断然拒用此名。有一阵子，《潘努治》几乎已经通过了。

===Original===

The *Man’s Magazine* was thought of, not as opposed to womanhood, but as intended to trump the *Gentleman’s*. But a hint was given to us that we might seem to imply that our periodical was not adapted for the perusal of females. We meant the word “man” in the great generic sense;﻿—but the somewhat obtuse outside world would not have so taken it. The *H.B.P.* was for a time in the ascendant, and was favoured by the lady, who drew for us a most delightful little circle containing the letters illustrated;﻿—what would now be called a monogram, only that the letters were legible. The fact that nobody would comprehend that H.B.P. intended to express the general opinion of the shareholders that “Honesty is the Best Policy,” was felt to be a recommendation rather than otherwise. I think it was the enterprising young publisher who objected to the initials﻿—not, I am sure, from any aversion to the spirit of the legend. Many other names were tried, and I shall never forget the look which went round our circle when one young and gallant, but too indiscreet reformer, suggested that were it not for offence, whence offence should not come, the *Purge* was the very name for us;﻿—from all which it will be understood that it was our purpose to put right many things that were wrong. The matter held us in discussion for some months, and then we agreed to call the great future lever of the age﻿—the *Panjandrum*.
When a new magazine is about to be established in these days, the first question raised will probably be one of capital. A very considerable sum of money, running far into four figures﻿—if not going beyond it﻿—has to be mentioned, and made familiar to the ambitious promoters of the enterprise. It was not so with us. Nor was it the case that our young friend the publisher agreed to find the money, leaving it to us to find the wit. I think we selected our young friend chiefly because, at that time, he had no great business to speak of, and could devote his time to the interests of the *Panjandrum*. As for ourselves we were all poor; and in the way of capital a set of human beings more absurdly inefficient for any purposes of trade could not have been brought together.

===Chinese===

《男人杂志》也议过——并非与女性为敌，而是要压倒《绅士杂志》。可有人点拨我们：这名字仿佛在暗示本刊不宜女性阅读。「男人」二字，我们取的是堂堂的类名大义；——无奈外面那略显迟钝的世界，未必肯这样领会。《H.B.P.》一度占了上风，深得那位女士青睐；她替我们画了一个可爱的小圆圈，把三个字母圈缀其间——如今该管这叫花押，只是那几个字母还认得出。谁也看不出 H.B.P. 是要表达全体股东「诚实为上策」的共同意见——这一点非但不碍事，反倒被看作一个优点。我记得反对这组首字母的是那位进取的年轻出版商——我敢说，绝非厌恶那句格言的精神。旁的名字还试了许多；有位年轻气盛、却太不知轻重的改革派提议说，倘不致开罪于人——而得罪的也尽是不该得罪的——《泻药》正是为我们量身定做的名号——他说这话时环视一圈的那副神色，我永生难忘；——由这一切读者自会明白：我们的抱负，原是要匡正天下许多不正之事。这事议了好几个月，末了我们一致同意：这个未来撬动时代的大杠杆——就叫《潘詹德鲁姆》。
如今要创办一份新杂志，头一个问题多半是资本。得报出一个不小的数目——远不止四位数——还要让雄心勃勃的发起人们把它念熟。我们可不是这样。也并非我们那位出版商朋友肯出钱、单把才思留给我们去筹。我想我们选中那位年轻朋友，主要是因为他当时谈不上有什么大买卖，能把时间全献给《潘詹德鲁姆》的利益。至于我们自己，个个清贫；论资本，再找出一伙做生意比我们更荒唐地无能的人，怕是难了。

===Original===

We found that for a sum of money which we hoped that we might scrape together among us, we could procure paper and print for a couple of thousand copies of our first number;﻿—and, after that, we were to obtain credit for the second number by the reputation of the first. Literary advertising, such as is now common to us, was then unknown. The cost of sticking up “The Panjandrum” at railway stations and on the tops of the omnibuses, certainly would not be incurred. Of railway stations there were but few in the country, and even omnibuses were in their infancy. A few modest announcements in the weekly periodicals of the day were thought to be sufficient; and, indeed, there pervaded us all an assurance that the coming of the *Panjandrum* would be known to all men, even before it had come. I doubt whether our desire was not concealment rather than publicity. We measured the importance of the *Panjandrum* by its significance to ourselves, and by the amount of heart which we intended to throw into it. Ladies and gentlemen who get up magazines in the present day are wiser. It is not heart that is wanted, but very big letters on very big boards, and plenty of them.
We were all heart. It must be admitted now that we did not bestow upon the matter of literary excellence quite so much attention as that branch of the subject deserves. We were to write and edit our magazine and have it published, not because we were good at writing or editing, but because we had ideas which we wished to promulgate. Or it might be the case with some of us that we only thought that we had ideas. But there was certainly present to us all a great wish to do some good. That, and a not altogether unwholesome appetite for a reputation which should not be personal, were our great motives. I do not think that we dreamed of making fortunes; though no doubt there might be present to the mind of each of us an idea that an opening to the profession of literature might be obtained through the pages of the *Panjandrum*. In that matter of reputation we were quite agreed that fame was to be sought, not for ourselves, nor for this or that name, but for the *Panjandrum*. No man or woman was to declare himself to be the author of this or that article;﻿—nor indeed was any man or woman to declare himself to be connected with a magazine.

我们盘算出：一笔指望从彼此身上刮拢的钱，够买纸、够印第一期两千册；——至于第二期，我们打算凭第一期的名声去赊。如今司空见惯的文学广告，那时还没听说过。把「潘詹德鲁姆」贴上火车站、贴上公共马车顶的花销，自然无从谈起。全国的火车站寥寥无几，连公共马车自己也还在襁褓里。当时以为，在几种周刊上登几则像样的启事也就够了；说真的，我们全体还浸在一股笃信里：《潘詹德鲁姆》尚未驾临，其降临必已妇孺皆知。我甚至疑心，我们想要的与其说是扬名，不如说是藏拙。我们度量《潘詹德鲁姆》的分量，用的是它于我们自身的意义，和我们打算倾注进去的心血。如今办杂志的先生女士们聪明多了。要的不是心血，而是大牌子上的大字——还要多多的牌子。
我们有的是心血。如今必须承认：对文学造诣这一摊，我们下的功夫，远不到它应得的份。我们要写、要编我们的杂志、要把它印出来，并非因为我们善于写、善于编，而是因为我们有想要播扬的思想。也许我们中间有些人，只是以为自己有思想。但想做点好事的大愿，我们人人心里确实都有。这一点，加上一份不算全然不健康的好名之心——要的不是个人的名声——便是我们的大动机。我不认为我们做过发财梦；虽然无疑人人心里都存着一点念头：经由《潘詹德鲁姆》的书页，或许能叩开文学之门。说到名声，我们完全一致：求名不求己身，也不求张三李四之名，只求《潘詹德鲁姆》之名。谁也不得自称是这一篇那一篇的作者；——说真的，谁也不得自称同一份杂志有牵连。

===Original===

The only name to be known to a curious public was that of the young publisher. All intercourse between the writers and the printers was to be through him. If contributions should come from the outside world﻿—as come they would﻿—they were to be addressed to the Editor of the *Panjandrum*, at the publisher’s establishment. It was within the scope of our plan to use any such contribution that might please us altogether; but the contents of the magazine were, as a rule, to come from ourselves. A magazine then, as now, was expected to extend itself through something over a hundred and twenty pages; but we had no fear as to our capacity for producing the required amount. We feared rather that we might jostle each other in our requirements for space.
We were six, and, young as I was then, I was to be the editor. But to the functions of the editor was to be attached very little editorial responsibility. What should and what should not appear in each monthly number was to be settled in conclave. Upon one point, however, we were fully agreed﻿—that no personal jealousy should ever arise among us so as to cause quarrel or even embarrassment. As I had already written some few slight papers for the press, it was considered probable that I might be able to correct proofs, and do the fitting and dovetailing. My editing was not to go beyond that. If by reason of parity of numbers in voting there should arise a difficulty, the lady was to have a double vote. Anything more noble, more chivalrous, more trusting, or, I may add, more philanthropic than our scheme never was invented; and for the persons, I will say that they were noble, chivalrous, trusting, and philanthropic;﻿—only they were so young!
Place aux dames. We will speak of the lady first﻿—more especially as our meetings were held at her house. I fear that I may, at the very outset of our enterprise, turn the hearts of my readers against her by saying that Mrs. St. Quinten was separated from her husband. I must, however, beg them to believe that this separation had been occasioned by no moral fault or odious misconduct on her part. I will confess that I did at that time believe that Mr. St. Quinten was an ogre, and that I have since learned to think that he simply laboured under a strong and, perhaps, monomaniacal objection to literary pursuits.
